response:
Yes—Reforms should prioritise purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management, alongside stronger licensing and quality standards. In my area, I’ve watched new Build-to-Rent blocks bring better maintenance, on-site managers, and clearer routes to repairs, which makes renting feel more secure and predictable. When a portion of units is covenant-controlled and allocated for genuinely affordable rents, these schemes can expand supply without sacrificing quality or long-term tenants.

Coupled with this, stronger selective licensing, robust inspections, and minimum energy and safety standards create healthier homes and a fair playing field for tenants and responsible landlords. Encouraging longer tenancies through contracts and tenancy deposit protections helps communities stay stable and reduces churn, which benefits local services and schools.

I know small landlords who want to do the right thing, and policy must guard against unintended burdens. Simplified compliance, phased introduction, and targeted support to upgrade a property to meet standards would help them participate rather than be pushed out.

Overall, the mix of well-managed Build-to-Rent, affordable covenants, and a clear, fair regulatory framework offers the best path to more affordable, good-quality homes.

Agree that reforms should increase supply of affordable, good-quality homes. We support purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure developments with affordability covenants and professional management because they offer stable, well-maintained homes for young renters. In my city, too many friends face short-term lets and sudden rent hikes; a BTR model with long leases, clear maintenance standards, and a housing management team would reduce insecurity and improve safety. Affordability covenants—rents tied to local incomes and capped for a defined period (e.g., 15-20 years)—would keep rents within reach for graduates and early-career workers while still attracting private investment. Mixed-tenure schemes that include affordable units help build inclusive communities rather than mono-tenure mini-blocks.

We also need funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside housing, not after the bricks go up. Coordinated delivery avoids crowded hospitals, underused schools, and long commutes. In practice, that means incorporating transport upgrades and new GP surgeries and primary schools into planning approvals and phasing, so new residents are service-ready from day one. This approach would help my peers rent more sustainably while contributing to vibrant, long-term neighbourhoods.

As an organisation working across rural and urban parts of England, we strongly support reforms to boost affordable, good-quality homes by ensuring every new development includes wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes, together with dedicate oldrr-person and supported-housing provision and student key-workerr accommodation. Our experience shows demand is highest for homes that are fully adaptable (M4(3)) and near good transport, schools, and NHS facilities, especially in rural communities where appointments require travel.. Reforms should include: 1) mandatory accessibility and adaptability standards for all new affordable homes, 2) funding and incentives for wheelchair-accessible social housing and for conversions of unsuitable properties, 3) planning reforms to enable small-scale, community-led and build-to-rent schemes in rural villages, 4) streamlined approvals and efficient procurement to reduce costs and deliver on time, 5) partnerships with local health and care providers to deliver supported housing in thr right locations, 6) retention of affordability via shared ownership and rent-setting controls. This approach would reduce isolation, support key workers, and deliver durable, cost-effective housing that matches local demographics and cultures.

I disagree with pushing more greenfield release or relaxing the Green Belt to boost housing supply. In our area, the most effective reforms would prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before any release of countryside land. We already have derelict mills, empty high‑street shops and unused offices that could be converted into affordable flats or supported accommodation, cutting the need to sprawl and protecting valued landscapes.

Key reforms I’d like to see: a brownfield‑first approach with a clear, time‑bound pipeline for converting vacant stock and faster planning determinations for such schemes; stronger powers or incentives to bring long‑term empty homes back into use; targeted grants or low‑interest loans for conversion of offices and shops into genuinely affordable homes; and guarantees that affordable units are built in regeneration schemes (not merely a token percentage).

All new homes should be built to high accessibility standards as a default (wheelchair‑accessible and adaptable where needed), with explicit provision for older people, supported housing, and student key‑workers where there is demonstrable local demand. Also, ensure rural and cultural needs are addressed with appropriate design and community facilities. Maintain Green Belt protections unless a robust case shows clear public benefit with high environmental gains.

Reforms should insist on funded, phased delivery of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside housing, ideally prior to or concurrent with development, to ensure service-ready communities; otherwise risk stranding new homes with poor access to essential services.

i strongly believe housing pressure in Wales is acute, and many families in our communities are paying too much or living in unsuitable conditions. To genuinely increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes, I think we need a multi-pronged package that puts community ownership, modern construction methods, and smarter planning at its heart, with careful piloting of rent stabilization so we can learn what actually works without stalling supply. 

Key reforms we would support, with recognition of local nuance:

- Accelerate and fund community-led housing (CLTs, housing co-operatives, self-build, and collaborative ownership). Public land and land held by charitable bodies should be offered to community groups on long leases or shared equity arrangements, with a simple, predictable process. A Welsh fund dedicated to community-led housing—combining grants, low-interest loans, and in-kind land support—could unlock schemes more quickly and keep homes permanently affordable. These models deliver long-term stewardship and price protection that market-led routes often miss, and they tend to mobilise local volunteer energy and local supply chains. We need clear milestones and reporting so communities know what to expect and funders can see impact.

- Embrace modern methods of construction (MMC) and self-build to increase quality and speed. Modular and off-site construction can deliver warmer, better-insulated homes with lower construction risk, while empowering local SMEs and craft trades. Welsh policy should enable early engagement between planning teams and MMC developers, create procurement frameworks favoring local firms, and provide training pipelines for carpenters, fabricators, and installers. When homes are built on site with good design input from residents, quality tends to improve and maintenance costs go down over time.

- Planning and development reforms that actually unlock supply. We need simpler, faster routes for small sites and community-led schemes, without weakening standards. A regional planning framework should require a meaningful portion of new developments to be affordable (for example, a baseline in the 20–30% range, with flexibility for very small sites) and remove unnecessary red tape for community-led projects. Early pre-application engagement with planners, predictable viability tests, and a streamlined consent pathway for reformulated, high-energy-efficiency designs would help. In practice, this means more permission-in-principle routes for community-led proposals and better guidance on site assembly from local authorities.

- Use land value capture and public land reform to fund affordable homes. Where planning uplift occurs, communities should share in the benefits. Reforming how uplift is captured could unlock a capital stream for genuinely affordable homes, particularly on brownfield and derelict sites. Public bodies should prioritise long-term leases or sale to community-led groups where it delivers durable affordability and local control.

- Targeted rent stability pilots with robust evaluation. Rent caps or stabilization can improve affordability on a short-term basis, but we must understand the risk to supply, investment, and landlord participation. I would support pilots in high-rent areas with clear evaluation frameworks, sunset clauses, and guardrails for ensuring new-build and social housing remain viable. Safeguards could include transitional subsidies to landlords, exemptions for new affordable housing, and performance reviews showing whether supply, maintenance, and quality are maintained or improved.

- Quality, energy performance, and local job impact. Any reform should attach minimum standards for energy efficiency, accessibility, and durability. MMC projects should be required to meet ambitious energy targets (EPCs or Welsh-equivalent standards) and deliver training opportunities for local workers to build resilience in the construction sector.

- Delivery bodies working together, with transparent measurement. An agreed, cross-sector implementation plan—between Welsh Government, local authorities, housing associations, and community groups—would set shared goals, milestones, and independent evaluation. Data should be published so communities see progress and policymakers can adjust approaches quickly.

What I’d like to see next is a clear pilot plan from the Welsh Government that identifies where these reforms would start (including a couple of ambitious CLT projects on underused public land), sets up MMC supply chains in key regions, and tests rent stabilization alongside strong safeguards. If these reforms are designed with communities at the centre and backed by accountable funding, we can deliver more affordable, high-quality homes faster without compromising long-term supply or quality.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. As a representative of our local housing organisation in England, I welcome the government changes aimed at increasing the supply of affordable, good quality homes. In our area the most effective reforms will be those that prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long term empty homes before releasing any greenfield land or Green Belt. This approach protects our landscapes, makes best use of existing infrastructure, and can deliver genuinely affordable homes more quickly. Below are the reforms we believe would work best here.

- Mandate a brownfield first approach in planning policy
- Strengthen and ring-fence the pipeline of brownfield sites for housing, including land owned by the council, housing associations and the private sector
- Create a national brownfield and empty-property register to identify sites that can be brought back into use with minimal delay
- Require local authorities to set clear annual targets for bringing long term empty homes and redundant commercial buildings back into residential use

- Incentivise regeneration and the conversion of vacant stock
- Expand grants and low interest loans for refurbishment and conversion of vacant offices, shops and other non residential buildings into high quality homes
- Extend and simplify permitted development rights for suitable conversions, with robust design standards, energy efficiency, and access requirements
- Make contributions from developers more predictable by reforming Section 106 and Community Infrastructure Levy arrangements so that affordable housing is deliverable on brownfield sites without creating unviable schemes for small builders

- Ensure high quality and affordable homes through strong design and sustainability standards
- Require homes created from brownfield sites to meet a higher energy efficiency standard (target EPC B where feasible) and be built to flexible, accessible designs (Lifetime Homes standards) where appropriate
- Establish a local design code that reflects our town centre character and landscape setting, so new homes fit in and complement existing communities while achieving modern standards
- Guarantee adequate space for parking, play and green space where needed, to avoid creating problematic overcrowding or poor living conditions

- Streamline processes while protecting landscapes
- Create a fast track planning track for brownfield infill and conversions with clear decision timelines and pre application support, so time spent in planning is not a barrier to delivery
- Align planning and housing delivery with a dedicated regeneration delivery unit at the local level to oversee brownfield projects, with performance benchmarks and regular public reporting
- Implement robust checks to ensure that the release of Green Belt only happens after every brownfield and empty property option has been exhausted, and that any release would be accompanied by compensatory landscape protections and local flood risk management plans

- Improve performance and accountability
- Establish measurable targets for homes delivered on brownfield sites each year, with quarterly updates to communities
- Require annual reporting on the number of long term empty homes brought back into use, the proportion of affordable homes on mixed schemes, and the quality standards achieved on repairs and conversions
- Create a dedicated fund to support councils and housing associations in acquiring and remediating derelict or contaminated brownfield sites so that schemes are deliverable within realistic timelines

In our area we already have several viable brownfield opportunities, including a disused mill by the river and a long unused office block in the town centre. We have seen what can be done when a council works with housing associations to convert these spaces into affordable flats with good insulation, modern heating systems and accessible ground floor accommodation. Bringing these properties back into use reduces vacancy, strengthens town centres and supports local services, while avoiding the environmental footprint of new greenfield development.

We also support targeted pilots that test early delivery models, such as small, community led regeneration schemes and modular construction on brownfield plots. When the economics stack up, these can bring new homes to market quickly and with energy efficient standards that reduce running costs for families.

Overall, our priority is to protect landscapes and avoid unnecessary Green Belt release. The reforms outlined above align with that aim while delivering real gains for the local housing market by making the best use of existing stock and preventing further sprawl. We look forward to working with the government to implement these reforms with appropriate funding, clear delivery routes and robust quality controls.

Living in England and renting in a town where new developments feel like a weekly headline, I’m not convinced the reforms being floated around Section 106, the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and viability testing will genuinely fix the shortage of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area. In fact, I think they risk letting developers duck delivery of on‑site affordable homes while still getting planning permissions. What I’ve seen locally is that promised affordable units often get pushed back or traded for cash contributions that don’t translate into real homes within our community. The viability tests themselves feel opaque, and there’s not enough independent scrutiny or real consequences when planned commitments disappear into a funding pot that never gets spent where it’s meant to be spent.

That’s why I believe the reforms should do more than tweak a few numbers. They should hard‑wire transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on‑site affordable homes and real infrastructure funding, while at the same time empowering genuinely affordable, community‑led ways to build homes quickly. In particular, I’d like to see a shift towards a robust, enforceable framework for Section 106 and CIL, paired with strong support for community‑led housing models that can scale with local needs.

What I’d like to see in practice

- Make on‑site affordable housing the default, with clear thresholds that can’t be easily gamed by viability claims. For most sites up to a certain size, 30–40% on‑site affordable homes should be the starting point, with higher percentages on larger sites. There must be strict timelines for delivering those units, and any in‑lieu payments should be a last resort, not a normal fallback. If cash contributions are allowed, they must be ring‑fenced and spent in the local area within a fixed timeframe on genuinely affordable homes and related infrastructure.
- Increase transparency and accountability. Publish viability appraisals and Section 106 agreements in a clear, machine‑readable format so residents can see what’s being promised. Create an independent scrutiny body to audit delivery against commitments, with real penalties for non‑delivery and a clawback mechanism if units are never built or if they’re replaced with more expensive options.
- Ring‑fence CIL funds for local affordable housing and essential infrastructure. Local authorities should provide annual reports on how those funds are spent and what affordable housing outcomes they’ve achieved in practice, with a clear requirement that a share of receipts is allocated to the specific area where growth is planned.
- Tighten accessibility of viability testing. Use standard benchmarks and limit the scope for cost inflation to inflate profits. Ensure that the tests are applied consistently across schemes and that approval decisions aren’t held up by endless appeals that delay delivery of homes.

Beyond reforming the existing system, I think we need to back models that can actually scale quickly and deliver high‑quality homes people can afford to live in.

- Community land trusts (CLTs) and housing co‑operatives. These models keep long‑term control of the land and housing in local hands, setting rents and sale prices at genuinely affordable levels. Land acquisition can be facilitated by local authorities transferring land at lower costs or through long‑term leases, with funding support for initial development. In towns nearby, CLTs have delivered small clusters of homes that stay affordable for generations, but they need more land, easier planning routes, and longer‑term public backing to scale.
- Self‑build and modern methods of construction (MMC). Allowing groups to design and build homes that suit local needs can speed up delivery and reduce costs, but only if planning processes are streamlined for custom build plots and MMC is given practical support—like pre‑approved designs, access to reliable modular suppliers, and public land ready for development.
- Public land and proactive local government involvement. A small number of plots set aside specifically for self‑build, CLTs or co‑ops on brownfield sites can catalyse quick wins without chasing market‑driven, profit‑led schemes that fail to meet local housing goals.

In short, I’m not convinced that tinkering with Section 106, CIL and viability testing alone will fix the housing crisis for my generation. We need a robust, transparent, enforceable framework that guarantees on‑site affordable homes and targeted infrastructure funding, plus serious investment in community‑led housing and modern construction methods. If policy makers can combine strong delivery obligations with real support for CLTs, co‑ops, self‑build and MMC, we’ll see more affordable, high‑quality homes appear faster and in the places people actually want to live.

Thank you for reading and considering the lived experience of young people trying to put down roots in our communities.

I strongly agree that the reforms proposed will most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area. A funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing is essential to create sustainable, service-ready communities. Without this, new homes risk being isolated or over-burdening existing services. For example, a new development could unlock more housing if a ring-fenced infrastructure fund delivered upgrades to rail or bus access, GP capacity and a primary school in parallel with the homes, preventing delays and overcrowding.

I also support purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. These models provide long-term rental supply with secure tenancies, high-quality management and on-site facilities, which helps essential workers and families plan their futures.

Finally, targeted finance, improved procurement access, a small-sites policy and planning support for SME and local builders would widen local supply and encourage diverse, community-led housing. By prioritising local small builders and simplifying approvals where possible, we can deliver more affordable homes that fit our area’s needs and character.

i really think rents in my area are rising quickly, and as a 18-24-year-old renting near Belfast, it’s hard to save for a deposit while paying bills. I think targeted rent stabilization pilots could help affordability without wrecking long-term supply if they’re closely monitored. Caps or slower increases in high-demand neighbourhoods should come with rigorous evaluation on landlord viability and new investment, with a clear rule that pilots end if they harm supply or reduce new builds. 

I also back stronger licensing, enforcement, minimum quality standards and longer tenancies. A straightforward safety and energy standard check, mandatory decent-condition guarantees, and clearer tenancy terms would improve lives. To protect small landlords, there should be phased compliance, affordable access to advice, and targeted grants for upgrades rather than blanket penalties.

Reforms to how planning obligations are handled need transparency and enforceable commitments—ensuring on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding are delivered. A public register of obligations and delivery milestones would help residents see progress and hold developers to account. I’d want these reforms piloted in a few council areas first, with clear metrics, before wider rollout.

From living in England, I think the reforms that would most effectively increase affordable, good-quality homes start with regeneration and brownfield use to the greatest extent possible. In our area there are several long-empty shops and a disused factory; converting those sites into well-designed flats would add homes without damaging green space and would reuse existing infrastructure. A strong brownfield-first policy, with faster remediation funding and clearer planning routes for conversions and small-scale infill, is essential before any Green Belt release. 

I also support mandating higher energy standards for new builds and supplementing this with a national retrofit programme for existing homes. The aim should be to cut bills and climate impact without pushing costs onto tenants or risking rents rising sharply; so simple subsidies or a ring-fenced retrofit fund are necessary. 

Finally, community-led approaches like community land trusts, housing co-operatives, self-build schemes, and modern methods of construction can bring affordable, good-quality homes on a faster timetable. They work best where there is land supply and predictable planning support, with training capacity to sustain them.

From where I live in England, I think the reforms proposed to increase affordable housing fall short because they rely on market levers without giving local SME builders practical tools. I disagree that broad national reforms alone will unlock supply; what works locally is targeted support for small, local builders: targeted finance with patient capital and lower upfront risk, procurement access that opens council and housing association frameworks to small firms, a clear small-sites policy that releases parcels of land and simplifies approvals, and planning support that gets schemes through quickly.

In practice, a small site near our town has been held up by rigid prequalification requirements for council tenders and by finance costs that push bids beyond what local buyers can afford. A local SME also reports that mainstream lenders demand large deposits and tight conditions, pricing out community-led projects. If authorities created a SME housing fund, guarantees for small bids, prioritised pipelines for sites under 0.5-1 hectare, and front-loaded planning advice plus a faster decision process, we would see more diverse, affordable homes.

We need real, targeted tools, not vague promises. Otherwise supply will creep up slowly at best and miss the communities that need it most.

From my vantage point in England, the most effective reforms would combine stronger quality and safety standards with practical support for smaller landlords, while leading with public investment to expand genuinely affordable social housing. Licensing and enforcement should target worst-acting operators and protect tenants, but not impose excessive fees on small landlords who maintain decent homes. In my area a couple of landlords keep older terraces well, but others neglect repairs; clear inspections, gas/electric safety checks, and energy efficiency standards must be enforceable, with penalties proportionate to the risk posed to tenants.

Longer tenancies would offer security, especially for older families and single pensioners, provided there are fair rent rules and a robust deposits system. For many households, this is a stepping stone to stability rather than a path to social housing.

A major programme of council and housing association building would deliver genuinely affordable homes and energy-efficient standards, reducing pressure on the private market. I would also support rent caps or stabilization pilots to assess impacts on supply and investment; any cap must be carefully calibrated to avoid choking new construction or driving landlords out.

Overall, a mixed approach—strong enforcement, longer tenancies, substantial public building programmes, and evidence-based affordability measures—seems most likely to increase supply of good-quality homes in the medium term.

absolutely i disagree with the current reforms; they neglect SME builders. We need targeted finance, easier procurement for local small sites, planning support, and stronger local data, accountability, and funded council capacity to monitor delivery and enforce commitments!

From a Scottish perspective, reforms that lean on more private development and volume targets don’t reliably deliver affordable, good‑quality homes for local people. I disagree with approaches that rely mainly on market‑led Build‑to‑Rent or mixed‑tenure schemes without durable affordability covenants and strong, professional management. Instead, reforms must put community‑led models at the heart: make public or community land available for community land trusts and housing co‑operatives, unlock land for self‑build, and support modern methods of construction so we can build faster without compromising quality. Where I live, a proposed Build‑to‑Rent block would risk high rents and weak upkeep unless affordability protections are baked in and long‑term stewardship is guaranteed. By contrast, a local cooperative’s self‑build project, backed by modular MMC and local supply chains, could deliver genuinely affordable, energy‑efficient homes and maintain affordability over decades. Real progress will require faster planning pathways, predictable funding for these models, and enforceable affordability covenants, not merely more units churned through conventional private development. The goal should be lasting homes that communities can manage and sustain.

From my experience as a renter and student in England, the biggest driver of affordability is energy costs and building quality. Reforms to increase supply should couple tougher energy standards for new builds with funded retrofits of existing housing, so tenants aren’t hit with endless bills while developers deliver better homes. A transitional period and upfront retrofit grants are essential to avoid pushing up rents or costs for landlords.

Key reforms I’d back:
- Energy standards and retrofit funding: set a fabric-first standard for new homes, with clear routes to heat pumps or other low-carbon systems where appropriate, and a national retrofit fund to upgrade insulation, windows and heating in older stock.
- Finance and procurement for SMEs: public-backed guarantees, affordable loans and a local build pipeline that prioritises local SMEs and small sites; ensure contracts include quality, long-term maintenance and compliance.
- Small-sites policy and planning support: streamline planning for sites of 5–40 homes, unlock underused land on council brownfields, and provide local authority planning ‘one-stop’ services so decisions aren’t dragged out.
- Diversified, mixed-tenure outputs and strong design standards, with tenant protections and upfront affordable housing contributions.

Overall, this conditional approach could raise supply and cut bills, but must avoid piling costs on renters or crushing small builders.

I welcome reforms that improve local data, monitoring and accountability to ensure affordable, good‑quality homes are actually delivered. In my area, the planning department is stretched and too many promised affordable homes sit in the pipeline or stall, leaving local people waiting.

Key steps would include:
- Better local data: annual housing needs assessments refreshed quarterly; a live pipeline showing sites with permission, in build, or stalled, and whether affordable quotas are secured.
- Transparent monitoring: public dashboards and quarterly delivery reports at ward level, so residents can see progress and hold developers to account.
- Stronger developer accountability: enforceable penalties for missed delivery of affordable housing; mechanisms to claw back land or reallocate sites if commitments are not met; ensure affordable units are genuinely designated and let to local people.
- More planning and enforcement capacity: increased funding to council planning teams, additional planners and inspectors, and quicker enforcement against breaches to avoid long delays.
- Delivery-friendly processes: support for small builders, streamlined pre-apps, and clearer conditions to accelerate schemes that deliver affordable homes.

In my ward, a site with promised affordable units has stalled for two years; these reforms would help avoid that.

Our organisation welcomes the proposed reforms to boost affordable, good‑quality homes across Northern Ireland. The mix of community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction offers a practical route to faster, value-for-money homes that communities can sustain.

Key reforms we support include:
- Releasing public land to community land trusts and co‑operatives on long leases, with capital grants, loan guarantees and dedicated advisory support. This would keep land in community ownership and preserve long‑term affordability.
- Streamlining planning and procurement for MMC and custom/self‑build projects: pre‑approved modular designs, fast‑track planning for affordable schemes, and standardised contracts to reduce build risk.
- Serviced plots and developer support for self‑build: guarantee serviced plots in new estates, plus access to low‑interest finance and training so more local households can build safely.
- Strong quality standards: require energy efficiency and durable materials, with clear warranties and aftercare.
- Finance and skills: ring‑fenced funds for CLTs/co‑ops; support for small local builders; upskilling programmes for trades.

In our area, a local community land trust secured derelict council land on a long lease and delivered 14 affordable homes in modular construction within a year, providing stability for families and revitalising neighbourhoods. These reforms would help more communities replicate that success.

To really boost affordable, good-quality homes, reforms must require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside housing. In my area, a proposed development of 1,500 homes is planned, but crucial transport upgrades and a new GP surgery were signposted to open after residents have moved in. That delay risks overcrowding and car dependency. A simple, enforceable approach would be to condition planning approvals on an Infrastructure Delivery Plan that ties each phase of housing to the timely delivery of services, funded by developers and public bodies where needed. This should cover bus/rail improvements or new services, cycle routes, primary and secondary school capacity, local health facilities, water, energy resilience and reliable broadband. For example, set milestones where 20-30% of homes unlock only after the foundational infrastructure is funded and operational, with independent delivery oversight and transparent reporting. This keeps housing affordable and sustainable, reduces traffic, and ensures communities are ready to welcome families from day one.

I want reforms that tackle the bottlenecks in planning, delivery and affordability. In my area, delivery is hampered by patchy data and slow decision‑making. Without reliable site inventories and quarterly delivery updates it’s hard to hold developers to account. I’d back a requirement for transparent dashboards showing numbers of affordable homes, tenure mix and expected completion dates, with penalties if milestones slip.

Public investment in council and housing association building programmes is essential to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. But funding must be predictable and long‑term, with ring-fenced pipelines and support for councils to procure and supervise schemes, not outsource risk to the private sector alone. Procuring locally, and ensuring a clear rent target linked to local incomes, would help communities.

I’m cautiously optimistic about community land trusts, co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction. They can accelerate supply, but require land access, access to finance and robust quality controls. Piloting them in suitable areas with clear governance and help to scale up would be sensible.

In short: better data and enforcement, public‑led delivery, and careful, supported use of alternative models to expand affordable, good‑quality homes.

Agree. To increase affordable, good‑quality homes, we need a package that raises standards and makes renting more stable, while not squeezing small landlords out of the market. In our area I see decent properties alongside damp, cold homes that shouldn’t be rented. Strengthening licensing and enforcement would push rogue landlords to upgrade, and the revenue from licenses could fund more inspections and tenant support. Clear, enforceable minimum standards on heating, insulation, damp, fire safety and annual gas checks are vital, as is requiring landlords to demonstrate repairs completed within agreed timescales. Promoting longer tenancies with fair rent reviews would give pensioners and families real security, reducing repeated moves and the cost of rehoming. This must be balanced with support for small landlords—reasonable license fees, grants or low-interest loans to upgrade properties, and simple processes to exit if needed.

I’d also support pilots of rent caps or stabilization tied to local earnings, with robust data to assess impact on supply. If designed carefully, pilots could stabilise affordability without deterring investment.

Rent caps risk chilling investment and reducing supply; pilot evidence needed. I prefer targeted Build-to-Rent with affordability covenants, mixed tenure and community-led models to raise truly affordable, quality homes.

From a Wales-based perspective, I disagree that the reforms as currently framed will reliably increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. We need fundamental shifts that reflect who actually needs homes and where. Key priorities are: wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable designs; more older‑person and supported housing; and student key‑worker accommodation, particularly in rural and culturally distinct areas where provision is thin and demand is high. The current approach feels generic and unlikely to fix delivery gaps on the ground.

Concrete steps would help more: require a clear minimum share of accessible/adaptable homes in new developments (ideally 15–20%), with lifetime standards and spaces ready for adaptations. Create a dedicated pipeline for supported housing for older residents and ensure student key‑worker blocks near essential services. In rural areas, support rural exception sites and modular builds that fit local needs, with good transport links and respect for local culture and language.

But reforms must be backed by better data and enforcement (as if that will ever happen). Councils need up‑to‑date, granular housing‑need data; developers must publish annual delivery dashboards and face meaningful penalties for missed commitments. Investment in planning and enforcement capacity is essential to stop delays and ensure promises become reality. Without these specific measures, reforms risk not delivering the affordable, good‑quality homes people actually need.

Agree. Reforms should prioritise community land trusts, housing co-operatives, self-build and modern methods of construction to quickly boost affordable, high-quality homes. Also mandate higher energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits to cut bills, support tenants and hit climate targets.

From a Scottish perspective, the most effective reforms would blend community-led housing with modern construction methods to boost affordable, good-quality supply quickly. In my area, a local community land trust has shown how land coming back into community ownership can deliver genuinely affordable homes with long-term stewardship, rather than being incentivised to chase market prices. To scale this, we need faster access to public land for CLTs and housing co‑operatives, with clear disposal routes and long‑term funding support (grants or low‑interest loans) so groups can plan confidently. Permit small, well-supported sites through streamlined planning coupled with predictable funding cycles, so the pipeline remains steady rather than episodic. Support for self‑build and co‑operative models, with clear technical guidance and access to reliable supply chains for modern methods of construction—timber-frame, modular, and off-site fabrication—would deliver high-quality homes more quickly while also generating local skilled jobs. On Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes, I’m cautiously hopeful if affordability covenants are robust and management is professional. Long‑term rents aligned to local earnings, transparent maintenance funds, and tenant participation should accompany any large schemes. With these reforms, we could see a meaningful, locally rooted uplift in affordable homes that last.

Thank you for considering reforms. I strongly support major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low-income households. In our area, private rents have risen faster than wages, and my neighbours on modest incomes face insecure housing. A steady supply of social rent homes would protect older residents like me from displacement and help keep communities intact. When our council completed a scheme of around two dozen social rent flats recently, local families could stay in the neighbourhood and energy bills fell due to newer, better-insulated homes. I also welcome rent caps or stabilization to improve affordability, provided they are designed with evidence from pilots and safeguards for supply and investment. A carefully tested cap, linked to local wages and energy costs, could prevent untenable rent rises without driving builders away. I would like to see pilots across a few councils with close monitoring of construction starts, maintenance funding, and landlord exit rates, so we can refine the approach before wider rollout.

From where I sit in England, as a retiree who has lived here most of my life, I’m not convinced that more of the same public money poured into council and housing association building programmes will reliably deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes. The big schemes often take years to plan and even longer to complete, and by the time a family is offered a home the rent levels, energy costs, and maintenance bills can make it unaffordable for those on very low incomes. I’ve watched local schemes stall because funding rounds faltered, or because the necessary infrastructure—schools, roads, healthcare facilities, and utilities—wasn’t ready. That is not a sustainable way to build communities, and I fear it simply shifts the problem rather than solves it.

What I believe would work better—though I recognise the need for safe, decent homes—are reforms that broaden how homes are funded, planned, and delivered and that tie new housing more tightly to the delivery of services people actually rely on every day. In my view, the following would be more effective in increasing affordable, good‑quality housing in our area:

1) Diversify funding and delivery models
- Encourage a mix of developers, housing associations, community land trusts, and co‑operative housing to deliver affordable units, with long‑term protections so rents stay within reach. It’s not sensible to rely on one model; a portfolio approach reduces risk of stagnation when grant rules change. 
- Allow revenue from market housing to cross‑subsidise affordable homes, but with strict guarantees that a substantial portion of units remain genuinely affordable in perpetuity or for a fixed very long term. I’ve seen schemes funded largely by public grants struggle when those grants disappear mid‑project.
- Make better use of public land by offering long leases or ownership shares to local groups who can deliver affordable homes quickly, rather than selling land outright to a single large developer who delays because of complexity and profit priorities.

2) Planning and site access reforms
- Set clear, binding development decision timelines so schemes don’t sit in planning limbo for years. A predictable timetable helps communities plan for schools and GP surgeries and gives builders a realistic window to bring projects forward.
- Prioritise brownfield sites and infill rather than greenfield acreage, with simpler rules for small and medium builders. Encouraging SME builders can increase supply faster than waiting for a few large firms to absorb land and risk.
- Remove overly onerous viability assessments that push affordable components off the back burner. If a site is viable with a proportion of affordable homes, let that be a stronger requirement rather than a negotiating chip that rarely lands in practice.

3) Infrastructure first, or at least upfront, not after the houses go up
- Infrastructure should be funded and scheduled in tandem with housing delivery, not as a postscript. A new estate needs transport links, GP capacity, schools, water and waste infrastructure, and reliable utilities from day one. Too often, families move in and then wait years for a bus route, a school place, or a cleaner drainage system.
- Explore developer levies, infrastructure bonds, and regional funds that front‑load essential services for large sites. This would prevent a mismatch between where people live and where services are available, and it would avoid the cycle where unsustainable new communities become a burden on local authorities.

4) Refurbishment and better use of existing stock
- Invest in upgrading and extending the quality and accessibility of existing affordable homes. Bringing derelict or under‑used council and housing association stock back into good condition can create immediate, stable housing without the long lead times of new builds. Energy efficiency upgrades and accessible design should be standard, reducing future cost burdens on residents.

5) Quality standards and resident protections
- Ensure every new and refurbished home meets high energy efficiency and accessibility standards. Older residents need homes that are warm and affordable to heat, with practical features that reduce maintenance costs.
- Strengthen protections to prevent the erosion of genuinely affordable rents when schemes are delivered through mixed funding models. Rent levels must be predictable and stable for households on very low incomes.

In my experience, what matters most to families is not the size of the grant or the glamour of a new estate, but whether the home is affordable to live in, is well connected to the services they need, and is delivered quickly enough not to keep families waiting for years. The reforms I’ve suggested focus on speed, fairness, and sustainability—recognising that good housing alone doesn’t create a thriving community unless the necessary services are in place at the same time.

I hope the government considers these practical reforms and tests them in local pilots before locking in a single, large public‑funded approach that may not deliver the long‑term, affordable homes our areas actually require.

Current reforms to boost affordable housing tend to focus on volume and speed, but without addressing accessibility and local demographics they won’t deliver real value. I believe reforms would be most effective if they prioritise wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes, plus dedicated provision for older adults, supported housing, and student key‑worker accommodation to serve rural and cultural needs.

In my area, it’s common to hear that even affordable new flats lack step‑free access or adaptable layouts. Families with a wheelchair user face long waits or forced adaptations after moving in. A village near me has a former care‑home site that was converted into flats with limited accessibility, leaving those with mobility needs stuck in unsuitable housing. Conversely, there are few truly mixed, on‑site supported options for younger workers who help keep services running in rural communities.

I’d push for: a planning rule requiring a meaningful share (e.g., 15–20%) of wheelchair‑accessible or easily adaptable homes in new developments; design standards that meet M4(2) and M4(3) such as level thresholds and flexible rooms; funding for on‑site care and co‑located services; and dedicated schemes for student‑key workers in rural areas to support essential services. Without this targeted approach, more homes won’t translate into better living for many residents.

There is a clear and growing need in our area to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. I welcome reforms that aim to stabilise rents where they are pushing families and individuals to the edge, but that also recognise and protect the incentives landlords and investors need to maintain and grow the housing stock. In my experience in England, the private rented sector has become more expensive and more variable in quality, while new homes take years to come on stream. A balanced package of reforms, tested through pilots, could help.

I support targeted pilots for rent stabilisation or caps, but they must be designed so they do not discourage investment or drive properties out of the market. A sensible approach would be to link any cap to local earnings growth or CPI and to review it annually. There should be exemptions for new-builds and for properties undergoing substantial energy efficiency upgrades or safety improvements, to avoid penalising landlords who are investing in better homes. We should also allow modest, predictable annual changes for existing tenancies that reflect genuine cost pressures, so landlords are not unable to justify upkeep.

Pilots must be evaluated rigorously. Local authorities could track vacancy rates, average rents, turnover of tenancies, and the rate and quality of maintenance, along with tenant satisfaction and energy performance improvements. If a cap starts to reduce the supply of rental homes, the pilots should be adjusted or paused. It is essential to guard against landlords exiting the market, converting stock to short lets, or letting properties fall into disrepair due to financial pressures. Providing a pathway for landlords who keep rents within a cap, or who invest in energy upgrades and decent standards, would help keep supply steady.

Quality and safety must be part of any reform. Rents should be linked to quality through mandatory minimum standards and robust enforcement. Properties should meet decent homes and energy efficiency standards (aiming for EPC C where feasible, with phased progress and government-supported retrofit funding). Grants or subsidies for essential safety and efficiency improvements would help landlords maintain properties and could be tied to long‑term tenancy commitments.

Beyond pilot rents, broader reforms to planning and development are needed to enlarge the affordable housing stock. Faster planning decisions, particularly for brownfield sites, and clearer, locally appropriate affordable-housing requirements on new developments are crucial. Encouraging Build‑To‑Rent and other long‑term rental models with affordable rent floors can stabilise markets while ensuring the supply of genuinely affordable homes. Local authorities should have access to predictable funding to bring forward land for affordable homes and to upgrade existing council housing to decent standards.

From a resident perspective, I have seen rents rise faster than wages in recent years, and families I know have had to move further away as costs become unaffordable. I have also observed well‑intentioned landlords who struggle to justify ongoing upgrades when returns are under pressure. A careful combination of pilots, exemptions for new builds and energy upgrades, better enforcement of quality standards, and strong planning reform could address affordability while protecting and growing supply.

In summary, I would support a package that starts with carefully monitored rent-stabilisation pilots, with clear exemptions and linked improvements for energy efficiency and safety, and is complemented by faster planning, robust affordable housing requirements on new schemes, and targeted incentives for landlords who maintain quality and supply. The evidence from pilots should drive decision‑making and adjustments, ensuring we increase affordable homes without strangling investment or reducing the number of homes available to rent.

To genuinely increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area, we need a twin track of expanding supply and stabilising rents in the short term. In my experience as a renter in England, rents have risen quickly while genuinely affordable options have remained scarce.. Reforms to planning and land release should br prioritisrd: faster planning decisions for brownfield sites; a clear requirement for affordable units on larger developments; release of publicly owned land with streamlined procurement; stronger use of Section 106 with transparent reporting on the actual outcomes. Support for smaller builders—through affordable finance, guarantees, and simplified procurement—could reduce bottlenecks andd diversify delivery. On price stability, pilots for rent caps or stabilisation could help affordability but carry significant supply risks, including landlord exit. I’d back time-limited, area-targeted pilots with robust evaluation, exemptions for genuinely new-build stock, and caps indexed to local wages or inflation. If the evidence shows distortion to investment or maintenance, we should pause. Pair any cap with incentives to upgradee existing stock to a decent energy standard and with protections for long-term tenants. In short, combine supply-focused reforms with carefully evaluated, limited testing of rrnts stabilization rather than immediate nationwide rollout.

I don’t think the best way to boost affordable, good‑quality homes is simply to pour more cash into traditional council or housing association building programmes. In my area, delivery is slow, planning barriers bite and long procurement cycles push up costs. Instead reforms should prioritise community‑led and modern construction approaches that can change supply quickly:

- Community land trusts taking land into local ownership to lock in long‑term affordability and protect against value‑driven rent hikes.

- Housing co‑operatives and self‑build groups giving residents real control over design, upkeep and running costs, with proven potential for better energy efficiency.

- Modern methods of construction and off‑site manufactured homes to speed up delivery, cut waste and raise quality, while still allowing local tailoring.

Concrete steps I’d support include releasing public land for CLTs and co‑ops at affordable terms, providing patient finance and guarantees for small builders, and simplifying planning for small, incremental developments. Funding should reward long‑term affordability, not just headcount.

In short, reform should enable community‑led models and efficient building methods to deliver quicker, higher‑quality homes that stay affordable, rather than more of the same from large‑scale public programmes.

Like many Scots, I want more affordable, good‑quality homes, but I disagree with sweeping reforms that speed up planning without protecting communities. Haste can mean poorer design, flood risk and loss of greenspace. Even well‑intentioned schemes risk eroding local input when decisions are rushed, and that undermines trust in new developments.

We also need more wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes, and housing that understands rural and cultural needs. Too many new flats lack step‑free access or flexible layouts for ageing relatives or students sharing. Delivery should not be a one‑size‑fits‑all exercise; it must reflect the realities of different parts of Scotland.

Infrastructure must not follow housing after the fact. We need funded, phased provision of transport, schools, GP services and utilities alongside or before housing to avoid crowded clinics and congested buses. In rural Scotland, promises about roads and broadband crumble when housing is built without accompanying services, pushing up living costs and eroding affordability.

Instead of broad deregulation, adopt robust standards: require a meaningful affordable quota, high energy efficiency, flood‑resilient design and mandatory accessible units; ensure local communities have real input through plan‑led processes. These safeguards are essential to deliver affordable homes that people actually want to live in.

I believe reforms could help address affordable housing, but they must be carefully balanced with protecting our landscapes and town character. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes could lower land costs and provide a predictable stream to fund genuinely affordable homes alongside essential local infrastructure—schools, GP surgeries, and roads. In my town there is publicly owned land near the high street that has sat idle for years; bringing it into use with clear affordable-quota requirements and local consent could deliver homes that neighbours can actually afford.

However, I want to see this approach used with caution. First, prioritise regeneration, infill, and conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before any greenfield release or Green Belt adjustment. There are many empty shops and barns on brownfield sites that could be converted without destroying countryside values. Any release should be accompanied by robust design standards, flood risk checks, and a local oversight body to ensure uplift funds are ring-fenced for housing and essential infrastructure, not diverted elsewhere. Pilot schemes with transparent reporting would help communities see the benefits before wider rollout.

I’m replying as a 60-year-old resident of England who wants to see genuine, deliverable housing—not more promises. I don’t oppose new homes, but I do oppose reforms that prioritise speed or market profit over real, local delivery and quality. If reforms are to increase affordable, good‑quality homes, they must strengthen local capacity, stop land-banking, and target regeneration before any greenfield or Green Belt release. Here’s what would actually help, in my view.

First, improve local data, monitoring and accountability. We need a statutory requirement for councils to publish transparent, real-time delivery dashboards showing progress on every major site, highlights of any stalls, and how affordable housing obligations are being met. A public, independent audit of large schemes should be routine, with clear milestones and penalties if delivery is late or conditions are not discharged. In our area, a 90‑unit site promised 40% affordable homes but has not progressed in two years—the public would benefit from a live tracker that flags such issues early so the council and developer are held to account, rather than letting schemes drift and taxpayers shoulder the cost of delays.

Second, prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant buildings before releasing greenfield land or weakening Green Belt protections. I understand the pressure to boost supply, but greenfield release tends to create longer planning processes, higher infrastructure costs and landscapes that communities value. Every local plan should include a robust brownfield-first pipeline, with concrete proposals for converting long‑term empty offices, shops and industrial units into homes, complemented by subsidies and simple, fast-tracked consents for viable conversions. In our town, several commercial properties have stood empty for years; with a practical conversion program and a tightened, performance‑based planning regime, those units could become affordable homes much sooner than new greenfield sites. If greenfield release is ever considered, it must be conditional on a landscape and biodiversity plan that’s enforceable and funded, not just promised on a glossy brochure.

Third, target finance, procurement access, and planning support for SME and local builders to widen the supply chain. Big developers may deliver at scale, but the risk is fewer affordable homes and less local apprenticeship opportunities. We need a stronger small-sites policy, with secured access to finance via council-backed funds, quicker and more transparent procurement rules, and public land allocated specifically for SMEs to bid on. I’d like to see at least a portion of new housing coming from sites under 0.5 hectares delivered through local builders who hire locally, with a streamlined planning route and pre-approved design and build standards. In practice, a local builder I know faced prohibitive planning fees and slow approvals on a modest 12‑home project; a dedicated SME fund and a simplified consent process could unlock similar schemes elsewhere without sacrificing quality.

Fourth, strengthen enforcement and delivery capacity. Planning departments need adequate staffing to discharge conditions, monitor construction timelines, and ensure affordable housing contributions are delivered on time and in full. Councils should be funded to act as active delivery bodies, not as passive bystanders waiting for developers to self‑police. Where commitments fall away, there should be enforceable remedies and, if necessary, clawbacks that fund interim affordable housing while long‑term sites complete.

Finally, deliver a credible, local‑first pipeline. Residents want to know when, where, and how homes will be built in their communities, with clear guarantees that conditions will be met, landscapes protected, and local jobs created. The reforms I’d support would require councils to demonstrate an evidence-based plan that prioritises regeneration and small builders, with greenfield release only as a last resort and with strict, enforceable safeguards.

I’m not against more housing, but I am against systems that look good on paper and fail the places and people who need them. Real reform means stronger local data, regeneration-first delivery, and genuine support for SMEs to build diverse, affordable homes that stay affordable and well‑built for the long term.

Yes, strengthen local data, monitoring and accountability; fund council planning and delivery to ensure developers keep commitments. Also prioritise regeneration, infill and converting vacant or long‑term empty homes before releasing greenfield land to protect landscapes.

it's outrageous that i oppose sweeping reforms; rent caps may help affordability but risk shrinking supply and landlord exit. Pilot evidence-based rent-stabilisation schemes, plus funded, phased delivery of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside new homes to build sustainable communities!

Yes, I support reforming finance access and small-sites planning to help local SMEs build more affordable, good-quality homes. Strengthen licensing and quality standards with longer tenancies, while safeguarding small landlords. Consider pilots on rent caps to boost affordability, with careful monitoring of any impact on supply.

To increase affordable, good-quality homes in our area, reforms should prioritise SME and local builders through targeted finance, easier procurement routes, and planning support for small-site development. In our district, a derelict site was brought back into use by a local SME through a pilot, delivering 12 affordable homes after procurement adjustments, showing what’s possible. A dedicated finance pot with grant or low-interest repayable loans, plus guarantees to cover higher pre-construction costs would help local builders who know the area best. Public procurement platforms should reserve a meaningful share of contracts for SMEs and local contractors, with simplified bid requirements and longer payment terms to improve cash flow. On planning, a streamlined small-sites policy, with explicit criteria for under-used land (0.5-2 hectares in rural or semi-rural areas) and fast-tracked validation, would unlock more diverse local housing. Local authorities should be empowered to offer pre-application planning advice and reduce delays through clear decision windows (12 weeks for outline, 18 for detailed consent).

I also back delivery of wheelchair-accessible, adaptable, older-persons, supported and student key-worker homes tailored to demographic, rural and cultural needs. These must be integrated in mainstream schemes rather than isolated pockets, with requirements for accessible design, flexi-use spaces, and proximity to essential services. Funding should cover both new build and retrofit in existing stock, avoiding sterilising existing communities.

From where I live in Scotland, I don’t think the proposed reforms that aim to simply loosen planning rules or push more units onto the market will reliably increase the number of affordable, good‑quality homes that families can actually live in long term. What would work much more effectively, in my view, is a serious push to build purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent stock with a meaningful proportion of mixed‑tenure housing, all carried out with affordability covenants and professional management. This approach gives us long‑term rental supply, predictable rents, and proper maintenance over decades, not just until the next market cycle.

There are a few reasons I’m convinced this is the right path. First, long‑term supply. When developers build homes specifically to rent, the properties are kept as rental stock for the long haul. Tenants aren’t at the mercy of a landlord who can sell up or convert units to owner‑occupation at the drop of a hat. In Scotland we’ve seen how churn in the private rental sector can push rents up and make it hard for households on modest incomes to plan for the future. A Build‑to‑Rent model provides stability: longer tenancies (with decent break clauses), on‑site maintenance teams, and a steady pipeline of new homes kept in rental use for the long term. I’ve heard from friends who live in such blocks in other parts of the country about better upkeep, quicker repairs, and clearer expectations around service charges and facilities.

Second, affordability and quality go hand in hand under this approach. If rents are anchored by affordable covenants—say, rents set at a level linked to local incomes and capped increases—then longer‑term renters aren’t priced out after a couple of years. It also means the investment is designed to stay affordable for families, pensioners, and key workers who contribute to our communities. Professional management matters too: a dedicated on‑site or nearby management team tends to deliver better repairs, easier access to information, clearer tenancy rights, and more consistent standards than individual private landlords who own a handful of properties scattered around a town.

Third, the mix of tenure within one development can strengthen communities and make services more affordable. A scheme that includes both rented units with covenants and some homes for shared ownership or affordable sale helps families stay close to schools, GP practices, and networks that matter in later life. It avoids the extremes of concentrated private rentals or long waiting lists for social housing, and it can be designed so that affordable units are not hidden away in peripheral pockets but integrated into the fabric of the area.

That said, there are guardrails we must insist on if we’re to avoid new problems. Any Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure programme should: require a meaningful share of units with covenanted rents affordable in the local context (for example a portion on large schemes, realistically 25–40% depending on size and locality); ensure long‑term rentals with secure tenancy rights and capped rent increases; mandate on‑site or easily accessible professional management with responsive repairs; guarantee high energy efficiency standards and accessible design; and provide clear avenues for tenants to raise concerns with independent oversight. Planning conditions should not be optional side‑bars but binding requirements with regular reporting to the Scottish Housing Regulator and to local communities.

In practice, we’d also benefit from releasing public or other well‑located land for Build‑to‑Rent projects, with planning gains that fund more affordable covenanted units in the same or adjacent developments. I’m not convinced that widening general planning rules or incentivising more for‑sale houses will deliver the long‑term rental stock we need, especially for older people like me who may prefer renting to owning as a way to keep flexibility and avoid heavy maintenance burdens in later life.

My own experience in nearby towns suggests that well‑run Build‑to‑Rent schemes, with mixed tenure and affordability covenants, can deliver better living conditions and more predictable costs for tenants than many traditional private rentals or recent speculative schemes. If policymakers want real progress on affordable, good‑quality homes, then they should make these Build‑to‑Rent developments the backbone of supply, rigorously backed by affordability covenants, professional management, and robust tenant protections. That approach, rather than broad deregulation or quick‑fix schemes, is what will keep families, pensioners, and communities secure in their homes for years to come.

I strongly support major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low‑income households. In our area, private rents have risen faster than wages, and waiting lists for council or social housing stretch for years. I’ve seen families I know down the street struggle to find secure, affordable homes, while a friend’s children still rent a cramped flat because there simply aren’t enough good-quality social homes available. A decisive, well-planned push to build social rented housing would not only relieve pressure on the private rented sector but also provide stability for children’s education, people’s health, and our local communities. The reforms I’d like to see are practical, deliverable and designed to last decades, not just cycles of funding.

What reforms would most effectively increase supply?

- Provide a long, ring-fenced capital programme for social housing. Councils and housing associations need multi‑year funding (ideally 10–15 years) with predictable allocations to plan and hire the right workforce. Lifting borrowing constraints on councils’ Housing Revenue Accounts (HRAs) and enabling sensible public borrowing would let delivery keep pace with need without chasing speculative profits. When money is available for genuine social rents, we can plan larger schemes and build much more quickly.

- Use land assets and streamline planning for social housing. Government and local authorities hold public land that could be released for genuinely affordable homes at scale. Set clear expectations that a significant share of new development on public or brownfield land should be social housing, delivered on a timely basis. Planning processes should be streamlined for schemes that include a substantial social rent component: quicker approvals, fewer duplicative hurdles, and a default presumption in favour of well-designed social housing where affordable homes are a material part of the plan.

- Ensure affordable housing is truly affordable and long‑term. Social rents must be anchored to household income and linked to long-term affordability, not subject to market fluctuations. I would favour a rent model where social rents are kept affordable for 25–30 years or more, with annual reviews tied to income where appropriate, and with protections against spiralling increases. Tenants should have secure, long‑term tenure, backed by reliable maintenance and clear service standards.

- Standardise designs and accelerate delivery without compromising quality. A framework of standard, modular or semi‑modular designs can reduce construction time and costs, while still delivering high-quality, energy-efficient homes. It’s important that speed does not come at the expense of durability or accessibility. Local firms and skilled trades should be supported, with apprenticeships and local employment woven into every major scheme.

- Build energy efficiency and decarbonisation in from the start. Social homes should meet high energy-performance standards and be adaptable for future improvements. A focus on insulation, heat pumps or other low-carbon heating, and durable building materials will lower running costs for tenants and reduce pressure on public services in the long term.

- Strengthen procurement, oversight and tenant involvement. A robust procurement framework with long-term partnerships between councils, housing associations and contractors can protect quality while controlling costs. Tenants should be invited to participate in design and governance through boards or resident panels, ensuring homes meet real needs and remain well maintained.

- Address supply chain and labour market pressures. Public investment should come with commitments to local training, fair wages, and safe working conditions. This not only helps deliver schemes on time but also strengthens the broader local economy, which is especially important in areas where average incomes are squeezed.

- Integrate support services with housing. Social housing delivery should be paired with access to tenancy support, employment advice, and health and welfare services where needed. That holistic approach helps sustain tenancies, reduces homelessness, and supports children's schooling and community cohesion.

In practice, these reforms would mean a steady stream of genuinely affordable homes that are there for the long term—homes that families can stay in as their circumstances change, rather than being forced back into the private market. It would also mean fewer churns in the private sector, less displacement of vulnerable residents, and a more stable, growing local economy driven by construction and long-term property management.

I understand there are budget pressures and competing priorities. However, without a long-term, public-led investment programme focused on social housing, we risk continuing with temporary fixes that merely shift the problem from one community to another. The positive impact of a serious, well-managed push to expand council and housing association stock would be felt for a generation: fairer access to decent homes, improved life chances for children, and communities that people are proud to be part of. I strongly urge the government to commit to these reforms and to provide the resources and the policy framework to make them happen.

I support reforms to unlock affordable, high‑quality homes: back community land trusts, co‑ops, self‑build and modern methods; reform S106, CIL and viability with transparency and enforceable on‑site affordable contributions; strengthen local data, monitoring and delivery capacity.

In my view, the reforms that would actually boost the supply of affordable, good-quality homes aren’t more rules for private landlords alone. Here in England, what we need first is a substantial, sustained push of public investment in council and housing association building to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rents for low‑income households. Without that, private sector tweaks risk shrinking stock or pushing rents up as landlords pass costs on to tenants. 

I’ve spoken with local small landlords and heard their concerns about licensing fees, stricter minimum standards, and longer tenancies raising costs and reducing viability. A few have already scaled back or sold up, which simply reduces the choices for tenants, especially the elderly and those on fixed incomes. 

What would help more reliably: fast planning approvals, targeted grants or low-interest loans to upgrade existing homes to meet quality standards (instead of punitive penalties), and a clear programme of new social housing on brownfield sites. Also, provide stable incentives for small landlords to stay in the market while we root out bad actors. This balanced approach would deliver real, lasting growth in affordable homes in our area.

I disagree with reforms that depend primarily on letting the market decide or on tinkering with planning permissions alone. The clearest way to genuinely increase supply of affordable, good-quality homes is to release surplus public land and capture planning uplift through levies or taxes to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure.

In our area, Council-owned sites sit dormant while demand grows. If these sites were released with conditions that deliver a defined share of affordable homes and with uplift funds ring-fenced for housing, transport and schools, we would see faster, higher-quality delivery than waiting for private land to drop in price. Relying on existing Section 106 agreements or the Community Infrastructure Levy has repeatedly fallen short—the uplift often accrues to developers rather than to genuinely affordable homes.

Key safeguards are essential: a public land bank with transparent disposal criteria, genuine price reductions for discounted sale, binding delivery timelines, and independent oversight of how uplift revenue is spent. Funds should be legally ring-fenced to affordable housing and local infrastructure, not absorbed into general budgets.

Please prioritise this approach, as it addresses land costs head-on and funds the services communities rely on.

From my perspective in England, a balanced approach to increasing affordable, good-quality homes is needed. We should deliver more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older people, together with supported and student key-worker housing that reflects local demographics, rural patterns and cultural needs. It’s sensible to build in flexibility so homes can reconfigure if family circumstances change, and to include energy efficiency from the outset.

However, I am cautious about greenfield releases and Green Belt changes. Landscapes matter for character, tourism and health, so any expansion should come after we prioritise regeneration of existing places.

My preferred reforms: prioritise infill, conversion and regeneration of vacant offices, shops and long-term empty homes before new greenfield development. In our town centre, several empty units have stood empty for years; converting them to affordable flats would support locals and keep streets lively without sprawling outwards. Make it easier to convert with design standards that protect character; require a portion of schemes to be fully accessible; offer incentives for retrofitting existing housing and for locally appropriate, modular, energy-efficient builds. Always involve communities early and ensure rural transport links are strengthened.

Across my area in England, I remain unconvinced that releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies will reliably deliver affordable, good-quality homes. On paper it sounds clever, but without teeth it’s just accounting gymnastics. If land is released, councils must secure binding delivery obligations—on-site affordable homes, or clear, ring-fenced funding for social housing and local infrastructure. Otherwise it becomes a windfall for developers, inflating land values and delaying or eroding affordable supply.

Similarly, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing needs to go further than cosmetic changes. Transparency is welcome, but without independent auditing and standard national benchmarks, viability studies can be used to whittle away affordable obligations. In practice, I’ve seen sites in our town where promises of 30-40% on-site affordable housing evaporated after viability assessments, causing years of delay and a lack of affordable homes for local people.

I’d rather see rules that require affordable housing as a default on publicly owned land, clear, enforceable funding for infrastructure, and a fast, standardised approvals process with independent oversight. That would really start delivering homes people can afford.

I disagree with reforms that push greenfield release before we make full use of regeneration opportunities in town centres. In our area, the real bottleneck is not a lack of land but a failure to bring vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes back into use. A former mill on the edge of town and several empty shops in the high street sit unused while families struggle to rent decent, affordable homes nearby.

Proposed reforms should prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant buildings before any Green Belt release.
