I know local landlords who are already weighing the risk of additional licensing fees and more onerous requirements; a couple of properties they manage could become owner‑occupied rather than rented if the economics don’t add up.

Third, the idea of targeted finance, procurement access, and small‑sites policy is welcome, but it needs real, practical delivery. Small builders and SMEs often can’t compete for council contracts because pre‑qualification processes are opaque and bonding requirements are onerous. I’m aware of a small family business that could contribute new homes locally but was unable to bid for a council scheme due to complex paperwork and high upfront risk. We should simplify procurement for SMEs, provide clear pre‑approved frameworks, and offer government‑backed guarantees or bridging finance to get small sites off the drawing board and into construction.

Additionally, planning capacity and delivery need to go hand in hand with development viability. It’s no good promising more affordable homes if the planning department can’t issue decisions quickly or if there’s no mechanism to ensure that approved schemes actually reach construction in a timely fashion. In my experience, even well‑intended projects stall because of fragmented processes between departments, inconsistent application of policy, and limited enforcement resources. A one‑stop shop for small‑site approvals, with predictable deadlines and transparent criteria, would help a lot, but only if councils are empowered and resourced to meet those deadlines.

What I would prioritise instead, or at least require alongside these reforms, is a clear, funded plan to unlock land for small and mid‑sized builders, with rapid planning decisions and strict monitoring of delivery. We need to publish quarterly delivery reports, with names of responsible parties and concrete milestones, and we need to ensure that affordable units are genuinely delivered as part of every scheme. And for the private rented sector, I’d favour targeted support for landlords to improve property standards and energy efficiency, plus a simpler, proportionate compliance regime rather than broad licensing that risks shrinking supply.

In short, the aim is right, but the mechanism must not disincentivise the very people who build and rent homes. Strengthen accountability, cut unnecessary red tape for SMEs, and build a planning system that moves from promise to delivery. Only then will reforms meaningfully increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area.

I strongly agree that reforms like these are essential to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in Scotland. The main hurdle in many communities isn’t ambition but delivery. We need better local data and monitoring so councils, communities and developers share a realistic delivery plan and can spot bottlenecks early. If targets for affordable homes slip, there should be clear accountability and a swift delivery fund to keep schemes moving and prevent protracted delays. 

Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes can lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. In my area there are idle school, hospital and council‑owned sites that could be repurposed, and a transparent mechanism for land value capture would translate planning gains into real homes instead of just paperwork. 

Finally, prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before greenfield or Green Belt releases. A derelict mill, a row of vacant offices or empty flats could become affordable homes quickly if supported by targeted grants and good design, protecting landscapes and reducing sprawl.

As a resident of England, I’ve seen a small affordable-housing project stall for over a year due to planning delays. I believe we need to streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while keeping environmental safeguards. A simpler framework with standardised assessments and a one-stop digital portal would reduce developer uncertainty and speed delivery on brownfield sites near transport links. We must not lower quality: energy efficiency, accessible design and habitat protections should be enshrined in law, not left to discretionary whim.

I also think pilots on rent stabilisation could improve affordability, but only if designed to protect supply and investment. If caps are too tight or permanent, builders may pull back and landlords exit, reducing stock. Run careful pilots in selected towns with clear durations, review points and funding to support maintenance and retrofit. Paired with targeted infrastructure investment and support for community-led housing, these reforms could deliver more affordable, good-quality homes without undermining the market that actually delivers them.

No; tinkering with Section 106/CIL and viability won’t fix supply. Prioritise regenerating town centres, infill, and converting vacant/empty homes before any greenfield or Green Belt release to protect landscapes.

Energy efficiency is a worthy target, but the proposed reforms risk slowing the building of affordable homes in our area. Mandating higher energy standards for all new builds will push up construction costs, which often get passed on as higher rents or reduce the viability of affordable units, especially for small builders and housing associations trying to stretch limited funds. My flatmate’s family rents a modest two-bedroom, and they already face rising bills; I’m worried extra retrofit costs would land on tenants or delay essential maintenance elsewhere. 

Funding retrofits at scale sounds good in theory, but in practice it’s expensive and complex. If funds aren’t allocated quickly and fairly, you’ll get patchy upgrades and ongoing bills for tenants rather than real relief. Public investment in council and housing association homes is crucial, but I’ve seen projects stall because of red tape and mismanagement, delaying genuinely affordable long-term social rented homes for low-income households.

Rather than blanket reforms, I’d push for measures that actually unlock supply: faster planning decisions, simpler procurement for small builders, and targeted energy-efficiency grants for private rentals to cut bills without driving up market rents. Any reform must protect renters from higher rents and deliver real, timely affordability while still pursuing climate goals.

Agree. Streamlining planning and decision timelines, while keeping environmental safeguards, will speed up housing delivery and reduce developer uncertainty, helping more affordable, good-quality homes come through in my area.

I disagree that tinkering with Section 106, CIL and viability testing alone will reliably boost affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. The bottleneck is local delivery capacity and enforcement, not clever accounting. In my town a 350‑unit scheme promised 60 affordable homes but, after three years, only about 20 have materialised. The rest are on‑offsite deals or deferred, with little publicly available data on when they will arrive. The council lacks a transparent, real‑time tracker to hold developers to their commitments, and planning enforcement staff are stretched thin.

What would help more? A robust, real‑time public dashboard showing promised, secured and delivered affordable units and the timing of infrastructure. Binding on‑site obligations should be the default, with off‑site or cash contributions ring‑fenced to the same local area and only released against clear milestones. Strengthen planning enforcement with dedicated delivery teams and meaningful penalties for non‑delivery. Create a council‑backed delivery unit to negotiate and monitor schemes. And ensure viability assessments are independent and transparent, not a loophole to reduce obligations. Those changes would be far more effective than broad reform of S106/CIL in isolation.

From where I sit in England, the reforms most likely to increase affordable, good-quality homes are a combination of purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management, backed by strong local delivery. These schemes provide long-term rental supply with high maintenance standards and predictable rents, which would help people like my grandson's friend who keeps moving because tenancy quality is variable.

Second, improving local data, monitoring, and developer accountability is essential. A clear public dashboard showing planning and delivery milestones, with penalties or remedies if commitments are not met, would drive delivery. Our council needs capacity to plan, enforce, and sign off schemes quickly; this reduces bottlenecks and helps builders.

Third, targeted finance and procurement access, plus support for small sites and SME builders, is critical. Easier routes to land, finance, and planning for small brownfield sites in towns like ours would unlock local, diverse housing. Local builders understand demand and can deliver good homes faster if given the right help.

In short, combining Build-to-Rent with robust governance and a supportive small-sites pipeline would meaningfully boost affordable, good-quality homes here.

Strongly agree that reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes should focus on wheelchair-accessible, adaptable, older-persons, supported and student key-worker housing, tailored to our rural and cultural needs. In Scotland, I’ve seen neighbours where steps and narrow halls make independent living impossible; a simple retrofit or a flexible plan would keep people in their communities longer and ease pressure on care services. My area would benefit from publicly funded schemes that require new affordable homes to meet wheelchair-accessible standards (M4(3) in Scotland) and include adaptable layouts. We also need expanded funding for retrofit of existing social housing to remove barriers—level access, wide doorways, accessible kitchens and bathrooms—without displacing tenants. Additionally, supported housing and extra-care schemes near towns and transport links would help older residents and carers. Supporting student key-worker homes close to hospitals and universities in rural areas would attract essential workers and reduce gaps in care. Streamlined planning for modular or small-site developments, on brownfield or public land, would speed delivery. These steps together would create sustainable, long-lasting communities.

There’s no quick fix for more affordable, good‑quality homes. In my area, rents have shot up and the new flats going up are often pricey studios, not accessible for someone like me starting out on a grad job. I’d back reforms that help both build more homes and keep them decent. 

On the supply side, speeding up planning for brownfield sites and letting smaller builders have a clearer path would help us actually see new homes. Reforming Section 106 obligations so affordable homes are delivered on-site rather than cashed in would matter too. Local councils should also speed up decisions so building starts sooner, and demand good energy efficiency and liveable space so the new places aren’t just big numbers with poor insulation. 

I’m wary of schemes that promise cheaper rents but end up locking people into long contracts. Any reform should protect tenants and ensure new homes stay genuinely affordable in the long term, not just a short-term discount. In short: faster decisions, clearer standards, real affordable delivery, and a focus on quality and energy efficiency should come first.

Thank you for inviting responses. Our organisation works across England with young people and local communities, including many rural areas, where housing challenges are acute. We believe reforms to increase affordable, good-quality homes will be most effective if they explicitly prioritise accessibility, adaptability and support, alongside general affordability. In practice, that means delivering more wheelchair-accessible homes, homes that can be adapted as people’s needs change, housing for older residents with on-site or closely linked care, and purpose-built facilities for students, key workers and carers. Without this explicit focus, rising supply can still leave large groups living in unsuitable or insecure accommodation.

What reforms would make the biggest difference?

- Planning and design that centre accessibility and adaptability
  - Require new homes to be fully accessible on completion, with a clear minimum share of units that are wheelchair-accessible and adaptable (easy future modification, wide corridors and doors, level access, well-designed bathroom layouts). This should not be a one-off standard but a design framework that remains affordable across schemes.
  - Embed aging-in-place and adaptable design across all tenures, not just specialist schemes, so families and individuals can stay in their homes as needs evolve.
  - Simplify and accelerate approvals for specialist housing projects (accessible, adaptable, supported housing and student key-worker schemes) through a fast-tracked planning route with clear performance targets.
  - Ensure compliance with quality standards for space, light, acoustic comfort and energy efficiency, so homes remain fit for purpose for decades.

- Targeted funding and viability models for specialist housing
  - Create ring-fenced capital funding for specialist affordable housing—accessible, adaptable, older-person and supported housing—paired with revenue support to make schemes viable near places people work and train.
  - Support retrofit programmes to convert existing blocks into wheelchair-accessible and adaptable units where viable, particularly in towns and rural market towns where land is scarce.
  - Promote delivery models that combine housing with on-site or near-site care and support services (housing with care, community hubs, or co-located health and social care facilities) to ensure residents can age in place and maintain independence.

- Land release, infrastructure and collaboration
  - Make public land available explicitly for specialist affordable housing and ensure infrastructure (transport, healthcare, schools, childcare) is in place or planned in step with delivery.
  - Strengthen partnerships between local authorities, housing associations, universities and NHS providers to pipeline schemes, including student key-worker accommodation and care-enabled options on or near campus and work sites.
  - Encourage modular, prefab and adaptable construction methods to reduce build time and costs while maintaining quality, with long-term warranties and aftercare.

- Rural and cultural tailoring
  - Policies should recognise rural needs: smaller but accessible units near services, good transport links to workplaces and campuses, and land-use policies that allow for rural exceptions sites where accessibility features are built in from the start.
  - Design and delivery must be culturally responsive: homes and neighbourhoods should reflect diverse family structures, languages, and community preferences; include community liaison roles and translation support where needed.
  - Transport arrangements and digital connectivity must be integral to schemes so residents can access education, employment and care without excessive travel.

- Student key-worker housing
  - Develop and fund student key-worker housing near universities, hospitals and other essential sites to relieve pressure on general student accommodation while supporting the retention of NHS staff, teachers and carers in local communities.
  - Offer flexible, affordable lease structures and access to rent subsidies or approved private sector energy standards to ensure cost remains manageable for those on lower incomes.

- Monitoring and accountability
  - Local authorities should publish annual data on the supply of accessible and adaptable homes by scheme, tenancy type and time-to-completion, plus resident satisfaction and maintenance metrics.
  - Independent appraisal of the performance and health outcomes of specialist housing to ensure schemes are delivering genuine benefits and value for money.

Evidence from our work supports these priorities. In a pilot programme with a local council, we helped convert a vacant block into three wheelchair-accessible flats with on-site storage and level thresholds. Occupancy occurred within six weeks of completion, and residents reported greater independence and reduced reliance on costly short-term care. In rural settings, where market housing is scarce, early delivery of adaptable homes tied to care-on-site services reduced out-migration and kept households connected to schools and work. Finally, a university town with a proposed student key-worker block demonstrated that proximity to hospital trusts and campus facilities substantially lowered transport-related expenses for low-income staff and students, while improving turnout for part-time shifts and study commitments.

Taken together, these reforms would not only increase the quantity of homes but also improve the quality of housing for people with changing needs, reduce the long-term care burden, and support cohesive, diverse communities. We urge policymakers to implement a holistic package that prioritises accessibility and care alongside affordability, backed by robust funding, clear delivery timelines and transparent monitoring. We would be glad to participate further in shaping pilots and the design of these schemes across different local contexts.

Thank you for inviting a response on how to increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes. Our organisation works with local authorities, housing associations, and community groups across England, so we see a spectrum of need—from dense urban areas to rural communities—and a variety of housing demands. In shaping reforms, we favour approaches that can unlock supply while protecting quality, supporting vulnerable groups, and giving councils the tools to plan strategically for the next decade.

First, reforming the planning and land-release system is essential. We need a clearer route to bring suitable land forward, with a strong emphasis on brownfield sites and small-scale sites that are realistically deliverable. A targeted planning framework could mandate a higher proportion of affordable homes on larger developments and streamline consent processes—without diluting quality standards. Local authorities should be empowered to use a fast-track, locally tailored tariff or levy model that funds new affordable rent homes and enables cross-subsidy for infrastructure. We appreciate pilots that test 20–30% affordable provision on suitable sites, with clear benchmarks and sunset clauses so developers are not priced out of the market over the longer term. Crucially, any reforms should be designed to reduce delays caused by lengthy viability assessments and to provide predictable outcomes so builders and housing associations can plan multi-year programmes.

Second, we should pair supply reforms with affordability protections that are evidence-based and temporarily scoped. Rent caps or stabilisation schemes can help households in the short term, but they carry real risks to investment and landlord engagement if they are too blunt or long-lasting. We support carefully designed pilots that are CPI-linked, time-limited, and accompanied by robust evaluation—with measures such as how many homes are brought forward, changes in rent levels over time, maintenance quality, and the rate of landlord exits. Any cap should be accompanied by guarantees that supply will not contract, including transition arrangements for existing tenants and a plan to scale-up new affordable homes to match demand.

Third, a strong emphasis on quality and adaptability is essential. Every new affordable home should be designed to last, with accessible and adaptable features by default. We support mandatory M4(2) and M4(3) standards where possible, with tiered targets to ensure that a meaningful share of homes is wheelchair-accessible and adaptable as needs evolve. This should apply across affordable rent, social rent, and disability-inclusive schemes. In practice, this means planning for lifetime homes, accessible entrances, non-slip surfaces, and smart design that allows easy adaptation for aging residents or carers on site.

Fourth, specific housing types must match demographic and geographic needs. We need more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes; more older-person and supported housing with on-site care where desired; and more student-key-worker accommodation near hospitals and universities to relieve pressure on general housing stock. In rural areas, community-led and self-build initiatives can unlock plots that larger developers overlook, provided there is strong local planning support and funding. We should promote modular and off-site construction to shorten build times and improve quality, while ensuring long-term maintenance is funded and managed well.

Fifth, funding and delivery models must be durable and transparent. Long-term funding streams, capital Grants for affordable homes, and reform of Section 106/2-for-1 planning contributions (where appropriate) should be aligned with local need assessments. Ring-fenced land, public-owned assets, and partnerships with housing associations can de-risk schemes and accelerate delivery. It is important that pilots are accompanied by independent evaluation and that successful models are rolled out with appropriate adjustments for different local contexts.

Finally, governance, data, and accountability matter. Local authorities should have access to clear policy guidance, standardised design specifications, and strong monitoring frameworks to track supply, quality, affordability, and resident satisfaction. We advocate a phased approach—pilot, evaluate, refine, and scale—so reforms can adapt to lessons learned. 

Overall, we can increase supply by coupling planning reform with quality standards and targeted, evidence-based affordability measures, while ensuring housing for older people, disabled residents, rural communities, and key-worker cohorts is not an afterthought but a core part of housing policy. We urge government to proceed with cautious, data-led pilots and to publish results openly, so reforms deliver both more homes and better homes that communities can be proud of.

Living in England and facing the reality of housing costs with friends and family, I believe reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with real transparency and binding obligations is essential to delivering affordable, good‑quality homes in my area. If developers know there will be enforceable on‑site affordable housing and guaranteed funding for infrastructure, we’ll actually see a tangible mix of homes rather than promises that never materialise.

I’d want: 1) a clear, locally appropriate affordable housing target within each planning consent, with strict deadlines and penalties for non‑delivery; 2) a strong on‑site requirement where feasible, ensuring a true mix of affordable rent and shared ownership rather than relying on off‑site contributions or cash in lieu; 3) independently assessed, published viability testing with accessible explanations of how figures are reached, and the right to challenge dubious assessments; 4) CIL funds ring‑fenced for local infrastructure and affordable homes, with transparent reporting on how money is spent and what outcomes are achieved.

In our town, infrastructure gaps—traffic, school places, GP capacity—can stall otherwise welcome new homes. With stronger, enforceable S106/CIL rules and open viability testing, new developments would better support communities, delivering affordable homes alongside the infrastructure we need for a good quality, sustainable place to live.

Living in Scotland, I see two consistent pressures shaping our housing market: a real shortage of affordable, good-quality homes and households facing higher energy bills in cold winters. I want reforms that combine ambitious energy standards, practical support for local builders, and sustained public investment in social housing so that affordable homes come with lower running costs and better long-term quality. The reforms below are what I think would move the needle most effectively in my area.

First, raise energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits across the board. A fabric-first approach for all new homes—clear, performance-based targets for insulation, airtightness, and efficient heating systems—would protect tenants from escalating bills while cutting carbon. In practice, that means net-zero-ready or lower-operational-cost standards, with mandatory heat pumps or heat networks where appropriate, plus robust building commissioning to ensure homes perform as designed. For existing stock, establish a dedicated retrofit fund focused on social housing and private-rented stock, prioritising blocks and estates with high fuel-poverty risk. The aim should be measurable bill reductions and warmer homes, not just ticking boxes. In our area, when a council-led retrofit project upgraded insulation and introduced efficient boilers in a block, tenants reported warmer flats and noticeably lower energy bills over the winter. Scaling that up would make new and existing homes genuinely affordable to run, which is essential if we’re to attract and retain residents in towns and communities facing depopulation.

Second, ensure finance, procurement access, and planning support are targeted at SME and local builders. Large regional firms often win big contracts, pushing small local firms out of contention and reducing local job opportunities. A targeted finance package for SMEs, streamlined procurement with local supplier quotas, and a “small-sites policy” that reserves a proportion of public land and public-funded developments for local builders would help diversify supply and keep building jobs closer to home. Planning support should include a one-stop pre-application service, faster decisions for small sites (under, say, 20 units), and guidance that simplifies conditions where appropriate. In practice, a small site on a former high street site near my neighbourhood could deliver 8–12 genuinely affordable homes if the local builder could access finance and navigate planning quickly; with some planning clarity and land access, this would become a real, deliverable pipeline rather than a dream.

Third, commit major public investment to council and housing association programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes. A stable, long-term pipeline of social housing is the backbone of affordable supply for low-income households and makes sense for tenants and for communities. This means predictable funding over 10–15 years, ring-fenced for new build and for the management and maintenance of existing stock, and ambitious targets for new social rent homes alongside energy-efficient design. In our area, the long waiting list for social rented homes underscores the need for a robust expansion programme, not just piecemeal projects. Modern methods of construction can speed up delivery while maintaining quality, and building to high energy standards in these homes will keep running costs affordable for tenants for decades. Local authorities, in partnership with housing associations, should have a clear, citizen-informed process to decide what mix of social rent, affordable rent, and other genuinely affordable options best meet local needs.

Finally, these reforms must be pursued together with strong community engagement and local learning. Put tenants at the centre of planning decisions, ensure access to training for local workers, and monitor impact on fuel poverty as well as on carbon reductions. Scotland has a strong track record of community-focused housing initiatives; if we amplify energy efficiency, empower SME builders, and back long-term council and housing association programmes, we can deliver more affordable homes that are cheaper to run, better for the climate, and stronger for local economies.

In short: higher energy standards and funded retrofit, targeted SME-friendly finance and planning support, plus big, stable public investment in social housing. If these reforms are implemented in concert, we’ll unlock a larger, more diverse local housing supply that remains affordable in the long term and kinder to tenants’ energy bills.

I strongly disagree that the reforms should prioritise relaxing landlord regulation or watering down enforcement as a quick fix to housing supply. Without robust licensing, clear minimum quality standards and regular inspections, any increase in supply will produce a lot of tired, poor-quality homes that tenants cannot live in. We need longer tenancies, yes, but not at the expense of safe, well-maintained homes; those protections should be matched by decent enforcement and viable options for genuine landlords, so small landlords aren’t pushed out of the market by disproportionate costs.

Reform of Section 106, CIL and viability testing also must be about transparency and enforceable obligations, not loopholes. Money collected should reliably fund on‑site affordable homes and essential infrastructure, with binding delivery timelines and penalties for non-delivery. Viability assessments should be independent, open to scrutiny, and subject to mandatory delivery targets before planning is approved.

In our area I’ve seen a large development promise 40% affordable units, but delivery has stalled and several units ended up off‑site or reduced in quality. Strengthening the conditions attached to planning gains, ensuring on‑site delivery where possible, and publishing delivery data would give tenants confidence and incentivise genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes rather than empty promises.

I live in England and I want to see more affordable, high‑quality homes in my area. I strongly support reforms that improve local data, monitoring and accountability, and that properly fund council planning, enforcement and delivery capacity so commitments are delivered. In my town a major development was granted outline consent with a stated 40% affordable share, but progress has stalled for years. There’s little public data on the current pipeline or milestone delivery, so residents can’t tell whether obligations are being met. A transparent local delivery dashboard, updated quarterly, would help everyone see permissions, starts on site, completions and the affordable units delivered, plus performance by the developers. Key reforms include: 1) binding delivery plans in Section 106 agreements with firm milestones and penalties; performance bonds to secure delivery if schemes stall; 2) extra funding for planning departments, case officers and enforcement teams, plus digital tools to track applications and enforcement actions; 3) faster enforcement when developers miss milestones and timely viability reviews; 4) closer collaboration between councils, housing associations and infrastructure providers to unlock sites. With stronger data and capacity, councils can hold developers to account and ensure promised homes are built, at genuinely affordable prices and well designed.

absolutely agree. Improve local data, monitoring and developer accountability, and fund council planning and enforcement to ensure delivery; plus major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable social rent homes!

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I’m wary of reforms that push housing numbers up without making sure the places we actually live in have the services to support them. In my view, the single most important reform is to make infrastructure and services a condition of housing delivery, not an afterthought. That means funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or even prior to new homes, so that new communities are ready to live in from day one rather than years later.

Why this matters here and now
- In practice, estates can come with a large price if people can’t get a school place, a GP appointment, or reliable buses. It’s not just an inconvenience; it affects affordability because people are forced to own more cars, spend more on travel, or move away when services can’t meet demand.
- I’ve seen new developments nearby where the roads and bus routes were promised later, while the primary school intake and GP capacity were already stretched. When critical infrastructure is delayed, households end up paying more long term for commutes, for private transport, or for private health care, which undermines the very idea of affordable, good-quality homes.
- Utilities capacity is another bottleneck. Even when homes look affordable on the price tag, a lack of reliable broadband, water pressure, or power capacity can make living there expensive and stressful. That diminishes the perceived and real value of new housing and risks leaving residents with a poor quality of life.

What reforms would make a real difference
- Infrastructure-led planning: require developers to fund and deliver transport, schools, healthcare facilities and utilities in a clear, phased plan that runs in parallel with housing delivery. Housing should not be occupied in large numbers until the critical services and infrastructure are in place.
- Enforceable timelines and milestones: planning approvals should come with binding delivery schedules for key infrastructure. If milestones aren’t met, housing occupation should be paused or rephased until services are delivered. This protects buyers, renters, and the wider community.
- Reform planning obligations to prioritise early infrastructure: strengthen the use and predictability of Section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) so money is ring-fenced for early-stage transport upgrades, school expansions, and healthcare capacity before or at the outset of new housing completions.
- Early and integrated transport investment: improvements to bus corridors, rail links, cycling networks and pedestrian access should be funded upfront. New housing should be accompanied by reliable, affordable public transport options that reduce car dependency and local congestion.
- Healthcare and education readiness: ensure capacity planning is built into the development brief. That means new or expanded GP practices, clinics, and schools with clear timetables tied to housing phases, not after residents have moved in and the system is already stretched.
- Utilities and digital inclusion: plan for upgraded water/sewerage capacity, electricity grid resilience, and high-speed broadband as a condition of planning consent, with works sequenced to match occupancy. Without this, “affordable” homes can become unliveable in practice due to outages, slow internet, or water pressure issues.
- Design for sustainability and quality: require high-quality, adaptable design and climate resilience in tandem with infrastructure. A service-ready community should also offer affordable, accessible homes that are well-connected to amenities and public spaces.
- Brownfield first, with local gains: prioritise existing brownfield sites and ensure any expansion on greenfield land comes with proportionate infrastructure guarantees. Local communities should see the benefits in the form of upgraded transport and services, not just more houses.
- Local accountability and community benefits: mandate community benefits agreements that include local job opportunities in the construction phase and ongoing service provisions, so the local economy and workforce can grow alongside new homes.

Illustrative example
In a nearby development, housing was approved with promised road and bus improvements and a new school in a future phase. The housing was completed, but the bus service rollout lagged, the primary school expansion was delayed by years, and GP capacity remained tight. Residents ended up commuting longer, paying more for travel, and feeling alienated from the town centre. If infrastructure and services had been funded and scheduled alongside housing, that first phase could have been genuinely affordable in practice and a better place to live from the outset.

Bottom line
We need a reform package that makes infrastructure and service readiness a core part of housing policy. Supply is essential, but not at the expense of what makes a place liveable and affordable. An infrastructure-led, phased approach would deliver not just more homes, but better homes in places where people can actually afford to live, and where schools, clinics, transport, and utilities work in harmony with the new communities.

I urge policymakers to guard against purely accelerating numbers of homes and to commit to this service-ready framework as a condition of all substantial housing schemes.

Public investment in council and housing association building programmes is the only credible way to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rents for low‑income households. In our area, waiting lists remain long, overcrowding persists and private rents rise faster than wages. We therefore urge reforms: - Sustained, ring-fenced capital funding to councils and housing associations to plan and build at scale, with access to public land and streamlined procurement. - Planning reform: fast-track approvals for social housing, with local targets and firm nomination rights to ensure allocations go to those in housing need. - Use modern methods of construction and strict energy efficiency standards to deliver durable, low-cost homes, faster. - Rents set at social levels tied to local incomes, with protections from rent shocks and clear governance to keep homes affordable. - Robust oversight by Homes England and local authorities to ensure value for money and high build quality. These steps would reduce homelessness, alleviate overcrowding and create resilient communities.

I strongly support reforms to increase affordable, good‑quality homes by releasing surplus public land and capturing the uplift in land value created by planning decisions through levies or taxes. Releasing council and other public land would lower land costs and speed up development, particularly if a meaningful share is ring‑fenced for affordable housing and local infrastructure. In my area there are several unused council‑owned sites that could deliver genuinely affordable homes for local families and for older residents who need to downsize but stay in the community. To fund the necessary services, levies or taxes should be used to capture planning gains—via Community Infrastructure Levy and appropriate section 106 contributions—so improvements to roads, GP capacity, schools and green space follow new homes. This approach helps ensure high design and energy efficiency standards, with accessible layouts for an ageing population. If the public sector leads on land release and ensures transparent use of uplift funds, it will reduce land costs, accelerate delivery, and strengthen local services for generations to come.

Disagree: Relying on market-led expansion risks affordability gaps and variable quality. We should push purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure with strong affordability covenants and professional management, but only alongside stricter planning timelines, robust local data, and enforceable delivery duties by councils.

Agree. In Wales, the main barrier to more affordable, good-quality homes is the slow, fragmented planning process. If we streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while keeping environmental safeguards, we can accelerate delivery and reduce developer uncertainty, which should translate into more affordable homes for local families. In my area, a small proposal for eight affordable houses dragged on because of multiple rounds of pre-application checks and consulting bodies. A single digital planning portal with clear, statutory deadlines for each stage would help developers plan and commit without endless delays. A one-stop pre-application advice service could iron out design issues early, cutting costly revisions later.

I’d support a standardised Welsh framework for affordable housing contributions that scales with project size and is linked to robust environmental protections, not a blanket veto. Keeping protections for green spaces and wildlife is essential, but predictable, streamlined rules will encourage small and medium builders to bring forward well-designed homes. If done right, these reforms would boost supply, improve quality, and help more families in Wales afford a good home.

Agree. The reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area are a dual approach: tighten and modernise the private rented sector, and back community‑led and modern construction models. First, strengthen licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards for private rental homes, with clear safety and decency requirements and regular inspections. Encourage longer tenancies to give families stability, while offering sensible protections for small landlords—phased implementation, simple compliance rules, and targeted support for essential repairs. This will raise standards in the current stock and reduce costly churn for tenants. Second, back community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build groups and modern methods of construction to unlock land quickly and deliver affordable, high‑quality homes. In our area, a local CLT on a disused site could deliver 20–30 homes within a couple of years, and MMC prefab housing could cut build times and improve energy efficiency. Combine this with planning reforms to prioritise brownfield land and provide faster consents, plus funding routes that share risk with communities. A diversified mix would provide secure, affordable homes while protecting landlord viability.

I strongly support reforms to get affordable, good‑quality homes built more quickly in our area, while keeping strong environmental safeguards. In practice, planning and decision timelines in Northern Ireland can be slow and uncertain, which discourages local builders and housing associations from bringing sites forward. Streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines with clear, published criteria would reduce wasted time and developer uncertainty, helping to bring brownfield and underused sites into use without weakening protections for countryside and wildlife. 

I also welcome practical routes like community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, and self‑build, alongside modern methods of construction such as modular or off‑site manufacture. These approaches can deliver genuinely affordable homes more rapidly and with higher energy efficiency, easing bills for older residents. In my area, I’ve seen neighbours struggle to downsize because suitable, affordable options are scarce; community‑led models can keep homes within communities and ensure long‑term affordability. 

If these reforms are paired with predictable funding and clear milestones, we could accelerate delivery of good‑quality homes that meet local needs, support neighbourhoods, and help people stay in their communities as they age.

To increase affordable, good‑quality homes in our area, I think a balanced mix of options would work best. Purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management can help sustain long‑term rental supply while maintaining standards. In our borough there are BTR proposals with 15–20% genuinely affordable units and on‑site maintenance commitments, which reduces the frequent turnover and neglect seen in some private blocks. The crucial factor is robust, transparent covenants and a duty to keep rents within reach of local families.

I also support community‑led models such as community land trusts and co‑operatives, plus self‑build and modern methods of construction. These approaches can deliver high‑quality homes more quickly and keep local control over pricing and design, provided there is viable funding and land supply and strong local management to sustain maintenance.

Lastly, continuing, long‑term public investment in council and housing association building programmes remains essential to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. That requires reliable funding, predictable delivery timelines, and high design and energy efficiency standards to prevent high running costs over time.

Taken together, a coordinated portfolio approach with rigorous governance and monitoring would be most effective in boosting supply while protecting affordability and local character.

To increase affordable, good‑quality homes in my area, I would prioritise reforms that ensure infrastructure keeps pace with housing. I support requiring funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing is released for occupation. Without these service‑ready conditions, new estates quickly create congestion, stretched GP capacity and underperforming schools, undermining sustainability and affordability. I would back a ring‑fenced infrastructure fund or adaptive finance that unlocks in stages aligned to site completion, with independent delivery bodies to monitor milestones. For SMEs and local builders, targeted finance, easier procurement routes and planning support are crucial to unlock small sites. Simple access to affordable finance, devolved planning powers, and a clear pipeline for small, local sites would diversify supply and encourage price competition. In my area, a roughly 150‑home scheme stalled by lack of bus service upgrades and a hospital expansion not yet funded shows why service readiness should precede or accompany housing. A Local Plan framework that ties infrastructure sequencing to SME‑friendly procurement would help deliver genuinely affordable homes with good quality standards, not just more units.

From where I stand in England, trying to find a place that’s affordable near where I study or work, I don’t think simply listing reforms like community land trusts, co-operatives, self-build and modern methods of construction will automatically deliver the affordable, good‑quality homes my area needs, fast. They’re worth considering, but they’re not a magic fix and they won’t reliably resolve the housing problem on a practical, local level without a lot of extra support and reform.

Here’s why I’m sceptical about relying on those reforms alone to shift the supply quickly:

- Land and cost barriers stay stubborn. Community land trusts and co‑ops can help households influence the price and governance of housing, but they need access to land at a price that makes sense for long‑term affordability. In practice, land costs and competition from private developers are still the main obstacle. If public land is released for these models but at the same time land prices rise elsewhere, the net effect on supply and price is uncertain.
- Planning and regulations slow things down. Even with fast‑tracked processes for modular builds, we still face lengthy planning consent, local opposition, and complex procurement rules. In my area, projects have stalled for years over design approvals or disagreements about land use. Without a streamlined, consistent national approach to planning for community‑led housing and modular builds, the promised speed remains illusory.
- Financing and capacity matter. Self‑build and co‑ops require people who can fund, manage and oversee construction, plus skilled trades. There aren’t enough local builders trained in modern methods, and access to affordable finance for self‑build schemes is patchy. That means even good ideas may delivered as small, scattered sites rather than a big leap in supply. If the system relies on volunteer committees and niche co‑ops, progress is uneven and slow.
- Quality and long‑term maintenance can be overlooked in the rush for speed. Modern methods of construction have potential to produce efficient, high‑quality homes, but only if there are strong quality controls, robust supply chains, and ongoing maintenance funding. If these conditions aren’t in place, we risk cheap options that don’t stand up to wear and the test of time.

That said, there are ways that these approaches could contribute meaningfully, but only as part of a broader, faster‑acting package:

- Unlock and prioritise public land for community‑led housing with simple, fast planning routes and upfront funding for initial costs. A clear, cross‑government pipeline that guarantees land supply for CLTs and co‑ops would help them scale beyond pilot sites.
- Allow modular and modern construction to feed into a national pipeline. A government procurement push, with pre‑approved designs, bulk orders, and guarantees on quality, could bring down costs and speed up delivery while keeping high standards on energy efficiency and durability.
- Lower barriers for small builders and self‑build projects. Streamlined planning for small‑scale, well‑designed plots, starter plots set aside for first‑timers, and access to affordable land and finance would help these routes scale more quickly than large, conventional developments.
- Align incentives to protect first‑time buyers and renters. If reforms focus too much on supply without protecting those who can’t buy, the gains will be hollow. We need affordable rents, longer secure tenancies, and options like shared equity or rent‑to‑own linked to genuinely affordable pricing.
- Build capacity and governance. Community models work well where there’s strong local leadership and professional oversight. Providing training, professional guidance, and ongoing management support will help these schemes stay viable and maintain quality.

In short, I think these reforms should be supported, but only as part of a coordinated strategy that also tackles land pricing, planning bottlenecks, financing, and ongoing maintenance. If the government truly wants to increase affordable, good‑quality homes quickly, it needs to couple these approaches with a rapid‑release land program, streamlined planning, and a robust pipeline for modern construction that guarantees price stability and quality from the start. As a young person trying to plan a future, I want to see concrete timelines and measurable targets, not just well‑meaning ideas that take years to translate into homes on the ground.

To increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area, reforms should combine speed with safeguards. Firstly, streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines but retain environmental protections and local influence. Establish clear statutory milestones for applications and a maximum decision window (e.g., 12–16 weeks for straightforward proposals), plus a digital, single‑point submission system and mandatory pre‑application engagement to help small builders and community groups. 

Secondly, require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing. In our town, a sizeable development was delayed because there was no commitment on a new primary place or bus links. A plan that ties infrastructure funding to development footprints, with enforceable delivery schedules, would deliver sustainable communities and avoid “fit‑and‑forget” estates that strain services.

Thirdly, mandate higher energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits to reduce bills and meet climate targets. Set ambitious EPC targets and create a dedicated retrofit fund for social and private rented housing so tenants don’t bear disproportionate energy costs during transition. In practice, higher standards now could be funded by efficiency savings over the life of the homes, offsetting upfront costs.

I believe reforming housing policy to back community-led models alongside well-managed Build-to-Rent would genuinely increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Encouraging community land trusts and housing co‑operatives, plus allowing more self‑build using modern methods of construction, would bring new homes in a way that prioritises long‑term affordability and good standards. I’ve seen a small CLT in our county secure land and deliver designed, affordable homes for local families, with the profits reinvested locally. Co‑operatives can give residents a real stake and help keep running costs predictable. 

On renting, purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management would stabilise rents and raise maintenance standards over time. For someone like me, who wishes to stay near community services, well‑managed BTR near shops and transport is a real asset and helps retain community cohesion.

Proposed reforms: faster planning routes for MMC and modular homes; release public land on long leases to CLTs and co‑ops; grants or low‑interest loans to support self‑build; require affordability covenants in large developments and establish a clear register of professionally managed BTR stock to guarantee quality.

From my experience in England, the quickest way to increase genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes is not simply to speed up planning, but to empower communities. I back community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build projects, and modern methods of construction such as modular timber and off‑site manufacture because they deliver affordable homes that stay affordable and maintain local character. Releasing surplus public land helps, but only if it’s made available on long‑term ground leases and the uplift in land value is captured through levies or taxes to fund affordable housing and essential local infrastructure. That approach avoids inflating land prices and supports genuinely affordable, well‑built homes for local people. Planning reform should streamline processes and decision timelines, but with strong environmental safeguards and real local involvement to prevent poor quality or speculative schemes. If councils can offer land to a CLT or housing co‑op at fair terms and apply a land‑value uplift levy, we’ll see faster delivery of affordable homes that actually last the test of time.

To increase affordable, good-quality homes, reforms should be paired with funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure new communities are sustainable from day one. I support reforms that stimulate faster, more affordable development, but only if there are credible delivery plans for essential services that households can actually access. Front-loaded or clearly ring-fenced funding for infrastructure—not just promises—would keep new estates from becoming car-dependent or service-deserted. Mechanisms could include upfront developer contributions directed to early phases, and a government-backed infrastructure fund that unlocks schemes when delivery milestones are met by councils and builders.

In practice, if a large estate is planned near my town, we’d need a new bus corridor or rail improvements, a primary school and a GP practice with capacity before occupiers move in, plus upgrades to water and energy capacity and climate-smart building standards. I’ve seen proposals approved without enough school places or transport, which creates long commutes and strain on services and ultimately harms affordability and quality of life.

Overall, I’d back reform aimed at boosting supply, provided there are robust, transparent plans and guarantees that services are funded and delivered in parallel with housing—otherwise targets risk becoming hollow.”

Agree. Improve local data, monitoring, and developer accountability, and strengthen planning enforcement and delivery capacity. Release surplus public land and capture planning uplift via levies to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. Pilot rent caps to raise affordability while evaluating risks.

I disagree with approaches that push housing numbers up without making sure the services to support them are ready. Reforms must require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure sustainable, service-ready new communities. If infrastructure is after the homes, residents face long commutes, stretched GP surgeries and schools, and overburdened water and power networks, which quickly makes affordable living untenable and undermines the purpose of new homes.

From my experience in England, a large estate was approved, yet a new primary school and extra clinic capacity were delayed for years. Parents and patients had to travel further, local buses were cut or overcrowded, and the whole area felt less affordable because you carry hidden costs—time, travel, stress. The only way to truly increase supply that remains affordable is to link it to upfront or well-timed infrastructure delivery and robust funding mechanisms.

I would back reforms that empower local authorities to require developers to fund and deliver enabling infrastructure in clear phased milestones tied to planning permission, and to secure long-term provision of roads, public transport, schools, clinics, and utility upgrades before or alongside housing. Only then will new homes be genuinely affordable and sustainable for communities.

Agree. To increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area, reforms should both raise the energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits of existing stock. When homes are built to high fabric‑first standards (strong insulation, airtightness, efficient glazing) running costs stay low, making rents more affordable and helping developers meet demand in a price‑sensitive market. A dedicated retrofit fund—with grants and low‑interest loans—should target private landlords and social housing, covering insulation, heat pumps and efficient boilers. This front‑loads improvements so bills fall in the long term and reduces the risk of tenants being hit by energy price spikes. In my experience, a block I rent in benefited from insulation and window upgrades funded by a local retrofit program; the bills dropped and the home felt much more comfortable. To scale this, planning for energy‑efficient schemes should be streamlined, energy performance standards should be the default for new builds (aiming for EPC A/B), and landlords should have clear, simple requirements to upgrade when tenancies change hands. Importantly, accompanying support must shield tenants and small landlords from upfront costs.

Reforms that would increase supply are hard to pick. In our Welsh town, people are worried about affordable homes near work and schools. Some say relax planning rules to speed up building, but I’m not sure that would help if it comes with worse quality or bigger costs later. I think a mix is needed: support for small local builders to take on affordable homes on brownfield sites, with clear expectations on energy efficiency and quality so new homes stay comfy and cheap to run. More social housing or shared ownership schemes tied to local incomes could keep homes affordable in the long term, not just for the first year. I’d also like to see money used to bring empty homes back into use and to upgrade existing stock so renters aren’t stuck in damp flats. Ultimately, reforms must come with strong infrastructure planning and guarantees about upkeep, so we’re not trading one shortage for another.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. As an organisation representing older residents in a small town in England, we see housing affordability closely linked to our daily quality of life. While new homes are welcome, many of our older neighbours live in Victorian terraces that are damp, poorly insulated and costly to heat, which consumes a larger slice of fixed pensions. Any reforms that increase supply should also guarantee energy efficiency and accessibility, so homes are affordable to run and suitable for ageing occupants. We hear from residents who cannot move because available properties are not suitable—stairs, no downstairs bathrooms, or no nearby transport links to shops and clinics. In our experience, planning delays, slow repairs in social housing, and a lack of mixed communities hamper mobility and neighbourhood sustainability. It would help if reforms encouraged retrofitting existing stock alongside new builds, prioritised accessible design, and ensured new homes are well connected to essential services. In short, supply must come with practicality: warmth, accessibility, and proximity to care.

I want more affordable, good-quality homes, but I’m sceptical about reforms that simply push things through planning and leave communities behind. In practice, speeding up decisions can come at the cost of quality, sites being released without proper infrastructure, and housing that doesn’t stay affordable in the long term. Any reforms need to be tightly balanced with robust protections for the environment, local input, and genuine long-term affordability.

First, on planning reform. There’s sense in reducing needless delay for straightforward schemes that fit a local plan, but not if the process becomes a shortcut for developers at the expense of design quality and neighbourhood character. In my area, I’ve seen delays largely driven by fragmented decision-making between adjoining councils and lengthy pre-application negotiations that aren’t well coordinated. Faster timelines risk cutting corners on infrastructure planning (roads, drainage, schools, GP capacity) and on the assessment of environmental impacts. The result can be a wave of new homes that the local services can’t support and that people struggle to afford once rents and service charges are added in. The better approach would be to streamline where it truly helps, but with enforceable, binding deadlines and a dedicated, adequately resourced planning service that can deliver quality decisions. A single, well-governed pre-application process with clear criteria and timelines would reduce uncertainty for developers without sacrificing environmental safeguards or local accountability.

Second, Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes. I recognise the potential for long-term rental supply, but the affordability covenant and management structures matter as much as the number of units. In some recent BTR projects locally, headline rents looked “reasonable” until you add in management fees, service charges, and restrictive covenants that can lock people into tenancies for long periods. If BTR is to genuinely help locals, it must involve strong, lasting affordability requirements—ideally 40 years or more—with a clear mechanism for transfer to more affordable housing when incomes change over time. It also needs professional, transparent management that keeps repairs timely, maintains communal areas, and protects tenants’ rights. Otherwise, we risk creating upscale rental enclaves that don’t help the people who actually live nearby or make it easier for local workers to afford a home.

A practical way to deliver would be to require a meaningful share of affordable homes within BTR schemes, not relegated to periphery blocks or special permission after the market has shifted. I would push for a minimum of 25–40% of units to be genuinely affordable, with rents capped relative to local incomes and linked to CPI rather than market fluctuations. There should be independent monitoring, regular reporting on vacancies, and a right for tenants to participate in management decisions where appropriate. The long-term stewardship of these estates matters as much as the architecture, and poor management can poison a community’s sense of belonging much more quickly than a purely new-build volume would.

Beyond these two levers, I’d like to see reforms that actually expand genuinely affordable housing and reduce land-price-driven inflation. That means public investment in social and council housing, and more use of public land for affordable homes. It also means reforms to capture some of the uplift from land value for the public good—so a site isn’t released without a strong payment that funds affordable housing, schools, and roads alongside the new homes. Councils should be empowered to acquire and assemble land where needed, rather than letting market leakage push up prices on sites that are perfect for affordable housing.

Infrastructure must come first. Too many developments come with a promise of later upgrades that never materialise, or they arrive years after people move in. Any reform package should tie planning approvals to deliverable infrastructure plans and funding: schools, doctor’s surgeries, waste water capacity, transport links, and green spaces. Without that, more homes simply strain existing services and erode quality of life.

In short, faster planning can help, but not at the expense of environmental protections, local input, or long-term affordability. The reforms I’d back would mix targeted speed with strong design standards, enforceable affordability covenants in Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes, a serious push for social housing funded publicly, and funding conditions that lock in infrastructure alongside housing. If these safeguards aren’t guaranteed, speeding up housing delivery will merely swap one shortage for another: a quick pipeline of homes that don’t stay affordable or maintainable for the communities that need them most.

Yes, I support piloting rent caps to improve affordability while carefully monitoring effects on supply, investment, and landlord exit. I also back community land trusts, housing co-operatives, self-build and modern methods of construction to boost affordable, high-quality homes quickly.

i really think from where I live in Wales, the most effective way to increase affordable, good-quality homes is to direct finance to local SMEs, unlock small sites, and simplify planning while keeping quality standards. In practice, a Welsh Housing Finance Agency or ring-fenced funding for small to medium-sized builders would make loans and guarantees available with longer terms, reducing the risk of starting on a modest site. A neighbour's son, who runs a small builder firm, has shown how banks demand scale they simply do not have. Procurement access should reserve a share of public and social housing contracts for SMEs, and allow consortia of local builders. Too often public schemes reward larger firms with complex bidding, excluding genuine local capacity. Small-sites policy should enable development on 1-5 plot sites, with streamlined consent and targeted grants for initial infrastructure. Planning support must be practical: pre-application advice, clearer timelines, and a simple digital process. We must guard against compromising quality or planning for the environment; measures should include energy efficiency standards and local materials. If piloted well, these reforms could boost jobs and bring down rents in our communities!

i strongly believe from my experience living in England, the rental market in our town remains tight, with few long-term options for families. I support greater use of purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure developments with affordability covenants and professional management. When rents are predictable and repairs are timely, it changes how people plan their lives and makes neighbourhoods more stable. A nearby BTR scheme with on-site facilities and professional management has been a real asset, though too many schemes still lean towards short-term private lets.

I also think reform to Section 106, CIL and viability testing is needed, but must be credible and enforceable. Local authorities should see transparent viability models, with explicit obligations to deliver on-site affordable homes and targeted infrastructure funding. If a scheme cannot support full on-site affordable housing, there should be clear, time-bound alternatives or phased contributions, not optional add-ons. In my council area, promised affordable units have repeatedly slipped, undermining trust.

A dual approach — robust Build-to-Rent plus accountable viability reforms — could deliver more genuinely affordable, good-quality homes without stalling development. I would like to see published delivery plans, independent monitoring, and clear delivery timelines!
I'm not sure what reforms would really boost affordable, good-quality homes here. I doubt quick fixes; needs careful planning, but I can't see a clear path.

I’m responding from England, 25-34, as an individual who wants genuinely affordable, good-quality homes in my area. I don’t think the reforms that lean heavily on traditional, large-scale public building programmes are the fastest or fairest way to meet need. If the goal is to boost supply quickly and keep homes affordable in the long term, we should empower communities to lead delivery and use modern, proven tools that are already working in pockets of the country.

First, community land trusts have proven that land can be kept in community hands and used to deliver genuinely affordable housing with long-term stewardship. What I’ve heard from local groups is that CLTs can negotiate land at lower cost, secure long leases to residents, and embed strong resident governance that keeps rents affordable even when market conditions shift. The reform I’d want is to make it easier for CLTs to access publicly owned land, fast-track planning for community-led sites, and provide low-cost finance and technical support to get schemes from idea to completion. If a plot sits idle because a big developer is in purchase negotiations, a CLT can step in and deliver homes that remain affordable in perpetuity, rather than a one-off sale at market value.

Second, housing co-operatives offer stable, long-term affordability and a sense of local ownership that public-build programmes often miss. In practice, co-ops can keep control with residents, set rents on a cost-recovery basis, and ensure energy-efficient design through collective decision-making. To scale this, I’d press for reforms that simplify conversion of rented stock into co-ops, allow more flexible financing tailored to co-op models, and provide grants or low-interest loans to support initial conversion and ongoing management. In my view, the best outcomes come when residents share responsibility for maintenance and budgeting, creating homes that stay affordable for the long term rather than being subsumed into market cycles.

Third, self-build and modern methods of construction (MMC) should be front and centre in reform. If local groups can access serviced plots, design support, and transparent procurement routes, they can build faster, with higher quality and lower waste. MMC can reduce construction time, improve energy efficiency, and lower running costs for households. The reform I’d want is to simplify planning for self-build plots, provide clear guidance on technical standards, and fund training so people who aren’t traditional developers can participate. The government can also incentivise small builders and community groups to use modular or off-site construction where appropriate, while maintaining rigorous quality and safety controls.

I’m skeptical about relying predominantly on large public investments in council and housing association building programmes as the core route to affordability. Those schemes can be slow due to procurement cycles, budget delays, and complex oversight, and they sometimes prioritise volume over long-term affordability and resident voice. There’s a real risk that funds are tied up in project-by-project spend rather than creating a sustainable ecosystem of affordable housing. A mixed approach that prioritises community-led delivery, supported by targeted public assistance (land release, finance, and technical support), would likely deliver more affordable homes more quickly and keep them affordable for generations.

In practice, reforms should prioritise: land and planning levers that favour community-led delivery; access to finance and procurement routes that unlock CLTs, co-ops, and self-build groups; and strong emphasis on quality, energy efficiency, and long-term affordability. If we can shift some of the power and resources to people who will actually live in and maintain these homes, we’ll build a more resilient and affordable housing market in the medium term, not just a few more units delivered under a top-down programme.

I strongly support reforms that improve local data, monitoring and accountability, and fund council planning, enforcement and delivery capacity to ensure commitments are delivered. In our area there have been promises of affordable homes tied to new developments, but delivery has dragged on while rents rise. A clear, open data dashboard showing units planned, completed, under construction and in long-term management would let residents see progress and where delays occur.

We should tighten how planning obligations and affordable housing contributions are used, with ring-fenced funds and penalties for late completion, and a requirement that viable schemes still deliver a meaningful proportion of affordable homes. The council needs more planning staff and better digital tools to scrutinise viability, monitor progress and press for milestones. Early collaboration with housing associations and robust long-term management agreements will keep schemes affordable and well maintained.

Finally, ensure the homes built are genuinely affordable and good-quality—well insulated, energy-efficient, accessible, and well connected to transport and services. These reforms would bring more genuinely affordable homes sooner and in better condition.

England needs reforms that make it easier for small and local builders to deliver diverse, affordable, good‑quality homes, while making sure councils can plan, monitor and finish what they start. In my area, the shortage of affordable homes is real and long‑standing, and I’ve seen how big schemes can flood the market but not necessarily bring down prices for local people. A package that targets finance, procurement access, small‑sites policy and planning support, alongside stronger data and delivery accountability, could shift the balance in favour of SME builders who know local demand and can work quickly to fill gaps.

I live in Wales and am in my late 50s, responding as an individual who sees across my town how housing costs, quality and availability shape daily life. I strongly support the reforms to reform Section 106, CIL and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding. Delivering the right homes in the right places requires that the agreements attached to planning permissions reliably deliver affordable housing and essential infrastructure, not merely raise hopes. The following points explain why and how I think this can work in practice.

First, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing must be clear, enforceable and transparent. Planning obligations should be enforceable with set delivery milestones and penalties if delivery slips. I would like to see a requirement that a meaningful proportion of larger schemes are built on-site as affordable homes, with targets monitored and publicly reported by councils. Where on-site delivery is not viable in a given case, the policy should allow off-site contributions but only if there is a robust, auditable delivery plan for high-quality, affordable homes in the same area and within a defined timescale. Viability assessments should be independently checked, and the underlying assumptions published, so local residents can understand why a project is allowed to slip or needs adjustments. In practice, I’ve seen developments where promised affordable units didn’t appear on site; clearer rules and stronger monitoring would help communities see the benefit of growth rather than feel they lose out. During the next round of planning, I would support simpler, faster reporting of how much is being collected through CIL and where it is spent, including improvements to local roads, schools and green space, so residents can see the direct benefits.

Second, we should explore rent caps or stabilisation pilots to improve affordability while protecting supply. In parts of Wales the private rental market has become the main option for many households, and rapid rent rises can push families from towns with good services to more affordable but more distant areas. A limited, carefully evaluated set of pilots could help test whether rent caps linked to inflation or local affordability bands improve stability without deterring investment or forcing owners to withdraw from letting properties. Any such pilots should come with robust monitoring: impact on new build starts, existing stock turnover, maintenance standards and investment in energy efficiency. The aim is to create a supported, predictable market so younger families, key workers and older residents can plan their lives without fear of sudden rents doubling.

Third, we must deliver homes that match Wales’s demographic and rural needs. This means more wheelchair-accessible and adaptable homes, as well as supported and student key-worker housing. In my area there is a shortage of properties that can be easily adapted for wheelchair users or for households needing additional care, which becomes a barrier for independent living. I would like to see a requirement that new developments include a proportion of wheelchair-accessible units and adaptable layouts, with features like step-free access, wide doors, level thresholds and lift access where appropriate. For older residents and those who require support, purpose-built homes with on-site care and flexible communal spaces can make a big difference to wellbeing and independence. Similarly, we need housing tied to essential workers—nurses, teachers, carers—so they can live near the services they provide, reducing commute times and sustaining local economies. In rural communities, bilingual design, integration with local cultural networks and proximity to public transport should be standard, not an afterthought.

Taken together, these reforms would strengthen the link between planning permission and real, affordable homes, while ensuring the supply chain remains attractive to builders and investors. They would also help communities in Wales stay vibrant: younger families, older residents and key workers able to settle and stay near schools, clinics and jobs. I recognise the need for evidence from pilots and incremental reform, but the direction is right and delivers practical, tangible improvements for our housing market. I hope policymakers will adopt these principles with clear metrics, oversight and local accountability so we can all see real progress.

I’m responding on behalf of a youth-focused organisation in England, and I’m writing to voice a clear disagreement with relying mainly on large-scale council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes. Yes, social housing has a role, but in practice these programmes move slowly, are exposed to political cycles and budget changes, and too often fail to respond quickly to where housing pressure is most intense in our communities. In my area, people on the housing list wait years for a social rental, while private rentals—the main option for many young people—can be damp, poorly insulated and unaffordable.
