In my own town, I’ve seen scattered support housing proposals stall because they aren’t financially viable without guaranteed carr packages. A clearer funding framework and longer-term commitments would givee councils and housing associations the confidence to build now rather than later. Third, I’d welcome reforms that explicitl link student accommodation to key-worker housing—especiallyy around hospitals and university campuses where there’s a high demand from NHS trainees, social care students, and other essential workers. A pilot approach could reserve a portion of student blocks for key-workers in training with long tenancies or flexible leases that align withh placrment schedules. The spaces would be designed to be easily converte to other usess if demand shifts. This would reduce the scramble for affordable, well-located accommodation and help attract and retain the staff needed in local services. Rural and culturally diverse areas face particular hurdles. Reforms shouldd enable small sites, including rural exception sites and repurposed buildings, to navigate planning faster while maintaining design qualityy and community cohesion. That could mran allowing more modular construction on smaller plots, simplified planning checks for affordable housing with accessible features, and targeted funding for retrofit of older rural housing stock so existing homes can be made accessibl and energy-efficient rather than rebuilt entirely. Quality and cost must go hand in hand. The reforms I’dd support would requiree lifecycle costing to be considered, not just upfront build costs. Accessibility and adaptability add long-term value by reducing future retrofits and social care needs. They should also incentivise high energy efficiency and durable finishes to keep running costs down for households on lower incomes. In summary, I want reformss thatt (1) guarantee a meaningful minimum of accessible and adaptable homes in all new affordable schemes, (2) fund and enable genuinely supported housing to keep people independent and in their communities, (3) pilot flexible student-key worke housing tied to local health and education needs, and (4) tailor rural delivery to small sites and repurposed buildings while preserving community character. If we can align planning, funding, and design standards around these principles, we’ll see a steady growt in affordable, good-quality homes that truly meet the needs of diverse residents in both towns and villages.

Agree. Strengthening licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards, while promoting longer tenancies, is the most practical route to boosting the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. In practice, tenants face inconsistent conditions and unstable housing when enforcement is weak; we’ve heard from residents about damp and repair delays, and we know rogue landlords still operate where oversight is limited. A stronger licensing regime with a clear national register and mandatory checks every few years would weed out non‑compliant properties. Local authorities must have adequate funding to investigate, enforce and use penalties to fund further improvements. Minimum quality standards should cover essential repairs, fire safety and energy efficiency (MEES/EPC requirements), with swift remedies for breaches and proactive inspections of high‑risk lets. Longer tenancies should be supported to improve stability—three to five year contracts with limited, predictable rent increases within fixed terms would help families and workers plan. Importantly, reforms must protect small landlords: phased rollout, exemptions for those with small portfolios, practical guidance, and accessible grants or tax relief for necessary upgrades. Balancing these elements will lift quality and supply without driving viable landlords out of the market.

I STRONGLY SUPPORT REFORMS THAT WOULD INCREASE THE SUPPLY OF AFFORDABLE, GOOD-QUALITY HOMES IN SCOTLAND, AND I BELIEVE ENABLING COMMUNITY LAND TRUSTS, HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES, SELF-BUILD, AND MODERN METHODS OF CONSTRUCTION WILL DELIVER REAL PROGRESS QUICKLY. IN MY COUNCIL AREA WE HAVE VACANT PLOTS AND DERELICT TERRACES THAT COULD BE BROUGHT BACK INTO USE THROUGH A COMMUNITY LAND TRUST; GIVING LOCAL RESIDENTS LONG LEASES AND DEMOCRATIC CONTROL WOULD HELP PRICE HOMES DOWN WHILE PRESERVING AN AFFORDABLE, SOCIAL PURPOSE. HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES CAN PROVIDE STABLE RENTS AND ACTIVE RESIDENT GOVERNANCE, WHICH KEEPS MAINTENANCE STANDARDS HIGH AND OUTCOMES LOCALLY ACCOUNTABLE.

FOR SELF-BUILD AND MODERN METHODS OF CONSTRUCTION, IT WOULD HELP TO STREAMLINE PLANNING, OFFER SERVICED PLOTS, AND IMPROVE ACCESS TO AFFORDABLE FINANCE. THIS COULD UNLOCK MULTIPLE HOMES IN A FEW YEARS AND REDUCE DEPENDENCY ON TRADITIONAL BUILDING SITES. MODULAR AND TIMBER-FRAME SOLUTIONS CAN CUT BUILD TIMES, IMPROVE ENERGY EFFICIENCY, AND LOWER RUNNING COSTS FOR FAMILIES—CRUCIAL IN OUR CLIMATE. SCOTLAND COULD PILOT SMALL, SERVICED SELF-BUILD PLOTS LINKED TO COMMUNITY ENERGY SCHEMES AND SHARED FACILITIES, ENSURING QUALITY STAYS HIGH.

OVERALL, A POLICY FRAMEWORK THAT UNLOCKS LAND FOR CLTS, SUPPORTS CO-OPS, SMOOTHS SELF-BUILD PROCESSES, AND FUNDS MMC IS THE FASTEST ROUTE TO MORE AFFORDABLE, HIGH-QUALITY HOMES ACROSS COMMUNITIES IN SCOTLAND.

absolutely i strongly support reforms that streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while retaining environmental safeguards. In my area, uncertainty and lengthy negotiations inflate costs and slow the delivery of affordable, good-quality homes for families and retirees alike. Key steps should include: 1) fix clear national standards and a fast-track route for schemes that meet them, with decisions within a set period (for example 12 weeks for straightforward proposals). 2) move to a single consent point by upfront agreeing planning permission and affordable housing contributions (s106) so protracted negotiations don’t stall schemes. 3) speed up pre-application processes with time-bound consultations and a single digital portal to track progress. 4) prioritise brownfield land and simplify the redevelopment of derelict sites, while maintaining strong safeguards for flood risk, biodiversity and local character. 5) create predictable infrastructure funding with upfront pooled contributions and a simpler Community Infrastructure Levy regime. 6) ensure design quality and energy efficiency remain mandatory, with proportionate environmental checks to avoid repetitive delays.

In practice, a recent 30-unit affordable housing proposal in our area was held up for years over off-site contribution discussions. A capped decision timeline and upfront funding agreements could have delivered those homes much sooner, boosting local supply and keeping rents affordable for longer-tenured residents like myself and my neighbours!

To increase affordable, good‑quality homes in our area, I think reforms in four connected areas would help, though they need careful design and funding to work for local SMEs: targeted, patient finance for SME builders; easier access to public procurement; a strengthened small-sites planning route; and practical planning support for councils. A not‑for‑profit or government-backed facility offering low‑cost, long‑term finance for land purchase and delivery milestones would reduce the upfront risk for local builders. Terms tied to delivery, with some grants for affordable homes, and risk‑sharing guarantees could unlock schemes that larger developers overlook. We also need streamlined procurement: councils could reserve a share of pipeline work for SMEs, simplify pre‑qualification, and publish clear, long‑range delivery plans so local builders can bid with confidence. The small-sites policy should be expanded to include more brownfield plots under 1 hectare, with permission in principle and fast pre‑app guidance, plus viability support that properly reflects local affordability pressures. Finally, councils need better planning resource and predictable timelines—planning performance agreements with clear deadlines, and viability tests that recognise local housing need and construction costs. In our area, a 0.5ha site sits stalled despite planning permission because finance and procurement hurdles outweigh the gains from delivery; addressing these gaps could unlock real, locally rooted housing supply.

absolutely affordable, good‑quality homes in our area will not come from a single policy, but a mix of community-led and modern construction approaches. I’d support expanding community land trusts and housing co‑operatives, especially in fast‑growing towns, where long‑term affordability can be protected and local control preserved. Self‑build schemes and modern methods of construction (MMC) could speed delivery and raise quality, provided plots are accessible and costs are predictable. In Scotland, that means clear land-release mechanisms, planning efficiency, and funding that covers training, energy efficiency and maintenance.

On affordability directly, I’m cautious about rent caps. Pilots could help assess impact on supply and investment, as caps can deter landlords or reduce maintenance if not properly designed. I’d favour targeted, time‑limited pilots with robust monitoring, regional tailoring, and sunset clauses. Practical steps: public land released with community‑benefit agreements; grants or low‑interest loans for CLTs/co‑ops; planning reforms to accelerate MMC builds; and a dedicated evaluation framework.

As a 25–34‑year‑old renter, I want quicker progress in visible ways—more genuinely affordable homes near jobs and public transport, with good quality standards and energy efficiency!

I’m strongly supportive of reforms that increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes. In our area, the private rented sector can be a safety net, but too many properties fall below standard, and short-term lettings push families out of stable housing. Strengthening licensing and enforcement, raising minimum quality standards and promoting longer tenancies would raise safety and reduce churn. To protect small landlords, the approach should be proportionate: clear, simple compliance routes, with scalable enforcement and access to advice rather than punitive penalties that drive exits. In my street, a family has faced repeated rent increases and short tenancies, making it hard to stay in the area.

We also need better local data and accountability. Councils should publish up-to-date information on housing completions, stalled sites and developer delivery, with penalties or performance bonds for late schemes. Investing in planning and enforcement capacity will help commitments be delivered, particularly for affordable units attached to market schemes.

Lastly, rent stabilization could help affordability, but we should test it via pilots, with robust evaluation to avoid reducing investment or delivery. If pilots show positive balance, scale up gradually with guardrails to protect viable rental stock.

it's outrageous that as a resident of Scotland in my late fifties, I see a persistent gap between promises and delivery on affordable homes in my area. Reform should start with better local data and monitoring so we truly understand current need and capacity. At present, our council only recently began publishing a quarterly housing delivery dashboard; it shows a shortfall between affordable units promised in new developments and those actually completed, which makes it hard to hold developers or authorities to account.

I would support measures that strengthen accountability for developers and ensure councils have the capacity to plan, enforce and deliver. This could include binding delivery milestones, penalties for missed targets, and clearer reporting on on-site versus off-site contributions. Providing ring-fenced funding for planning and enforcement staff would help prevent delivery bottlenecks from eating into actual homes.

A practical step would be a local delivery partnership—bringing the council, housing associations and community bodies together early in the process to secure commitments up-front and track progress transparently. In short, better data, stronger oversight and funded planning capacity are essential to increase affordable, good-quality homes!

From where I live in England, the most effective reforms would be a practical mix of smarter design standards, local-led delivery, and faster construction methods, all tailored to our real needs: accessible homes for wheelchair users, adaptable homes for an ageing population, genuinely affordable options for first-time buyers and renters, plus targeted solutions for rural communities and culturally diverse areas.

First, we need homes that work for people from day one. Wheelchair-accessible and adaptable design should be the default, not an afterthought. In new sites, a meaningful share of affordable housing should be built to wheelchair-accessible standards (and easily adaptable for mobility aids as families’ needs change). That means wider doorways, step-free routes through living spaces, accessible bathrooms, adjustable kitchen layouts, and robust entry systems. In practice, I’d like to see a formal policy requiring a minimum proportion of each affordable development to meet M4(3) accessibility standards, with ongoing retrofit support for existing stock where feasible. We also need energy-efficient, low-maintenance homes that stay affordable long-term, so high-performance insulation and heat networks are part of every new build.

Second, reform the delivery models to expand capacity quickly without sacrificing quality. Community land trusts (CLTs), housing cooperatives, self-build groups, and modern methods of construction (MMC) offer routes to speed and ownership models that keep prices closer to local incomes. But these approaches need enabling policies and real capital support. Locally, land held by authorities or public bodies is often tied up; carving out land for CLTs or co-ops on a lease or below-market basis, with clear, simple transfer processes, would unlock a lot of supply. I’d push for a dedicated fund to seed CLTs and co-ops, with rapid-planning signs and streamlined procurement for MMC units. For self-build schemes, councils should be allowed to designate plots with straightforward planning routes, backed by a one-stop planning service and technical guidance on foundations, damp-proofing, and energy standards.

Modern Methods of Construction should be scaled up, especially in rural areas where transport costs can price traditional builds out of reach. A national MMC fund could support regional factories or modular hubs, create skilled jobs locally, and guarantee a pipeline of compliant, quality-controlled units. It’s not just about faster builds; it’s about consistent quality and long-term maintenance. Local authorities will need training and planning oversight aligned with MMC, plus procurement frameworks that prioritise durability, accessibility, and retrofit potential.

Third, planning and funding processes must stop being a bottleneck. We need faster, predictable decisions on developments that genuinely deliver affordable housing and meet accessibility criteria. Clear timeframes, consistent viability tests that prioritise social value over purely financial returns, and a requirement for affordable housing contributions that reflect local need (not just the cheapest option on offer) would help. Rural exception sites should be easier to release, with guarantees on long-term stewardship by communities or housing associations to avoid sites being lost to market delivery.

Fourth, target rural and culturally diverse areas with tailored approaches. Rural housing needs are not the same as urban demand: distance from services, schools, healthcare, and public transport must be factored into site feasibility. We should pilot mixed-use developments that include community space, care facilities, and culturally appropriate housing designs for different communities. This could involve simple, scalable adapted housing with local cultural features embedded in the design, rather than one-size-fits-all brick-and-plaster boxes.

Finally, the system should keep a close eye on outcomes. Councils and housing associations should report annually on accessibility features delivered, dwellings adapted or retrofitted, energy performance, and true affordability (including rent-to-own and shared-ownership options). Data on disability needs, aging populations, and rural housing gaps should drive planning choices, not just current housing numbers.

Concrete examples from practical experience back up these points. A nearby community land trust has ambitions to build 12 homes, including four fully accessible units, but faces planning delays and a lack of seed funding. A student-working population is discussing co-op ownership on a campus-fringe site, but there’s been little guidance on how to combine self-build elements with professional oversight to maintain safety and energy standards. Meanwhile, a modular-housing project in a neighbouring county shows promise for rapid delivery, yet procurement rules and local authority procurement cycles currently slow it down.

If reforms can combine accessibility by default, community-led delivery with realistic funding, and MMC-supported rapid construction—while simplifying planning and supporting rural housing contexts—I believe we could markedly increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes that meet real needs in our area.

i strongly believe from my vantage in England, living in a mixed area with aging housing stock and rising energy bills, reforms to increase supply of affordable, good‑quality homes need to address energy costs and quality at the same time. I broadly support mandating higher energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits. If new homes meet robust standards and existing homes are upgraded through grants for insulation, heat pumps, and draught‑proofing, bills fall and tenants aren’t squeezed by disproportionate costs. This helps meet climate targets and protects vulnerable households.

I also back stronger licensing and enforcement to raise minimum quality standards, but with caveats for small landlords. Any regime should avoid crippling compliance costs and offer phased timelines and practical support.

Encouraging longer tenancies can help households stay settled while giving landlords a viable model if costs for compliance and upgrades are shared. On supply side, targeted finance, better procurement access, and planning support for small sites would enable SME and local builders to deliver diverse, local housing. In practice, I’ve seen a local SME struggle with planning checks; streamlined processes and ring‑fenced energy grants would make a real difference!

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. As a resident of England aged 65+, I strongly support reforms that increase affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes could lower land costs and create a dedicated fund for affordable housing and essential local infrastructure such as GP surgeries, schools and public transport.

In our village there is an unused council site near the high street. If released, the uplift could fund 20–25 modular flats at ground level with two bedrooms and flexible living space, designed to be lifetime-friendly. This would help older residents who wish to downsize but stay in the community, and would free up family‑sized homes elsewhere.

We also need more wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes tailored to older persons, supported living, and student‑key‑worker housing. Homes with step‑free access, wider doors, accessible bathrooms and space for a carer would make daily life safer and easier. In rural areas, close proximity to schools, clinics and transport is crucial for families and care workers.

Taken together, these reforms would deliver better, fairer housing and stronger communities.

From a Scottish residents’ organisation representing older people and tenant groups, we see both promise and risk in proposals to increase affordable, good‑quality homes. We think reforms should be piloted and evaluated, not rolled out nationwide at speed.

Regarding rent stabilization, pilots that test caps or stabilisation in areas with acute affordability pressures could help families manage bills. However, they must be time‑limited, well‑targeted, and subject to independent evaluation. We’d want clear safeguards to prevent sudden exits by landlords or reduced investment in repairs; include exemptions for essential upgrades and provide transition support for small landlords.

On energy standards, raising standards for new builds makes sense and aligns with climate goals. We also need robust funding for retrofits of older stock to keep bills down for tenants and to ensure homes stay livable. Tie subsidies to level of improvement and guarantee protection against rent increases tied to compliance costs.

Also, unlock sites by simplifying planning rules and supporting modular or brownfield development, so supply doesn’t shrink while we raise quality. Overall, a measured, evidence‑led approach will serve both tenants and a cautious, salvageable supply chain.

I disagree with proposals that rely mainly on increasing ownership or widening the private rental market without ensuring long‑term affordability and quality. In Scotland, the most effective way to boost affordable, good‑quality homes is to foreground purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent (BTR and mixed‑tenuree schemes, with affordability covenants and professional management, to secure sustained long‑term rental supply. BTR units are designed to be rented long term, with on‑site or dedicated management teams that maintain blocks, respond quickly to repairs, and keep common areas well maintained. When rents are tied to affordability covenants for 20–40 years, we avoid the boom‑and‑bust cycle of the private market and provide real stability for families and local services. Reforms should: (1) require a significant allocation of BTR and affordable mixed‑tenure on new large schemes; (2) guarantee long‑term affordability through enforceable covenants; (3) unlock patient, long‑term financing and provide government backing to reduce costs; (4) mandate professional management and energy efficiency targets; and (5) prioritise brownfield sites with streamlined planning for BTR while protecting local communities. From local experience, high‑quality, well‑managed BTR offers better maintenance, predictable rentss and longer tenancy rights than much of the current private rental stock. This approach would deliver lasting supply and fairness moree effectively than measures focusing primarily on ownership or speculative private renting.

From where I sit in England, affordable, good‑quality homes for local people should come from builders who know the area and understand the local market. The reforms you’re proposing—targeted finance, easier procurement access for SMEs and local builders, a small-sites policy, and extra planning support—sound reasonable in theory, but I’m unconvinced they will deliver the homes we actually need here without creating new problems or delays.

Targeted finance sounds helpful on paper, but it risks distorting what gets funded and who benefits. If money is tied to specific targets or to particular schemes, there’s a real danger it diverts attention from genuinely viable projects that fit local needs. In my town, two viable 20‑25 unit schemes stalled when the funding criteria shifted mid‑way, forcing the developers to rework plans or seek more expensive private finance. That kind of uncertainty pushes up all-in costs and lengthens construction timelines. If we are serious about affordability, we need financing that is flexible, transparent, and has clear sunset clauses so funds don’t linger in a policy loop that can become self‑fulfilling and slow the market.

Procurement access for SMEs is a laudable aim, but the reality is that local builders often face a heavy, costly climb just to bid for council‑led or housing association projects. The paperwork, pre‑qualification, performance bonds, insurance, and long payment terms all eat into slim margins. In practice, Frameworks tend to be dominated by established national firms with the resources to navigate the system, leaving small local builders unable to compete on cost or reliability. I’ve seen a small 12‑home site get moped up by a bigger contractor because the SME couldn’t afford the up‑front bid costs or the bonding requirements. The result is fewer, not more, affordable homes and a higher risk of cost inflation across the sector.

The small‑sites policy could help unlock land closest to communities, but it’s a high‑risk route if not paired with real infrastructure release and viable planning economics. Small plots often come with disproportionately high per‑unit costs for access roads, sewer connections, and other infrastructure. If viability assessments don’t reflect those realities and if developers still face heavy local charges through planning gains, you end up delivering a few homes at a higher price rather than a steady stream of affordable units. In effect, the policy could simply redistribute where the profits lie without delivering the volume of affordable homes you’d expect. I’ve seen small sites that looked promising on paper stall for years while the cost of patience and red tape climbs.

Planning support sounds straightforward: more resource and faster decisions. But simply adding staff won’t fix the core issues unless decisions are made on a predictable basis and built into a streamlined framework. The backlog in planning departments isn’t just about capacity; it’s about the quality and consistency of decisions, and about the requirement for affordable housing contributions that can kill viable schemes for local families. When a planning decision feels arbitrary or is pulled into long negotiations over S106 contributions or viability matters, local builders lose confidence and delay starts. We need a planning system that is transparent, time‑bound, and with clear design expectations that don’t punish small, locally oriented builders for factors beyond their control.

If we want to truly increase supply from SMEs and local builders, the reforms should be recalibrated around deliverability, not just access. My practical suggestions would be:
- Finance that is flexible and time‑limited, with robust governance and sunset clauses, but without criteria that pick winners and distort market incentives.
- Procurement reform that genuinely lowers barriers for local SMEs: lower bid costs, shorter qualifying periods, longer payment terms, and a dedicated SME‑friendly track within frameworks so local firms can compete on value, not just on price.
- A realistic small‑sites policy that is paired with early‑stage infrastructure funding, simplified viability tests that reflect the true costs of small plots, and predictable planning contributions that don’t wipe out margins.
- Planning reform that accelerates decisions only when design quality and local character are protected, with measurable targets, clear guidance, and sufficient funding for planning departments to maintain consistent, fair judgments.

Above all, any reform must be about deliverability and quality, not just rhetoric about “inclusivity” or “localism.” Without coherent funding, fair procurement, viable small sites, and a planning system that moves quickly and transparently, we’ll end up with more empty promises and fewer affordable homes across our streets. I want to see homes built by local builders who know the area, with quality standards, energy efficiency, and long‑term affordability—not schemes that look good on paper but stall or fail to meet real local needs.

I’m not convinced that tinkering with Section 106, CIL and viability testing will actually deliver more affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Even with more transparency, the system still lets developers down‑size or swap on‑site affordable housing for cash contributions, and viability figures are often debated behind closed doors. In my town, schemes that were meant to deliver a solid chunk of affordable homes end up reducing the on‑site share or diverting funds to other parts of the country, leaving local families waiting years for homes, schools and GP capacity that never materialise.

What would help more is enforceable delivery, not just better reporting. Set clear on‑site affordable housing quotas with firm deadlines, and impose meaningful penalties for late or non‑delivery. Ring‑fence contributions for local infrastructure and housing, and require public, independent viability reviews so numbers aren’t hidden in private assessments. Use land owned by the council or housing associations to speed up delivery, with modern standards on quality and energy efficiency. In short, real delivery duties and direct local investment would do far more for affordable homes than further tweaks to the tariff and viability system.

I strongly support reforms that release surplus public land and capture planning uplift to fund affordable homes and local infrastructure. In Scotland there are council-owned sites and brownfield plots that sit idle while rents rise and new homes remain out of reach. Releasing land on transparent terms and applying uplift levies or taxes funded from planning gain could bring the cost of land down, helping councils build more affordable housing and upgrade local transport and GP capacity without extra pressure on households.

I also back targeted finance, procurement access and a robust small-sites policy to empower SME and local builders. A streamlined, well-supported planning route for small sites, paired with access to finance and guaranteed local procurement opportunities, would unlock diverse housing—from family homes to affordable rented flats—built by people who understand our communities. A practical example would be a local authority–community housing collaboration with a dedicated SME framework and a modest uplift levy ring-fenced for affordable homes and schools. For young people like me, these reforms could deliver genuinely affordable options near work, study, and transit, helping to stay in Scotland rather than moving away for somewhere cheaper.

Yes, I support reform. Mandating higher energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits will cut bills, help meet climate targets, and prevent tenants and landlords from bearing disproportionate costs while improving housing quality and long-term affordability.

From our organisation representing older residents in Scotland, we do not believe that more public investment in council and housing association building programmes is the most effective way to raise affordable, good-quality homes. In our rural and coastal communities, these schemes often suffer slow planning, procurement delays, and a poor match with dispersed populations (as if that will ever happen). Long lead times mean households wait years for a secure home, while ongoing maintenance costs still fall on cash-strapped local authorities.

We also question the emphasis on wheelchair-accessible, adaptable, older-person and student key-worker homes delivered as a separate category. Demand is scattered and budgets struggle to keep step with real needs, particularly in remote areas where travel to employment and services is limited. A better approach would be to unlock supply by:
- simplifying planning and speeding up approvals;
- enabling small- and mid-sized builders and community groups to build where people live, with realistic timescales and local input;
- using surplus public land with robust, long-term affordability safeguards; and
- insisting on universal design in all new homes so accessibility is built in, not bolted on.

Additionally, prioritise rapid repairs and energy upgrades to existing stock to reduce waiting lists and running costs for vulnerable residents. If reforms focus on these levers, we’ll see more homes faster, in the places that matter most to people here.

I live in Scotland and, as a young person, I’m sceptical that simply loosening planning rules will fix affordable housing. A real change requires that new homes come with funded, service-ready infrastructure up front. We need a phased approach where transport networks, schools, GP capacity, water, waste and broadband are planned and funded before large estates are approved, not after people move in and find services overwhelmed. In our area, a recent estate opened with more houses but the local primary is already at capacity and the bus service is infrequent; that makes new homes feel unaffordable in practice because you can’t get around or access essential services easily.

We also need more purpose-built Build‑to‑Rent and other mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. This would expand long-term rental supply and keep standards high, instead of letting existing stock be pushed into short-term lets or pressured markets.

Finally, release surplus public land and ensure planning uplift funds local infrastructure and affordable homes. Levies or taxes should be designed to lower land costs for developers while delivering real community benefits, not swallowed by councils’ general budgets. Without this full package, we’ll build more homes that aren’t genuinely affordable or sustainable for families across Scotland.

From our organisation representing young residents across England, we strongly welcome reforms to boost affordable, good-quality homes. The most effective steps are:

- Local data, monitoring and developer accountability: a live planning-delivery dashboard for each area showing approvals, starts and completions, with quarterly public reports. Link funding and approvals to delivery milestones and publish penalties for non-delivery to stop schemes stalling.

- Council capacity and enforcement: ring-fenced funding for planning and enforcement teams to accelerate decision-making and secure affordable housing as part of viability conditions, with clear deadlines.

- Regeneration and brownfield first: prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant buildings and long-term empty homes before releasing Green Belt or greenfield sites; protect landscapes and strengthen town centres. In our city, converting a long-empty cinema into flats demonstrated how regeneration can deliver housing quickly with local jobs.

- Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure: support purpose-built rental schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to increase long-term rental supply and stability.

This package would deliver more affordable homes, better quality, and longer-term stability for young residents.
I’d like more affordable homes, but I’m unsure which reforms would work here. Local input and careful planning matter, please avoid rushed schemes.

absolutely reforms should focus on two linked strands: raising energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits to cut bills, meet climate targets and avoid pushing costs onto tenants and landlords. Mandating higher energy standards for new homes, aligned with the Future Homes Standard, and a fabric-first approach would mean fewer cold flats and lower bills for tenants from day one. At the same time, sustained funding for retrofits—insulation, draught-proofing, heat pumps and better controls—would improve existing private rentals and student housing, reducing energy bills and fuel poverty.

In my experience as a renter, bills in winter are already high and some flats feel drafty and poorly insulated. This reform would help, but it will only work if councils can deliver. We need better local data and monitoring: publish annual dashboards on EPC performance, retrofit progress and affordable-home delivery, so residents can see results. We also need stronger developer accountability: binding delivery timelines and penalties for missed milestones, with upfront obligations to share delivery plans. And please fund planning, enforcement and delivery capacity in local authorities, including support for small builders, so commitments actually materialise and rents don’t rise to cover higher standards!

Reforms to mandate higher energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits could be the right lever to deliver affordable, good-quality homes, but they must be designed to avoid placing disproportionate costs on tenants or landlords. In my area of England, energy bills bite privatr rrnters and small landlords alike, and poor insulation is the main reason homes feel expensive to heat. If new homes are required to meet higher energy standards, and older stock is funded to be retrofi with insulation, draught-proofing, and heat pumps where appropriate, we would see lower bills and better comfort in winter. The challenge is upfront cost. Without substantial, targeted funding, developers pass costs on, or landlords raise rents to cove them. I’d back a national retrofit fund to cover insulation, window upgrades, and heating-system improvements in existingg stock, with money allocated to the dwelling, not tenants, to avoid sudden rent increases. We also need practical delivery: trained local crews, clear timetables, and a planning regime that speeds energy-efficient improvements without compromising safety or quality. A phased approach—top standards for neww builds within a few years and an accelerated retrofit programme for older homes—could extend affordable living without compromising climate goals.

From where I live in England, I don't think the answer lies chiefly in bigger public building programmes by councils and housing associations. In practice, these schemes take years to plan, fund and deliver, and even when completed they often don't reach the households who need homes most urgently. My friends and colleagues who are renting locally face rising rents and insecurity, and waiting lists for social housing feel endless. Instead,, reform should focus on enabling steady growth in good-qualityyy affordable homes by the private rented sector, with protections that don't squeeze landlords' viability to the point theyy withdraw from letting. That means targeted enforcement againstt the worst practices, but avoiding blanket, hard licensing that pushes decent small landlords out. It also means not sacrificing quality standards, but ensuring that tenancies can be longer with predictable costs. On planning, I want faster decisions on small-brownfield sites with light-touch checks and retained environmental safeguards, rather than sweeping deregulation that risks bad quality. Overall: unlock delivery by sensible incentives and clearer, faster routes for small developers and investors, while protectingg tenants and ensuring standards.

Agree: I think rent caps or stabilization can help affordability if designed carefully. In Northern Ireland, rents have risen faster than wages in many areas, making private rental less affordable for families like mine. A cap could provide immediate relief while arrangements to maintain supply are tested. However, I’m aware caps can discourage investment or prompt landlords to withdraw, especially if maintenance costs rise. Therefore, I support targeted pilots in 2-3 NI districts to measure impact on supply and outcomes for tenants. 

Design details: cap linked to either local median earnings or CPI plus a modest margin; allow increases for major improvements or renovations, new-builds for a set period, and long-term tenancies (3-5 years) rewarded with stable rent; include exemptions for landlords undertaking essential upgrades or where withdrawal would reduce much-needed supply. Consider a sunset clause and robust monitoring. 

Evaluation framework: monthly reporting of rental stock, vacancy rates, new-build completions, tenancy length, maintenance quality, energy efficiency, and tenant hardship indicators. If pilots show improved affordability without harming supply, roll out with appropriate guardrails. 

Complementary reforms: accelerate planning, subsidies for energy retrofit, incentives for landlords to upgrade properties, and strict enforcement of minimum standards. Also invest in social housing and enable schemes that bring older stock into affordable use while private market reforms are tested.

I think reforms should focus on better local data and stronger monitoring of delivery, with accountable developers and funded planning capacity to ensure commitments are kept. At the same time, we need more wheelchair-accessible and older-person homes tailored to local needs, while simplifying planning timelines but preserving environmental safeguards.

In Scotland, I’d prioritise decent energy-efficient upgrades and retrofit of existing homes; new builds alone won’t solve affordability, especially for older residents. Planning reform should simplify processes while protecting character.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. Our organisation supports reforms that would increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes while helping households cut bills and meet climate targets, but they must not pricing people out or slowing development. Mandating higher energy standards for new builds—aiming for very low running costs and good indoor comfort—should be tied to a clear delivery plan and phased to avoid cost shocks in a tight market. For existing stock, a substantial national retrofit fund is essential, covering social housing and the private rented sector. Insulation, draught-proofing, efficient heating (with heat pumps where suitable) and proper ventilation can substantially reduce energy bills and improve living conditions, but only if finance is accessible and decisions are outcome-based rather than box-ticking. Our pilots show that long-term savings can offset upfront costs when subsidies or low-interest loans are available; without this support, developers may pass costs to rents or scale back schemes.

We also need planning reforms that require a meaningful portion of affordable homes in new developments and streamline approvals for energy-efficient designs. Investments in local training and procurement are vital to prevent bottlenecks in the supply chain. Finally, robust protections for tenants—clear reporting on energy upgrades, caps on rent impacts, and guarantees of quality—are essential to ensure these reforms deliver genuinely affordable, high-quality homes.

I strongly support reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Strengthening licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards, and promoting longer tenancies, while ensuring small landlords can operate viably, would protect tenants and reduce churn. A clear national framework for private rented licensing, with proper resources for councils, would tackle rogue operators and ensure properties meet safety and energy‑efficiency standards, cutting costly repairs for families. Longer fixed‑term tenancies (3–5 years) would give families stability and help local schools and services plan ahead, provided there are fair, transparent rent reviews. For small landlords, sensible phased requirements and access to guidance or small‑grant support to upgrade homes would help them adapt without being forced out of the market. On the supply side, I back prioritising regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before releasing greenfield land or Green Belt, to protect landscapes. In our town there are underused mills and former shops that could become well‑designed flats with sensible planning and investment, which would deliver mores roofs without compromising local character. Overall, this brownfield‑first approach, paired with stronger standards and longer tenancies, offers credible, sustainable gains.

I live in England and am a pensioner, and I strongly agree that the reforms most likely to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes are bold, publicly funded building programmes led by councils and housing associations. A national programme, funded over a decade or more, would deliver genuinely affordable rents and secure, long‑term tenancies for low‑income households, including pensioners like me and families on modest incomes. In our area there is a council‑owned site near good transport links that could provide around 120 one‑ and two‑bedroom flats with modern energy‑efficient standards, accessible design, and damp‑free quality. If funded with predictable grants and ongoing maintenance money, such schemes could be delivered quickly by local authorities and housing associations, creating jobs and stabilising rents. I’d like to see reforms that speed up planning on brownfield sites, make it easier to use public land, and reinvest Right to Buy receipts into replacing homes rather than selling off stock. A clear pipeline and ring‑fenced funding would finally turn ambition into homes for those who need them most.

Reforms should prioritise releasing surplus public land, using planning uplift levies/taxes to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and infrastructure, and helping SME builders via targeted finance and small-site access; only after regenerating, infill, and converting vacant buildings, not greenfield or Green Belt releases.

From a lifetime in Scotland, I see that affordable, good-quality homes are essential for older folk to stay independent. I know neighbours who had to move when rents rose above what their pension could cover. I support reforms that test how to improve affordability without driving away investment or causing landlords to exit the market. In particular, pilots of rent stabilisation could be worth trying, but only with tight safeguards: temporary caps, linked to local incomes, exemptions for new-builds and major refurbishments, and clear triggers for lifting or adjusting them. We must gather robust evidence on effects for maintenance, investment, and tenant mobility before wider rollout, and be wary of unintended supply reductions.

Second, reform the planning system to align housing with services through phased delivery. Planning permissions should be granted with a binding delivery timetable that ties the release of housing to the completion of agreed infrastructure. If a developer or consortium cannot meet the triggers, there should be a proportionate mechanism to adjust phasing or funding, rather than simply accelerating housing and leaving services lagging.

Third, reform developer contributions to ensure that a meaningful share goes to local services in the area where the homes are built. We need more predictable, transparent mechanisms—stronger and more flexible S106 agreements and Community Infrastructure Levy where appropriate—so that every large site delivers sustainable capacity. Fourth, embed long-term, cross-agency delivery boards for new communities. These boards would bring together council planners, schools and academy trusts, NHS providers, transport authorities, water and energy utilities, and developers. Their job would be to agree a master plan with measurable milestones for infrastructure and to monitor delivery across all phases, not just housing. In my view, this joined-up approach is essential to avoid the disconnect I’ve seen elsewhere where a new estate is almost ready but the bus service, GP hours, or school capacity hasn’t kept pace.

Fifth, set clear quality and sustainability standards for homes, including energy efficiency, accessibility and use of modern construction methods that reduce running costs for households. Sixth, target transport-led and service-ready locations. By contrast, estates built with housing alone quickly faced capacity issues that fed long commutes and frustrated neighbours. These experiences underline why infrastructure-first reforms—funded readiness, phased delivery, and joined-up governance—are essential to truly increasing the supply of affordable, good-quality homes that people can live in, and stay in, for the long term.

From an organisation’s perspective, the reform package that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area needs to be pragmatic, well-targeted and capable of delivering the right mix of housing quickly. I see two interlocking strands that deserve emphasis: first, delivering more wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable and specialist housing to meet demographic and rural needs; second, unlocking innovative, community‑led routes that can scale up affordable provision rapidly through new delivery models and modern construction methods.

A. What we need to deliver on the ground for people and communities
- A genuine mix that includes much more than traditional social or affordable housing: we must build wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes for older people, with supported housing where needed, and student key‑worker homes to stabilise the local economy and services. Too much stock is designed for the average household and then retrofitted, which is costly and slow. Housing policy should require a portion of new affordable units to be designed to M4(3) wheel‑chair adaptable standards where appropriate, with flexibility for future care needs and easy conversion if a household’s circumstances change.
- Rural and cultural sensitivity: in rural areas and for communities with specific cultural needs, housing must be designed and sited to reflect travel distances, local services, and supporting infrastructure. This means allowing targeted small‑site development, co‑housing, and community‑led models that can work within or adjacent to village envelopes without sacrificing environmental quality or agricultural viability.

B. Practical reforms to unlock supply quickly and cheaply
- Support for community‑led models: community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, and self‑build groups have repeatedly demonstrated that they can deliver affordable homes with longer‑term affordability and better local buy‑in. Government should simplify land transfer to these bodies, guarantee appropriate grant support or low‑interest loans, and provide predictable, long‑term funding streams that enable them to acquire land and mobilise building quickly. A rights‑to‑build framework should be complemented by streamlined procurement and planning processes that prevent delays while maintaining high design and environmental standards.
- Modern methods of construction (MMC) and off‑site manufacture: MMC can shorten delivery times, improve quality and reduce long‑term maintenance costs. We need clear procurement roadmaps and funding pilots that encourage local authorities and housing associations to use MMC where appropriate, plus the creation of regional MMC hubs to build capacity and reduce costs through standardised components. For rural and high‑cost areas, MMC offers a viable route to affordable homes without compromising design quality.
- A responsive planning and land supply system: reform planning to prioritise delivery of affordable, accessible homes and to reduce duplicated requirements across authorities. That includes faster planning decisions for local authority‑led or community‑led schemes, clearer density expectations that balance infrastructure constraints with housing needs, and land value capture mechanisms that recycle uplift into affordable supply—without undermining the viability of small builders and community groups.
- Land and infrastructure alignment: to scale supply, we need more publicly owned land available at affordable terms for community groups and small builders, with a timetable for release and clear developer requirements. Where infrastructure constraints exist, targeted public investment should be front‑loaded to unlock sites (schools, GP capacity, transport links) so that new homes don’t hit viability walls at the end of the process.
- Retrofit and existing stock: alongside new builds, faster adaptation of existing housing stock for accessibility and energy efficiency will reduce vacancy and under‑utilisation in the system. Grants or loan guarantees for retrofits of social/affordable homes—and incentives for private landlords to improve tenures—would complement fresh supply and ensure long‑term quality.

C. What success would look like and how we measure it
- Outcomes over outputs: we need to track not just numbers of homes built, but the proportion that are wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable, or designed for supported living; the long‑term affordability period; and resident satisfaction with design quality and access to services.
- Local delivery capacity: reforms should build capacity in local authorities and community groups, with training and expert guidance on MMC, adaptive design, and heritage/district‑level constraints.
- Flexibility and resilience: planning and procurement processes should be resilient to market shifts, with contingency funding for prolonged periods of uncertainty (for example, economic downturns or regional growth fluctuations).

In short, I’m convinced we will get substantially more affordable, high‑quality homes if we couple a clear mandate for accessible, adaptable housing that serves older and disabled residents with a vigorous push to community‑led delivery and modern construction methods. This approach respects rural and cultural contexts and prioritises speed and long‑term affordability, not just short‑term construction targets. A coherent, well‑funded package of reforms along these lines would markedly improve local housing supply and quality over the coming years.

I live in Scotland and I’m replying as an individual. First, transparency and independence in viability testing are essential. Too often, viability assessments can appear to be shaped by developers’ interests, with the methodologies, inputs and assumptions kept opaque. If we are reforming viability testing, we must insist on a statutory, independently overseen process. That means published methodologies, clear inputs (land values, build costs, market assumptions), and an accessible, independent review of outcomes. Without that, the promised “more transparent” approach will simply become a new layer of paperwork that still favours profit over people who need affordable homes.

Second, on‑site affordable housing should be the default, not the exception. Cash contributions (commuted sums) may help infrastructure in theory, but in practice they frequently delay or dilute the delivery of affordable homes. In many local discussions I’ve heard, a large proportion of affordable housing ends up in the form of cash payments rather than actual on‑site units in the same development, and that slows down the supply of genuinely affordable homes in the places where they are most needed. If on‑site delivery is to be preferred, we must set firm delivery triggers, require a meaningful minimum percentage (not a token 5–10%), and ensure that if a site finishes viability improvements, the affordable units are still built rather than diverted to a later date. There should also be transparent reporting so communities can see when, where and how affordable homes are being delivered.

Third, reforming how we capture uplift from planning and land value needs to be carefully targeted. I welcome the idea of capturing uplift to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure, but I’m wary of levies or taxes that simply raise costs across the board and make land development even less attractive in already tight markets. If uplift capture is used, it must be tightly ring‑fenced for affordable housing and essential local infrastructure, and it must apply to clear, well‑defined land parcels where uplift is created by planning permission, not by speculative land banking. The revenue should be credible, stable and long‑term, with proper governance so communities can see tangible improvements in schools, GP capacity and roads.

Releasing surplus public land has potential, but the process needs reform as well. Public land should be brought into use quickly for affordable housing or for joint ventures with housing associations, with clear timelines and community input. Too often land release is slow and fragmented, which defeats the purpose of bringing down land costs and delivering timely affordable homes. Any land‑release framework should include transparent valuations, public accountability for sale terms, and a requirement that a substantial portion of the resulting homes are affordable in perpetuity or for a defined period.

In Scotland, we also need to recognise that housing delivery isn’t only about the private sector. If the market alone is relied upon, affordable homes will remain episodic and unevenly distributed—often in the towns and cities where land costs are highest. A more effective approach would combine targeted public land reuse, stronger public‑private partnerships with housing associations, and strategic, council‑led development that prioritises affordable housing alongside infrastructure and service improvements. That may mean more upfront public investment or land assembly by local authorities, with long‑term stewardship to keep homes affordable and well maintained.

In short, I oppose reforms that rely mainly on tinkering with viability tests, cash contributions in place of on‑site affordable homes, and broad uplift levies without strong safeguards. If reforms are to work, they must be transparent, independently verified, and designed to deliver real, timely affordable homes on site, supported by credible funding for infrastructure. Public land should be released quickly and used in ways that maximise affordable housing outcomes, and uplift capture must be targeted, accountable and ring‑fenced for housing and essential local services. Only then will we see a genuine increase in the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area.

Affordable, good‑quality homes are in short supply in my Scottish area, and I think a balanced reform package could genuinely widen both supply and security. I live in England and I’m responding as an individual. I’m in my late 30s and like many others I want to see more affordable, good-quality homes in my area so families, key workers and first-time buyers aren’t priced out. I believe reforms that release surplus public land and capture the uplift from planning decisions are the most effective way to increase supply and fund the infrastructure that accompanies new housing.

First, releasing surplus public land is a pragmatic, fast route to lower land costs and speed delivery. The key is to have clear, time‑bound triggers and safeguards: identify suitable sites, ensure high design quality and long-term maintenance, and require a substantial proportion of the homes to be affordable. Crucially, this must be accompanied by repurposing corridors for walking and cycling, and by investing in the local primary school and GP capacity that would be stressed by new residents.

Second, we should capture the uplift in land value created by planning permission to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. At present the tools exist—Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and Section 106 obligations—but they are not always used to their full potential or are inconsistently applied. A clearer, more robust uplift capture would ensure that the public benefits of a change in use or density are shared with the community. A levy or tax on uplift should be proportionate and ring-fenced for affordable housing and essential infrastructure (roads, drainage, school expansions, GP surgeries, and green space). This would lower the overall landed cost for developers and reduce the need for creeping budget skews, while ensuring that new communities are well‑served and sustainable.

To make this work, I’d welcome reforms to how the levy is calculated and collected. A single, predictable framework across planning authorities would help small and large developers alike. For example, a portion of the uplift from rezoning or higher-density schemes could be allocated to a local Infrastructure and Affordable Housing Fund. This fund would be transparent, with annual reporting on how much is raised, where it’s spent, and what homes are delivered. It should also include safeguards to prevent delaying schemes through complex approvals or overbearing conditions.

Third, the design and quality of affordable homes must be non-negotiable. Releasing land and applying uplift capture should come with robust planning conditions that require passivhaus-level energy efficiency, accessible design, durable materials, and a long-term maintenance plan. Mixed-tenure developments that include social rent, affordable rent, shared ownership and, where possible, shared equity help communities feel stable and inclusive. I’d also like to see guarantees that local employment and procurement obligations are part of these schemes, so the benefits reach local people.

Fourth, governance and pace matter. The government should incentivise rapid progress by setting clear milestones and penalties for delays, while offering support for early-stage viability work. A cross‑sector delivery board with representatives from councils, housing associations, local healthcare providers and residents would help maintain momentum and accountability. Local communities should have a meaningful say in site selection and design through well-advertised consultation and design workshops.

In practical terms, here are the reforms I’d push for:
- Identify and release surplus public land quickly, with priority to sites near transport, schools and town centres, delivering a minimum affordable-housing share (for example, at least 40% on public-land sites) with a clear timetable.
- Expand and reform uplift capture: implement a predictable planning uplift levy, proportionate to the value added by planning permission, ring-fenced for affordable housing and essential infrastructure, and harmonised across regions to avoid a postcode lottery.
- Strengthen existing tools (CIL and Section 106) to ensure funds are actually collected and spent on agreed infrastructure and affordable homes, with simpler, faster processes for developers.
- Set quality expectations: require high energy efficiency standards and inclusive design, with long-term maintenance provisions.
- Improve delivery governance: a dedicated delivery body or taskforce to track sites, publish milestones, and report publicly on outcomes and value-for-money.

Why this matters to me personally: we’ve watched land cost pressures push up rents and mortgage deposits in recent years while waiting for the right combination of site availability and funding. If surplus public land can be brought into productive use and uplift is fairly shared, I believe we’ll see not just more homes, but better-designed, better-integrated communities that don’t leave local services starved. The combination of land release and uplift capture could unlock a generation of affordable housing alongside the infrastructure our towns need to thrive.

If implemented well, these reforms could turn vacant or underused public assets into thriving neighbourhoods, help young families stay local, and support essential services without relying solely on higher private rents or ever-higher public debt. Second, set and enforce minimum quality standards across the private rented sector. In practice, I’d welcome multi-year tenancy defaults with regular, affordable rent reviews tied to transparent criteria, and safeguards against unreasonable eviction practices.
