That should be paired with land release on public or brownfield sites, and reforms to affordable-housing requirements to ensure a meaningful share goes to those in most need.

To genuinely raise the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area, reforms should centre on improved local data, stronger monitoring, and sharper accountability for developers, backed by funded planning and enforcement capacity in councils. Key steps: 1) create transparent, open data dashboards that track housing supply, affordable completions, and land-banking by site, updated quarterly; 2) make S106 affordable-housing obligations binding with clear milestones, performance bonds, and penalties for missed deadlines; require on-site delivery or timely alternative; 3) compel regular progress reporting from developers on affordable units and quality standards, with independent verification; 4) ring-fence affordable-housing receipts for local delivery, not general budgets; 5) boost council planning and enforcement capacity with protected funding for planning policy teams, development management and building-control; 6) empower councils to accelerate, but not compromise on quality, with streamlined consent for sites meeting robust design and space standards. In my experience, a large development on the edge of town has stalled because data was incomplete and enforcement was thin; with a proper dashboard and a delivered enforcement plan, households would have known when and where homes would be built and maintained. These reforms would protect residents, ensure promised affordable homes are delivered, and speed up delivery without sacrificing quality.

Yes. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies would lower land costs and fund affordable homes and local infrastructure in our area, unlocking sites for genuinely affordable housing while improving roads and schools.

As a pensioner living in England, I read the idea of reforms to boost affordable, good-quality homes with a mix of interest and caution. I’m not persuaded that the two main reform routes suggested will automatically deliver what my community needs. In fact, they could make matters worse for local people and for the long-term quality and affordability of housing.

Releasing surplus public land and using planning uplift through levies or taxes to lower land costs and fund housing and infrastructure sounds sensible in theory. In practice, I fear it would push up the price of land still further instead of making genuinely affordable homes available where they are truly needed. When councils release land, the most attractive sites tend to be near town centres or along major roads, where developers can build quickly. But these sites can also be prone to flood risk, higher maintenance costs, or poor access to local services. My own town has seen public land offered for development near a river corridor that requires expensive flood risk management and long-term maintenance. The funds raised through uplift or taxes may not cover the full cost of delivering the infrastructure—roads, GP capacity, schools, and public transport—that new housing actually requires. In the end, the affordable homes may be a fraction of what’s promised, and residents will still bear the burden of higher taxes or service cuts elsewhere to fund the rest.

There’s also a real risk that “uplift” revenues become a treasury feeding trough rather than a dedicated investment in the places that need it. If the money isn’t ring-fenced for affordable housing and local infrastructure, it will be used to plug gaps in other budgets. That can undermine local accountability: communities see new housing but don’t always see the promised improvements in roads, sewers, schools, or bus services in a timely way. In our area, the pace of hospital and school expansion has lagged behind housing growth in recent years, so even when affordable units are delivered, the surrounding services can’t cope. I fear public land release will become a mechanism for increased density rather than a coherent plan to create sustainable, well-served neighbourhoods.

The other reform—streamlining and simplifying planning and decision timelines while retaining environmental safeguards—is also attractive in theory, but I’m wary of the cost to quality and local control. Shorter timelines can mean rushed design and less opportunity for neighbours and local groups to have their say. My experience is that communities aren’t just a nuisance; they’re the people who hold local values and character together. When planning pressure intensifies, there’s a danger that important aspects—like the preservation of heritage, local green spaces, drainage and flood management, and true energy efficiency—get cut back to save a few weeks. I’ve seen recent applications approved in nearby villages where designs look impressive on paper but fail to respect the character of the area, the need for accessible housing for older residents, or long-term maintenance expectations. Environmental safeguards are essential, especially with climate risks rising; they must not be reduced or treated as an afterthought in a race to deliver more homes faster.

Another concern is infrastructure capacity. It’s not just about more houses; it’s about decent electricity, reliable water and sewerage, sufficient school places, robust health care access, and reliable public transport. If planning is accelerated without corresponding investment in infrastructure, new communities risk becoming overstrained and less affordable in practice because residents bear higher costs and poorer services.

What would I like to see instead? First, a stronger link between land release and explicit, ring-fenced funding for affordable housing and infrastructure, with transparent oversight and local accountability. Land should be released only on sites that are sustainable, with defined access to public transport, flood resilience, and existing or planned services, and with a requirement for high-quality design that respects local character. Second, a genuine focus on quality: a standard that new homes are energy efficient, accessible, well-insulated, and durable, with climate resilience built in. Third, real involvement of communities through community land trusts or housing associations that can steward and maintain affordable homes long term, ensuring that tenures match local need and aren’t merely a transient market fix. Fourth, targeted use of levy revenues to fund infrastructure that actually serves the new residents—roads, bus routes, GP expansion, school places, and flood defence—rather than letting it disappear into general budgets. Finally, a sustained investment in planning departments themselves—more staff, better training, and clearer guidance—so that decisions are well-considered, consistent, and capable of delivering high-quality housing while protecting the environment.

In short, I’d rather see reforms that prioritise sustainable, well-designed, affordable homes in the right places, with strong local input and robust infrastructure behind them, than schemes that rush through development at the expense of local character and long-term affordability. If the government wants meaningful reform, let it be reform that guarantees quality, not just speed; that protects green spaces and flood risk, and that ensures affordable housing is genuinely affordable for the people who need it most in our communities.

I strongly support reforms that push up the supply of affordable, good-quality homes and make sure they are part of well-planned, sustainable communities. In my experience here, the problem isn’t only about building enough houses, but about delivering the right kind of homes with the necessary streets, schools, health services and buses in place for people to actually live there comfortably. The reforms I’d like to see fall into a few practical strands.

- Improve local data and monitoring so we can see what is actually being delivered. Councils should publish a real-time housing delivery dashboard showing planning permissions granted, starts on site, completions, and the share of affordable homes on each scheme. It would also track delays and the reasons for them. Residents should be able to see whether a development is on track to meet its promised infrastructure and service commitments. In our area, there have been schemes granted permission but with slow starts and uncertain delivery of affordable units; more transparent data would help authorities, developers and residents understand the true progress and where action is needed.

- Strengthen developer accountability and delivery commitments. Planning obligations should be binding with clear milestones and penalties if milestones aren’t met. I’d like to see performance bonds or penalties that are proportionate and convertible into funds for affordable homes or local infrastructure when delivery slips. The affordable-housing element should be protected from being watered down or shifted to later phases. Where a developer misses milestones, there should be a straightforward route for councils to secure replacement delivery through other partners or to reallocate resources to ensure the obligation is fulfilled.

- Increase council planning and enforcement capacity. Councils often struggle to supervise complex developments, negotiate affordable housing, and secure timely delivery of infrastructure. Providing dedicated delivery teams, more planning staff, and digital tools to manage cases would help. If councils can coordinate planning, highway, education and vitality services more effectively, it reduces the risk of new estates being bought with all the houses but few buses, fewer GP hours, or a lag in utilities capacity.

- Require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing is completed. A development should be considered service-ready, not merely revenue-ready. This means upfront or staged funding for a reliable bus service and cycling routes, a new or expanded primary school and adequate primary and secondary places, sufficient GP capacity, and the necessary water, sewage, and broadband capacity. In practice, this could involve a formal service-readiness test tied to planning permissions and occupancy milestones, with obligations that infrastructure is funded and delivered in tandem with homes rather than tacked on later.

- Embed sustainable design and maintenance as a condition of delivery. Quality matters as much as quantity. Design codes that ensure energy efficiency, good daylight, accessible spaces, and a robust maintenance fund for a number of years after handover help communities thrive. It’s frustrating when a new estate looks good on opening day but suffers from poor drainage or neglected public realm after a couple of winters.

- Engage communities throughout the process. Local residents know what works for their area and where pinch points will occur. I’d welcome clearer forums for community input on phasing plans, school capacity projections, and transport changes, with a transparent method for incorporating feedback into delivery milestones.

For example, on a recent large scheme near our town, promises of a new primary school and a GP practice were not matched quickly by service provision. The result was longer trips for families and stretched local services even before all homes were occupied. A framework that links infrastructure funding and service capacity to each phase of a development would help prevent exactly that sort of mismatch.

Ultimately, these reforms should make sure that new homes are affordable in reality, not just on paper, and that the people moving in have the roads, schools, healthcare and utilities they need. If the government can empower councils with data, resources and enforceable delivery duties, we can build genuinely sustainable communities where affordable homes sit alongside good services and real opportunities for local people.

Agree. To increase supply of affordable, good-quality homes, we should mandate higher energy standards for all new builds and fund retrofits across the existing housing stock. Higher standards will raise construction costs slightly, but the long-term energy savings for tenants and landlords will be substantial, helping keep rents affordable while cutting bills and emissions. In my area, newer developments with strong insulation and efficient heating have kept energy bills manageable even in cold winters, while older, draughty terraces absorb most of a tenant's budget on heating. A national retrofit fund, with grants or low-cost loans for private rentals, would unlock upgrades to many properties that are currently energy-inefficient. Planning policy should require developers to meet EPC targets and support heat pumps or heat networks where suitable, not just for council housing but across private stock. This approach would boost the quality and availability of homes without displacing tenants and would help meet climate targets faster.

From my perspective in England, I disagree that major public investment in council or housing association building programmes is the most effective way to deliver affordable, long‑term social rents. Such schemes often take years to plan and deliver and can lock funds into procurement processes rather than speeding up local solutions. They risk mismatching units to local need and can dampen private investment appetite.

Reforms should prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before any greenfield or Green Belt release to protect landscapes and avoid sprawling growth. In our area there are several empty pubs and a disused mill that could be refurbished into high‑quality affordable flats within months, not years. Converting these sites is faster, cheaper and far less disruptive than building on greenfield sites.

Specific reforms I’d support:
- streamline planning for conversions of vacant offices, shops and industrial buildings into housing; provide fast‑track approvals with clear local design standards.
- raise penalties or taxes on long‑term empty homes and offer private‑sector retrofit grants rather than new council building programmes.
- require private developers to include affordable housing in private schemes, with long‑term affordability guarantees, and ensure high energy efficiency and quality.
- prioritise brownfield and infill before Green Belt release; only permit greenfield where essential.

From where I live in England, addressing the shortage of affordable, good‑quality homes clearly needs a mixed approach. I’m glad to see a focus on community-led models alongside stronger long-term rental supply. I think reforms should support both ends: community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build, and modern methods of construction to speed up high‑quality supply; and purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to stabilise long‑term rental markets. The best outcomes will come from enabling those routes to scale in a way that keeps quality, affordability and local engagement at the centre.

Key reforms I’d like to see fall into a few interlocking areas:

1) Planning and land reform to unlock land for community-led housing
- Create a fast‑track planning track for community‑led housing (CLTs, co‑ops, self‑build groups) and guarantee a pipeline of suitable soil and brownfield land (public land and derelict sites) allocated to these schemes on long leases with social‑value criteria. 
- Simplify land assembly for community groups and allow affordable land to be leased to them at terms that recognise the long‑term social benefit, with clear guidance on what constitutes an affordable return.
- Require local authorities to publish a forward plan showing where land is available for affordable, community-led housing, reducing speculative land banking and improving certainty for neighbourhood groups.

2) Governance, stewardship and quality
- Ensure long‑term stewardship of community‑led housing through robust governance (e.g., 99‑year leases or equivalent, transferrable covenants) and access to professional advisory support for boards.
- Tie design and maintenance standards to higher energy efficiency and high‑quality construction, with independent quality checks and resident feedback loops.

3) Modern methods of construction (MMC) and self-build plots
- Fund and facilitate local MMC facilities or partnerships to speed delivery, with guarantees on quality and supply chain resilience. Encourage timber-frame and other low‑carbon options where appropriate, with skilled local training pipelines for trades.
- Create serviced plots for self‑build and custom build with shared infrastructure costs covered by an early‑stage capital pot, plus clear guidance on planning intake, to reduce delays and uncertainty for individual buyers.
- Promote standardised components and procurement frameworks to make smaller builders viable and to shorten build times without compromising quality.

4) Build‑to‑Rent (BTR) and mixed‑tenure schemes with strong affordability covenants
- Encourage purpose‑built rental schemes with a clear long‑term ownership and management model, and require a significant, clearly defined share of affordable rents (for example a minimum 20–30% affordable units) integrated into the development.
- Mandate professional, localised management with published service standards, tenant protections and predictable rent trajectories linked to local affordability benchmarks.
- Tie new BTR schemes to energy efficiency, climate resilience, and social value commitments (e.g., apprenticeships and local procurement).

5) Financing and incentives
- Provide patient capital for CLTs and small‑to‑mid‑sized builders, including grants, low‑interest loans, and guarantees to mobilise land and delivery quickly.
- Consider targeted tax reliefs for community‑led housing purchases of land, and streamlined VAT and stamp‑duty arrangements where homes are genuinely affordable and subject to long‑term affordability covenants.
- Support local and regional housing investment funds that blend public funds with pension fund and private investments, with clear performance and governance requirements.

6) Local delivery, jobs and monitoring
- Tie new housing supply to local job creation and skills, with apprenticeships and training funded as part of the delivery model.
- Build in robust monitoring: housing delivered, timeframes, energy performance, tenant satisfaction, and long‑term affordability outcomes should be published annually.

In practice, I’ve seen the potential and the hurdles. In our town, a derelict site owned by the council could be transformed into affordable housing via a CLT, but land cost and planning timetables have slowed progress. A nearby district approved a Build‑to‑Rent project with a portion reserved for affordable rents, and residents appreciate the professional management and maintenance standards, yet the rent levels for the lowest‑paid key workers remain a concern. If reforms can remove the land and planning bottlenecks for community groups while ensuring quality, governable, long‑term rental stock, we could see a real increase in genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes in a reasonable timescale.

Overall, the reforms should empower communities to shape their housing while ensuring that modern construction and professional tenancy management deliver reliable, high‑quality homes for the longer term. That balance between community ownership and well‑regulated market delivery feels essential to me.

I’m responding as an individual living in England, and I’m speaking against relying on releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes as the main way to boost the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area.

First, the premise that simply releasing public land will automatically lower land costs and unlock a wave of affordable homes is optimistic at best and risky at worst. Public land parcels are not all in the same class. Some sites are awkward, contaminated, or poorly connected to town centres and services. Others are small and fragmented, or they sit on land with complex ownership and legal constraints. Selling these parcels off can raise quick revenue for councils, but it does not guarantee affordable homes, good-quality design, or long‑term value for local people. In practice, I’ve seen council-owned sites marketed with the expectation of “uplift” from developers and yet the affordable share ends up smaller than promised, or the delivery is delayed while infrastructure like roads and schools struggle to keep up. When the site is public land, there should be a presumption in favour of genuinely affordable homes and long‑term stewardship, not just a quick sale to the highest bidder.

Second, capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes (the so‑called uplift from land value or S106/CIL-like mechanisms) sounds neat on a whiteboard, but it rarely delivers predictable, affordable housing at the scale needed. Planning contributions are negotiated on a site‑by‑site basis and can be absorbed into the overall viability of a project. In a tight market, developers push back on contributions, claiming increased costs make schemes unviable. The result is more uncertainty, more delays, and fewer sites that actually deliver affordable homes. Even when funds do reach infrastructure or affordable housing, they are not always ring‑fenced in a way that ensures local residents see the benefit where they need it most—often in the same neighbourhood where the homes are being built.

There’s also a genuine risk that this approach displaces public value into a fund that is harder to scrutinise. If uplift revenue goes into a general pot rather than being earmarked for local affordable housing and critical infrastructure, it becomes a bargaining chip in larger, more contentious schemes and the gains cannot be reliably tracked by local residents. In my area, the infrastructure promised to accompany housing uplift—schools upgrades, expanded GP capacity, road improvements—has lagged behind the development timetable, leaving local services strained and residents frustrated.

What would work better, in my view, is a more direct, accountable approach to affordable housing paired with smarter use of public land and a clearer, more predictable mechanism for funding infrastructure. Key elements could include:
- A strong, public-led pipeline of affordable housing on surplus public land, prioritising council housing and high‑quality, low-energy homes built to durable standards. The aim should be long‑term stewardship, with rents that genuinely reflect local affordability and with protections against future sell‑offs.
- Empowering and funding housing associations and community land trusts to deliver truly affordable homes on public land, with ongoing oversight by residents to maintain affordability in perpetuity.
- A fast‑track planning system for affordable housing schemes, with strict viability tests that protect the affordable share and with upfront commitments on delivering essential infrastructure alongside housing.
- A transparent, local infrastructure fund tied to development—where uplift contributions are clearly allocated to the specific schemes that generate them, monitored by communities and augmented with long‑term public investment where needed.
- Strong quality standards, including energy efficiency, design that fits the local area, and access to public transport, so that new homes are affordable to run and properly integrated into their neighbourhoods.

In short, while I recognise the appeal of using public land and uplift revenues to finance affordable housing, the reality is that without tight safeguards, predictable delivery timelines, and direct, locally accountable investment, this approach can fail to deliver the homes we need where we need them. A more hands‑on, capability‑driven strategy—prioritising truly affordable housing, public land stewardship, and ring‑fenced infrastructure funding—seems far more likely to produce lasting, genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes for my area.

I welcome reforms that would genuinely boost the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area. As someone retired but deeply concerned about where the next generation will live, I believe we can achieve more by tightening up planning data, holding developers to account, and unlocking land that the public already owns. The goal should be homes that are genuinely affordable, well built and properly connected to essential services and transport.

First, we need better local data, monitoring and accountability. A single, transparent delivery dashboard for every local authority would be transformative. It should show how many homes are needed, how many have planning permission, how many are actually completed and how many of those are genuinely affordable, site by site Obviously.... Independent audits would check that promised affordable units are delivered and kept. In our town we have an approved site that has sat idle for years while the land value climbs and the groundwork costs rise; a public report on why it hasn’t progressed would put pressure on all parties to move forward. If we can see milestones and penalties clearly laid out, it becomes easier to make sure commitments are not forgotten or deferred indefinitely.

Second, strengthen planning enforcement and delivery capacity. Our council’s planning staff are stretched, which slows decision-making and undermines confidence. We need dedicated funding to recruit and retain more planning and enforcement officers, and to create a small, agile delivery unit focused on affordable housing. This would help prevent land-banking and ensure that when a scheme is approved, the build-out happens on time and to a high standard. A clear requirement for developers to start on site within a defined period, with penalties for long delays, would stop schemes lingering in limbo. There should also be robust oversight to ensure that obligations tied to planning permission—such as affordable housing, infrastructure improvements, or highway works—are actually delivered, not merely paid for in the long term.

Third, release surplus public land and capture planning uplift to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. The public sector already owns land that, with sensible reform, could unlock affordable homes much more quickly. Surplus school sites, council-owned car parks, and hospital grounds should be released under transparent terms with a dedicated portion for affordable homes. Importantly, the uplift in land value created by planning permission should come back to the community. Mechanisms such as the Community Infrastructure Levy or other land-value capture tools should be used to fund affordable housing and essential infrastructure—roads, GP surgery capacity, school places and public transport improvements—so the cost of new homes doesn’t fall entirely on buyers. In practice, this could mean a site with a guaranteed 30% affordable homes funded by uplift receipts, plus investment in the local infrastructure that makes the area viable for families and older residents alike.

Fourth, ensure quality and suitability for older residents. We need homes that are energy efficient, accessible and adaptable, with good insulation, low running costs, and proximity to shops and medical services. It’s not just bricks and mortar; it’s about creating communities where people can stay as their needs change. The reforms should explicitly support high-quality, lifetime homes on affordable plots that are well integrated with public transport and community facilities.

Finally, align incentives with delivery. Simplify processes for small and mid-sized builders to participate in affordable housing schemes, as well as major developers, but with transparent requirements and measurable outcomes. If these reforms are implemented with proper funding, accountability, and a clear link to land value uplift, we can significantly increase the number of affordable, good-quality homes without relying on uncertain market fluctuations.

In summary, better data and accountability, stronger enforcement and delivery capacity, and a clear mechanism to release public land and capture uplift to fund housing and infrastructure are practical, deliverable steps. They reflect what I’ve seen locally: where costs are managed and commitments are enforceable, schemes can move from planning to finished homes in a way that benefits ordinary people and the community as a whole.

absolutely i am not persuaded that the proposed reforms will increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in my area. Strengthening licensing and minimum standards risks squeezing small landlords out of the market, which would reduce the overall number of rental properties and push up rents for those who remain. In practice I’ve seen this: a private rental in our street sat vacant for eight weeks after new licensing checks, and a neighbour, who owns two rental properties, told me the administrative costs are now so high he’s considering selling one and moving to a simple buy-to-let mortgage rather than manage multiple properties. Enforcement creates uncertainty and can deter new landlords from entering the market. If licensing is kept, it must be tightly targeted at rogue operators, with clear fees and predictable timetables, not blanket schemes. Longer tenancies could help tenants, but only if landlords retain enough cash flow to remortgage and upgrade properties. A more effective path is to remove planning barriers, incentivise building on brownfield sites, and invest in council housing, while keeping standards practical and costs reasonable for small landlords!

i really think from rural Scotland, I’m worried that the current reform ideas won’t actually shift the dial on affordable, good-quality homes for people like me and my neighbours. We need reforms that deliver more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes, as well as older-person, supported and student key-worker housing, all tailored to our demographic reality, the geography of rural areas, and our cultural needs. Too much of the discussion feels abstract and urban-centric, which simply won’t work here where a decent home is often several miles from the nearest GP, school, or job. 

A few concrete concerns and proposals:

- Make accessibility non-negotiable in new builds and major renovations. All new homes should meet lifetime-home standards, with a clear target that a substantial minority (roughly 15–20%) are fully wheelchair-adaptable, with wide access, step-free routes, reachable controls, and adaptable bathrooms. Even for homes that aren’t wheelchair-adapted from day one, design must enable easy future adaptation without ripping the place apart. In our congested rural towns, this would save families from moving when mobility changes, and would reduce the need for costly retrofits later on.

- Fund rapid retrofit of existing stock, prioritising rural areas. Many homes in villages are older and not easily accessible; retrofitting to accessibility and energy efficiency needs is essential. Separate grants or a dedicated budget line for Disabled Facilities-style improvements should be ring-fenced and streamlined so approvals don’t drag on for years. Waiting lists in some councils are already long and that’s unacceptable when someone ageing at home is at risk.

- Expand and localise supported housing and integrated care in community settings. We should see more purpose-built, adaptable homes for older people and those needing on-site or nearby support, with flexible tenancy models and on-site care linked to local NHS/social care services. This isn’t “soft policy”; it holds the line on hospital admissions and delayed discharges, which in turn protects families and local health budgets. In small towns, co-locating carers’ housing with care facilities helps staff stay in the area and keeps services sustainable.

- Create student key-worker housing linked to rural essential services. There’s real pressure on workers who keep schools, care homes, and health services running in our communities. If we can provide affordable, well-located housing for student nurses, trainee teachers, and other key workers near hospitals or care hubs, it stabilises local services and reduces long commutes. We should offer incentives to developers for these purpose-built blocks—perhaps through planning bonuses or targeted funding—while ensuring rents remain genuinely affordable for frontline staff.

- Tailor housing to rural and cultural needs. That means designing homes that work with local character and weather, and making space for cultural practices and language needs where relevant. It could involve flexible room layouts for multi-generational living, accessible community spaces, and partnerships with Gaelic organisations or faith groups to ensure mosques, churches, and meeting halls have accessible, usable spaces. Community-led approaches, including community land trusts or housing co-ops, can help preserve the local character while expanding supply.

- Streamline planning and release suitable land. In rural Scotland, land release near town centres and in brownfield sites often stumbles on planning delays and infrastructure gaps. Reform should accelerate permission for accessible housing projects, ensure infrastructure (roads, water, electricity) is promised upfront, and allow modular construction to bring down costs while maintaining high accessibility and quality.

- Measure, learn, and report on outcomes. Any reform package should include concrete targets for accessible and adaptable homes, plus annual reporting on progress in rural areas. That data is crucial to adjust policy and ensure money is spent where it makes a real difference.

In short, the reforms that would actually increase supply and improve quality here are those that embed accessibility and adaptability into the backbone of new builds, fund rapid retrofits, invest in supported and student key-worker housing in rural settings, and recognise our cultural and geographic specifics. If the reforms stop at generic brownfield incentives or urban-focused targets, we’ll keep seeing growth in numbers of houses that don’t work for a large portion of our communities. I urge policymakers to embed these priorities as non-negotiable conditions in the housing reform agenda.

I strongly support reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing to secure on-site affordable homes and essential infrastructure, with greater transparency and enforceable delivery obligations. Too often, affordable housing figures are negotiated behind closed doors or softened in viability assessments, leaving communities unsure what will actually be delivered. Reforms should require on-site affordable units unless a robust, time-bound off-site alternative is agreed with strict delivery covenants and penalties. In my area, a medium-sized development funded by CIL outlined 30% affordable housing in its planning papers, but the final delivery and timing were not clearly tracked. A public dashboard showing commitments, delivery milestones, and actual completions would help residents and councils hold developers to account. Improved local data and monitoring—paired with a dedicated enforcement capacity in planning teams—would also close the gap between promises and delivery. Beyond housing, I want infrastructure funded upfront: school places, GP capacity, and road improvements tied to planning obligations. With these reforms, younger households like mine would have a fairer chance of staying local, and communities would grow sustainably.

Agree: Reform to prioritise wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older residents and key workers; raise energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits to cut bills; strengthen licensing and quality standards while promoting longer tenancies to protect both tenants and small landlords.

Living in Wales and navigating housing costs as a young adult, I see why an ambitious reform programme could help. I’m open to major public investment in council and housing association building to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes, but only if rents stay truly affordable and maintenance is guaranteed. The idea should come with strong protections against future rent spikes and high service charges, and with durable, well‑designed homes that meet energy standards.

Crucially, any new housing must be service-ready. I’d want funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing so communities aren’t stranded. In my area, new estates often lack a reliable bus link or GP access, which makes everyday life and long-term sustainability harder.

Practical reforms I’d back include prioritising brownfield sites, faster planning, and a clear requirement for energy efficiency and modern construction methods to cut running costs. We should also ensure local jobs and training for the build and management of these homes, and a mix of tenures to avoid stigma.

This approach could work, but delivery and ongoing maintenance must be transparent and locally accountable.

In our part of Scotland the gap between what people can afford and what is built is widening. Waiting lists for social housing are longer, private rents bite harder, and new homes often feel designed more for investors than for families trying to put down roots. I think the reforms that will work best are those that put land and housing into community hands, while also embracing modern ways of building so we can get quality homes on the ground quickly. I support community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build, and modern methods of construction as practical, accountable ways to grow affordable, good‑quality supply in a way that communities can sustain long term. 

Community land trusts offer a real hope of affordability that lasts. When a local group can acquire land at a realistic, community‑friendly price and place homes on it with long‑lasting affordability covenants, rents or prices stay within reach even as market pressures rise. Crucially, communities have a say in the siting, design and ongoing management of those homes, which tends to create more stable neighbourhoods. There are active pilots across Scotland supported by the Scottish Government and by organisations like Community Land Scotland, aimed at turning vacant or marginal sites into affordable housing through community ownership. In my own area I’ve spoken with residents who are forming a CLT to bring a derelict site back into use. They want to keep the development small and well integrated with the surrounding village, with a governance structure that ensures affordability for the long term. 

Housing co‑operatives are another route worth backing. They combine democratic control with a strong social ethos, so residents aren’t just renting—they have a stake and a say in management and future allocations. A village co‑op model I’ve heard about would allow a mix of tenures, with socially rented homes alongside ownership or shared ownership options, all governed by members. This approach tends to create a resilient community where maintenance and stewardship are kept local, which helps prevent fundamental reversals in affordability if economic winds change. 

Self‑build and modern methods of construction offer a route to speed and higher quality, not compromise. Group self‑build projects can pool local skills, spread costs, and reduce procurement risk, while giving people ownership of the design from the outset. Modern methods of construction—especially panelised timber and modular systems—can dramatically cut on‑site time, reduce waste and produce very high energy efficiency. In a few Scottish pilot schemes, modular timber homes have gone up in a matter of months and demonstrated excellent airtightness and low running costs, which helps keep homes affordable over the long term. There is potential to replicate this approach more widely if regulatory, planning and procurement bottlenecks are addressed. 

To realise these benefits, we need targeted reforms that streamline how land and funding can be deployed for community-led housing, without sacrificing quality or safety. Key measures would include:
- Land and planning: make land release to CLTs and co‑ops straightforward, with long‑term protection for affordability. Require a portion of public or major development sites to be offered to community groups at affordable terms, with fast‑tracked transfers and pre‑application planning support so schemes can move quickly from idea to shovel‑ready.

i strongly believe i am writing as an older resident living in England to say I strongly support reforms that would increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. First, targeted finance and better procurement access for small‑ and medium‑sized builders would unlock a lot of local potential. If there were a dedicated finance channel backed by local authorities or Homes England that prioritised SME bids, with clear, simple procurement routes that recognise social value and local employment, we would see more of these schemes move from drawing board to bricks and tiles. A “local‑first” procurement approach—where councils reserve a chunk of work for SME builders and provide support through the planning process—would keep money circulating in the community and deliver homes that reflect local needs and character.

Second, reforming small‑sites policy and providing planning support is essential. Planning departments should have streamlined processes for sites under a certain size, with pre‑application advice and a planning in principle route where appropriate. This would reduce delays and the risk of sites sitting idle for years. Local authorities could publish clear checklists showing what is required and how viability will be assessed, so small developers can plan with confidence. Importantly, small sites should be encouraged to deliver a genuine mix of affordable tenures, including some homes for first‑time buyers and older residents, designed for accessibility and energy efficiency. In practice, a light touch planning framework, paired with dedicated planning officers who understand SME needs, would speed up approvals without compromising quality.

Third, I welcome reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations. The current process can feel opaque, and affordable obligations sometimes end up diluted or deferred. If viability assessments were published in a consistent format, with independent scrutiny and a clear mechanism to appeal, communities could see that the costs of land, construction, and required affordable provision are balanced fairly. Crucially, obligations to deliver affordable homes and the necessary infrastructure—on site where possible, with credible in‑lieu options where needed—should be enforceable and time‑bound. We should also see a more predictable pooled approach to CIL and other contributions so the money actually reaches schools, GP surgeries, and transport improvements in a timely fashion. When local residents can rely on better funded and sooner‑delivered infrastructure, new housing becomes much more acceptable to the wider community.

Finally, encouraging purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management is key to increasing long‑term rental supply. Build‑to‑Rent, when properly regulated, offers stable tenancies, high standards of management, and reliable maintenance regimes, which are especially important for older residents who want to stay in their own communities. These schemes should carry robust affordability covenants, so rents remain genuinely affordable for a long period, and be backed by professional, local management that addresses repairs quickly and keeps shared spaces well cared for. I am encouraged by recent local examples where BTR developments include well‑designed family and accessible units, with on‑site facilities and on‑going resident engagement led by the managing company. A commitment to long‑term stewardship, with transparent reporting on rents, repairs, and energy efficiency, would make these schemes an enduring asset rather than a temporary boost.

Taken together, these reforms would help us build more homes that families can afford, near schools, trains, and amenities, with the quality to last. I’d urge policymakers to align finance, planning, and housing delivery in a way that supports local builders, protects tenants, and ensures that every new home contributes to a healthier, more inclusive neighbourhood. Thank you for considering these points.

From where I sit in England, with family and neighbours watching the monthly bills rise and the stock of affordable homes shrinking, I think reforms should follow a careful three-pronged approach: raise energy standards for new builds and back them with solid funding for retrofits, test targeted affordability measures with robust evaluation, and unlock public land together with planning uplift to fund genuinely affordable housing and local infrastructure.

First, mandating higher energy standards for new builds makes sense if it is paired with real, accessible funding to retrofit existing stock. Climate targets and savings on bills won’t be achieved if the costs land solely on tenants or small landlords. A staged, evidence-led pathway would work best: clear targets aligned with UK carbon budgets, but with exemptions or staged requirements for small landlords who cannot absorb steep upfront costs. Funding should come from a mix of public grants, low-interest loans, and perhaps a proportion of energy supplier obligations, with a straightforward burden-sharing mechanism rather than letting rents spiral. In practice, I’ve seen new-builds fetch higher rents in our area, and elderly tenants worry about energy-efficient measures being used as a lever to push rents up further. So any policy must ensure the cost of improvements does not simply transfer to tenants, and it should prioritise practical measures like solid-wall insulation, draught-proofing, efficient heating systems, and proper ventilation, delivered by a trained local workforce. Above all, outcomes should be measured in actual bill reductions and comfort, not just compliance checks.

Second, on affordability tools like rent caps or stabilisation: I’m open to pilots that stabilise costs in the short term while we learn how to protect supply and investment long term. Any rent control should be time-limited, regionally targeted, and designed with protections so that landlords still have a reason to maintain and upgrade properties. It’s crucial that pilots include rigorous independent evaluation and a clear exit strategy if rents rise or stock is diverted away from rental use. We must avoid a scenario where price controls trigger reduced maintenance, lower quality standards, or landlords exiting the market, which would worsen supply just when affordability is most needed. Pairing pilots with strong supply-side reforms—faster planning, clearer land release, and public investment to cover legitimate maintenance costs—could help balance short-term affordability with long-term stock growth. In my experience, affordability schemes work best when tenants have stability without risking poorer-quality housing or fewer new homes being built.

Third, releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift could unlock a material amount of affordable housing and essential local infrastructure. I would support a transparent, rapid disposal of suitable public plots for genuinely affordable homes, with a clear proportion reserved for social or affordable rent and shared ownership. Planning uplift should be captured in a way that funds local schools, GP capacity, transport links, and flood defences, not diverted into general budgets. A well-designed land value capture mechanism would help ensure the gains from planning permissions aren’t captured by landowners alone, but reinvested locally. Importantly, local communities must be involved and design quality safeguarded; we should not swap one set of problems for another by simply building more without infrastructure to support it. In many districts there are publicly owned sites that sit idle or are used for low-intensity purposes; unlocking these for genuinely affordable homes, alongside the necessary infrastructure, could make a real difference.

To make this work, I’d like to see a clear national framework that still respects local discretion: a predictable timetable for energy standards and retrofit funding, well-designed pilot schemes with published results, and a straightforward process for disposing of public land with enforceable affordable-housing commitments. All these reforms need robust monitoring, a focus on quality of life for current residents, and safeguards against unintended consequences for supply. If done well, they could deliver good-quality homes that people can afford, reduce bills, and strengthen local communities instead of pulling resources away from other essential services.
