My worry is that without proper funding and streamlined processes, these reforms could push up rents or slow development, especially for small developers. To work, I’d like to see ring-fenced capital for retrofits, a simple, predictable grant pathway rather than annual bidding rounds, and transitional support for smaller sites. Also, allow flexible approaches—such as off-site or modular solutions and phased implementations—to avoid delaying supply.

If these safeguards are in place, the proposed reforms could improve both the quantity and quality of affordable homes without falling into the trap of placing disproportionate costs on tenants or landlords.

I strongly support these reforms. Strengthening licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards, alongside promoting longer tenancies, is the fairest way to lift the quality of private rents and give families real security, without squeezing viable small landlords out of the market. In our area, too many older properties fall short on safety and energy standards; a clear, well-funded national framework would raise that baseline for everyone. I also welcome limits on excessive fees and a measured, phased approach so small landlords can adapt, with proper guidance and practical support to upgrade homes.

On supply, prioritising finance, procurement access and a small-sites policy makes sense for local SMEs and local builders. Local authorities could offer loan guarantees or easier planning routes for sites up to about 10–15 homes on brownfield land, plus dedicated pre-application planning advice so projects don’t stall. I’d like to see procurement that favours SME builders and local firms, with a predictable pipeline of affordable homes from new schemes. In our town we have potential small sites that could deliver ten affordable homes quickly with sensible planning support and capital backing. Together, these steps would deliver more affordable, good-quality homes while supporting small landlords and local builders alike.

Housing costs in my town in England are rising faster than wages, and it’s easy to feel stuck—the kind of squeeze that makes starting a family or staying here feel uncertain. I’ve been trying to relocate from a rented apartment into something more secure for a few friends and colleagues, but eve with decent salaries, the deposits and rent levels push affordability out of reach. I’m open to ambitious reforms that could unlock land for genuinely affordable homes and fund the local infrastructure we need, but I’m wary of policy changes that look good on paper and end up slowing development or pushing land prices up elsewhere. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift could be part of the answer if done carefully. Councils own sites that sit idle for years—old schools, garages, council offices, even car parks—that could be repurposed for mixed-tenure housing, with a clear, time-boun plan showing how the site will deliver affordable homes alongsidr market homes. In my area, for instance, there are several small council-owned sites that could be redeveloped with a meaningful affordable component without eating into grren space. If uplift from planning permission—essentially the extra value created when a site is rezoned for higher-density or different use—were captured through a levy or a taxx and ring-fenced for affordable housing and local infrastructure, that couldd reduce the need to compete for scarce subsidy pot after subsidy pot. The idea of a predictable, dedicated stream of funding is appealing, especially to help upgrade locall roads, schools, and green spaces that genuinely serve the new residents too. But the mechanism has to be designed to work in practice, not just on a whiteboard. Planning uplift must be predictable, transparen and proportionate. It shouldn’t simply raise land prices to the point where developers target more land or bigger profits elsewhere, or deter small builders who could deliver affordable homes alongside market units. It would help if the uplift capture was modestly phasedd and tied to deliverability milestones—so money flows only as homes are completed and rents or prices are set at genuinely affordable levels for local residents, not just a nominal percentage on paper. A few concrete guardrails would matter: - Clear definitions of affordability and delivery timelines, with benchmarks that local people can understand and hold the council to account. I’d like to see affordable homes pegged to local incomes, with a mix of social rent, affordable rent, and starter/shared ownership options. - Ring-fenced, auditable funds for housing and infrastructure delivery in the same locality. Annual reporting should be public, with independent oversight to prevent leakage into general budgets. - A balanced approach to land release. Prioritise brownfield and previously used public land first, with green space protected unless there’s a compelling public benefit case. Ensure there’s a transparent process for selecting sites and implementing designs that fit the local character. - Support for small and medium-sized builders. Large developers might be able to absorb uplift more easily, but local, smaller builders are often best at delivering a steady stream of affordable homes if the rules are workable and the upfront costs are manageable. - Delivery of infrastructure in parallel with housing. It’s onee thing to fund a new block of flats; it’s another to secure a funded upgrade to the local road network, flood defenses, or a new GP surgeryy in time for the residents moving in. - Environmental and quality standards. Sustainability should be baked in from the outset—energy efficiency, flood resilience, and high-quality design—so that new homes are affordable to heat and maintain, and don’t require retrofits that add to the burden on households. Personally, I’ve seen how the current Section 106 approach can lead to unpredictable negotiations and delays, with affordable housing sometimes being a secondary consideration after pricing. A clearer, more reliable uplift mechanism could reduce the variability and make the delivery of affordable homes a more certain outcome, not an aspirational add-on. It would also help communities see the benefits of new development rather than perceive it as an encroachment on local character and services I’d also want to see pilots in a few willing authorities to test different levy rates, eligible site types, and governance arrangements. If a pilot shows that uplift capture can fund a ring-fenced affordable housing supply and reliable local infrastructurr without deterring growth, I’d be inclined to support expanding it.. The key is to move from “more land value capture” rhetoric to measurable outcomes: actual extra homes affordablr to local households, better roads and schools, and a planning system that incentivises good development rather than bottlenecks it. Ultimately, reforms need to make a real difference for people like me who are trying to get a foothold in the housing ladder. If we can deliver a steady stream of genuinely affordable homes on surplus public land, funded by transparent uplift levies and paired with robust protections for local infrastructure and greenspace, it could be a meaningful step forward. But the risk of unintended consequences—price inflation elsewhere, slow delivery, or weak accountability—means we should tread carefully and test monitor, and iterate before a nationwide rollout.

We support reforms that prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before releasing greenfield land or Green Belt areas. In our area, derelict mills and disused offices sit alongside rising housing need, so a brownfield‑first approach is essential to protect landscapes while boosting supply. Key reforms we’d back are: 1) A mandatory brownfield‑first planning framework with faster, clearly time‑bound decisions for conversions and infill schemes, plus simpler routes for change of use where design and infrastructure standards are met. 2) Strong incentives to bring empty homes back into use—levies on long‑term empties, grants for conversion, and local matching funds to fund repairs and energy retrofit. 3) Requiring affordable housing on brownfield schemes (roughly 30‑40%, depending on local need), with a mix of social, affordable rent and mid‑market products, to ensure genuinely affordable supply. 4) Use of public land for affordable housing with robust delivery deadlines and safeguards against leakage into market sale; community land trusts and co‑housing models could play a role here. 5) Investment in infrastructure and high design/energy standards to ensure quality, accessibility and landscape protection, with strict protections for conservation areas and Green Belt boundaries. 6) Transparent reporting and local accountability to track brownfield capacity, delivery timelines and delivery of affordable homes.

From our organisation’s perspective across communities in England, reforms that lean heavily on market-led supply will not reliably deliver affordable, good-quality homes quickly enough. The emphasis should shift to empowering community‑led approaches that keep homes affordable in the long term.

We strongly support expanding community land trusts, housing co-operatives and self‑build projects, complemented by modern methods of construction. These approaches stabilise prices, give local people a say in design and stewardship, and can speed up delivery through modular and factory-made components. To realise this, councils should be able to allocate public land at low rents to CLTs and co‑ops, with long leases and strong local governance.

Planning and procurement rules should be updated to accelerate community‑led schemes and streamline MMC approvals without compromising safety or energy efficiency. A national framework for modular design and quality checks would help councils approve high‑quality builds faster.

We also need robust minimum quality standards and longer tenancies to protect tenants, while providing targeted support to small landlords to transition during the shift. Strengthened selective licensing and enforcement against poor practice are essential, but must be paired with genuine transition support.

There is real evidence in our area that well-supported CLTs and co‑ops deliver genuinely affordable homes with lasting community benefit. Reform should prioritise local, community‑led delivery and stronger standards to ensure affordable, high‑quality housing for the long term.

I live in England and want to see more affordable, good‑quality homes built locally. Reforms should target finance, procurement access, small‑sites policy and planning support to help SME and local builders increase diverse, local housing supply. Local builders often lack patient, affordable finance and access to procurement routes that favour big firms. A dedicated fund or guarantees for SME builders, plus streamlined, local procurement frameworks that shortlist small firms, would unlock more homes on brownfield land in our town centres. 

Better data and accountability matter too. Councils need robust delivery dashboards showing planning approvals, starts, completions, and affordable‑home delivery against commitments. If developers miss milestones, there should be clawbacks or penalties and targeted support to unlock stalled sites. 

And we should grow purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with long‑term professional management. Affordability covenants tied to rents, secure maintenance, and clear tenancy rights would stabilise rents and quality for renters like my friends and colleagues. 

In practice, I’ve seen small sites delayed by planning backlogs and lack of local knowledge within authorities. A package of support—financial, planning, and performance monitoring—would get more genuinely affordable homes built faster, with better quality and long‑term management.

I disagree with reforming Section 106/CIL and viability testing; tighter obligations could slow schemes and raise costs, reducing affordable supply. We should strengthen enforcement of quality, extend tenancies, and examine rent caps via pilots with clear impact data.

Agree. Reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area centre on releasing surplus public land and ensuring the uplift in land value created by planning is captured to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. In our district there are disused council sites and former NHS parcels that sit idle; bringing them forward with clear timetables would unlock more homes without pushing up private rents. The planning uplift should be ring-fenced: a transparent levy or Section 106/CIL mechanism that guarantees a substantial portion of affordable homes on all larger sites and funds for neighbourhood roads, schools and flood defences. 

I also back mandating higher energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits. The Future Homes Standard, plus grants or low‑interest loans for insulation, heat pumps and boiler upgrades, would cut bills and help meet climate targets while avoiding excessive costs being passed to tenants or landlords. In my experience, energy costs are a real burden; better-quality, energy-efficient homes keep bills down and attract families to sustainable developments with well-planned infrastructure.

I favour reforms that prioritis regeneration, infill, and converting long-term empty properties before any Green Belt release, with strong investment from councils and housing associations to deliver genuinely affordable social rents. Support community land trusts, co-ops, self-build and modern methods of construction, with robust planning and quality standards.

I’m concerned that pushing large public investment into council and housing association building programmes isn't the right way to secure genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. In my area, the promise of new social homes has repeatedly been slowed by procurement, overspends and governance hurdles, while existing housing stock decays and energy bills rise for tenants. Debt taken on by local authorities to fund new builds can become a budget burden for decades, crowding out money for repairs or supported housing services people actually rely on. Too often, land costs, fees and complex planning add months or years to delivery, meaning households lose years of stability. 

Reforms should instead prioritise accelerating repairs and energy efficiency in the current stock, and streamlining planning processes without sacrificing safety and design quality. Any expansion should be tightly targeted to those in greatest need and come with long-term affordability guarantees and maintenance funding. I’d resist schemes that rely on new-build consortia funded by public debt without clear, enforceable safeguards for residents.

Release surplus public land, capture planning uplift to fund affordable homes and infrastructure, and simplify planning while encouraging private-sector delivery with robust quality controls; avoid heavy, public-building programmes that risk inefficiency and long-term costs.

I welcome reforms that would deliver more affordable, good-quality homes that are wheelchair-accessible, adaptable, and suitable for older people, plus supported housing and student key-worker accommodation close to work and services. In my area, the shortage is acute, and too many families face long waits or have to move into unsuitable homes. Any reform must be rooted in practical, deliverable steps that recognise rural realities, community needs, and cultural diversity.

First, planning and land allocation should actively promote accessible and adaptable homes as a standard rather than an afterthought. I would like to see a robustly enforced minimum proportion of affordable housing built to accessible and adaptable standards (and for suitable developments, wheelchair-accessible units). These homes should be designed so that people can stay in their homes as needs change, with features like step-free access, wide doorways, with bathrooms and kitchens ready for easy adaptation. In rural areas, where land is scarce, allowing small, well-served rural exception sites with clear local connection criteria would help communities where demand is most acute. The aim must be to avoid “one size fits all” housing and instead require a mix that reflects the makeup of each community, including older residents, disabled people, students, and key workers.

Second, targeted funding and delivery models are essential. There needs to be dedicated capital for extra-care and other supported housing, with on-site care where appropriate, so older and more dependent residents can live independently for longer. We should also unlock retrofit funding to bring existing stock up to accessible standards and to reduce energy bills, which is a big concern for households on modest incomes. I would support incentives for modular construction and local-authority partnerships to accelerate delivery while maintaining quality. A portion of Right to Buy receipts should be ring-fenced to replace sold homes with new affordable, well-designed units, including wheel-chair-friendly homes, rather than letting stock shrink.

Third, the housing design must reflect the diverse needs of our communities. New homes should incorporate lifetime homes principles and universal design, with adaptable layouts that can be reconfigured for carers or family needs. This is especially important for older people, but it also helps families stay together as circumstances change. In areas with strong cultural or community identities, we should encourage flexible common spaces, appropriate community rooms, accessible outdoor space, and clear wayfinding. For student key-worker housing, think of schemes near hospitals and universities that provide affordable rents linked to income, with safe cycle routes and reliable bus links to critical workplaces—sokey workers can live near where they work without paying the premium that currently pushes them away from apprenticeship and early-career opportunities.

Fourth, rural delivery and local capacity are crucial. Local authorities should be empowered to use small sites and conversions (for example, repurposing redundant public buildings or shops) to create accessible flats, with planning and procurement streamlined for speed without compromising safety. Local partnerships—housing associations, universities, NHS trusts, parish councils and community land trusts—could jointly deliver mixed schemes that include older-person housing, supported options, and student accommodation, all designed to be affordable and well-integrated into town or village life.

Finally, robust oversight and meaningful involvement will help ensure these reforms work. The government should publish clear targets for accessible, affordable housing delivery, tied to funding streams and planning performance, with regular monitoring and public reporting. Residents should have a meaningful role in design decisions, and schemes should include on-site or nearby support services when appropriate, to prevent isolation and hospital admissions.

In short, I’m strongly in favour of reforms that prioritise accessibility and adaptability, ensure adequate supported housing is available, and deliver affordable accommodation for students and key workers near essential services. If these reforms are backed by long-term funding, local collaboration, and rigorous delivery standards, we can make meaningful progress toward the kind of homes our ageing population—and our communities more broadly—really need.

I’ve lived in a town in the south of England for many years, and I’ve seen housing pressures bite hardest where supply is slow and poorly maintained. To increase affordable, good‑quality homes, reforms should prioritise purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. These can deliver long‑term rental supply with predictable rents, decent repairs, energy efficiency, and clear tenant protections if backed by robust planning conditions and enforced standards.

At the same time, I’d want reform to start with regeneration, infill, and the conversion of vacant offices and shops and long‑term empty homes, rather than releasing greenfield land or disturbing Green Belt landscapes. In my area there are dormant sites and empty homes that could be brought back into use with targeted funding, simpler approvals for brownfield projects, and requirements to deliver affordable units alongside market homes.

Any reform should tie affordability to the homes in perpetuity and insist on professional management, good design, and adequate infrastructure—schools, GP capacity, and transport links—so communities aren’t left with poor-quality stock just to hit numbers. A cautious, phased approach that protects landscapes while unlocking regeneration seems the most practical path.

absolutely our organisation represents residents across England and we want reforms that genuinely increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. A mixed approach is needed.

On one hand, major investment in council and housing association building programmes can deliver long‑term social rents for low‑income households and create stable communities. But the funding must be predictable, efficient and accompanied by strong design and retrofit standards, so homes are energy‑efficient and affordable to run for decades. In our area, procurement delays and spiralling costs have undermined projects; simpler procurement routes, shared building standards, and longer‑term funding commitments would help get homes built sooner without compromising quality.

On the other hand, we must prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes before any release of greenfield land or Green Belt. In a town near us, a derelict office block with 40 potential homes has stood empty for years while families struggle with local overcrowding. Bringing such assets back into use, alongside converting empty homes, can deliver quicker, well‑located homes with less environmental disruption.

Finally, enforce stringent quality controls, establish robust local monitoring, and ensure affordability remains protected over the long term!

To increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in my area, the reforms that would work best are: substantial public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rent homes for low-income households; encouragement of purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to increase long-term rental supply; and streamlined planning processes that speed up delivery while keeping environmental safeguards.

In practice, that means ring-fenced funding for social housing so building can start quickly, simpler and faster planning approvals, and standardised Section 106 obligations that prioritise genuinely affordable units. Build-to-Rent should include long-term leases and high management standards so residents feel secure and well supported. Redeveloping brownfield sites with quality standards (thermal efficiency, modern insulation, and clean energy) can deliver better homes faster and reduce pressure on greenfield areas.

From my own experience, delays in planning have pushed potential projects back by months, while private rents in the area keep rising. If we can combine robust quality with predictable timelines, we will create affordable homes that families can stay in long term and communities can rely on.

I strongly support reforms to ensure more affordable, good‑quality homes. In particular, Section 106, CIL and viability testing should be more transparent and enforceable. Viability assessments must be independently reviewed, with on‑site affordable housing as the default where viable, and robust, ring‑fenced contributions for infrastructure if on‑site delivery isn't possible. When contributions are required, money should be earmarked for local schools, roads and GP capacity, paid promptly, with clear triggers and penalties for delays. In our area, I’ve seen schemes where obligations were diluted later; this must not continue. 

Second, local data, monitoring and accountability must improve. Councils need dedicated planning and enforcement capacity, and transparent public data on what was promised and what is delivered. A simple online dashboard showing planning obligations and delivery milestones would help residents and builders. 

Lastly, encourage Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. Long‑term ownership can guarantee quality and provide reliable rental options for families, not just quick sales.
Yes. Reform Section 106, CIL and viability testing with transparent, enforceable on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding to deliver more affordable, good-quality homes in my area.

I welcome reforms that prioritise regenerating our existing towns and villages before releasing any greenfield land or Green Belt. There are already places in our area where a little imagination and targeted investment could unlock many affordable, good‑quality homes without eroding our landscapes or the character of our communities. In practice, this means a brownfield‑first approach backed by practical planning reform, better use of empty homes, and smarter funding that rewards quality, not delay.

What I’d like to see:

- Put brownfield land and long‑term empty homes at the front of the queue. There are several sites nearby—a disused mill near the river, a vacant high‑street shop, and a former office block—that could be transformed into affordable flats or supported housing with modest remediation. If government policy makes brownfield regeneration the default, with clear targets (for example, a substantial annual share of new homes built on brownfield land), local authorities would be better equipped to plan and deliver.

- Strengthen planning levers that make infill and conversions easier, but with guardrails for quality. Permit more office-to-residential conversions and development on small, well‑chosen infill sites through streamlined pre‑application advice and permissive, design‑led development orders, while ensuring historic or conservation areas retain their character. This should be paired with robust energy and accessibility standards and a requirement for good design that fits the local context.

- Use empty homes as a live resource. A clear, simple framework to bring long‑term empties back into use could include penalties for long‑term vacancies, targeted grants for conversion, and incentives for landlords to retrofit for affordable rent. In our town, a shop that has stood empty for years could be converted into a small affordable housing block with ground‑floor community space, if a viable financial model exists.

- Make affordable housing genuinely affordable and well‑built. Reform viability testing so that affordable housing contributions are not a victim of protracted negotiations. Encourage tenure diversity—affordable rent, social rent, or shared ownership—on brownfield sites, with high standards for energy efficiency (and the retrofit of existing homes where appropriate) to reduce bills for households.

- Strengthen infrastructure alongside growth. It is not enough to approve homes if schools, GP services, waste drainage, and transport cannot cope. I’d like to see reforms that require pooled funding for infrastructure tied to housing development, supported by a clearer, timelier mechanism for Community Infrastructure Levy or Section 106 contributions that actually deliver the facilities local people need.

- Local voice and landscape protection. Maintain a strong emphasis on landscape and green space preservation. A ‘brownfield first, landscape‑led’ rule should be enshrined in policy, with mandatory consideration of local plans, environmental net gains, and climate resilience. New homes must have good access to public transport and avoid tunnel visions of sprawl that damage the countryside.

- Enable delivery through public land and community models. Where local authorities hold surplus land, release it for housing with strong affordable shares, and support community land trusts and housing co‑ops that can deliver long‑term stewardship and community benefit.

In summary, the most effective reforms for increasing affordable, good‑quality homes in our area would start from regenerating vacant and underused spaces, then infill and conversions, with greenfield or Green Belt release considered only after brownfield opportunities and housing needs have been fully addressed. Practical planning changes, targeted use of empty homes, improved funding for infrastructure and retrofit, and a strong emphasis on design quality and landscape protection will help ensure new homes fit well with existing communities and protect the countryside for future generations.

i strongly believe living in England and currently looking for my first long‑term home, I can see how the gap between wages and rents makes it hard to save for a deposit and to stay in one place. It’s essential that any scheme comes with strong tenant protections, transparent reporting, and independent evaluation so we can see what actually happens to the number of homes available to rent and the long‑term quality of those homes.

- Increase public and affordable housing supply: expand capital investment in affordable homes, especially on publicly owned land and in partnership with housing associations. Require a meaningful share (for example, 25–40%) of affordable units in new developments where viable, to ensure a pipeline of truly affordable homes alongside market homes.

- Stabilise and improve the private rented sector (with incentives for landlords): offer grants or tax relief to upgrade energy efficiency and safety in existing rental stock, and create longer‑term tenancy options where both tenants and landlords feel secure. Strong deposit protection, fair eviction rules, and clear maintenance responsibilities would build trust and reduce turnover, helping landlords keep properties in decent condition.
- Targeted rent support where needed: combine rent stabilisation pilots with targeted housing assistance for those on the lowest incomes, so affordability improves without relying solely on people’s savings or loans to cover rent. This helps people stay in the area where they study or work while councils invest in new homes.
- Local empowerment and performance monitoring: give local authorities the levers to tailor solutions to their area, while mandating regular, independent evaluation of both affordability and supply outcomes. The focus should be on net increases in available homes, not just temporary rent relief.

From my own experience, I’ve seen rents rise quickly in my city, even as job prospects feel uncertain for young people starting out. A stable, predictable rent level would make budgeting easier and would help people like me save for a deposit or for a move to a place that suits our needs—without trapping us in rising costs. I’m not against landlords or investments—in fact, sensible, well‑regarded landlords should be part of the solution. But we need reforms that increase the number of affordable homes available and keep homes good‑quality, safe, and energy‑efficient.

In short, a balanced package that pairs targeted rent‑stabilisation pilots with a robust supply‑driven reform programme—planning speed, public land release, modern construction, and landlord support—offers the best chance of genuinely increasing affordable, good‑quality homes in our area while protecting investment and opportunity for landlords and developers. The ultimate goal should be more homes that people can actually afford to rent and live in long term, with clear safety and quality guarantees.

From my perspective as a pensioner in England, I believe the most effective reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes lie in getting more use from what we already have, not a rush to greenfield sites. Regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant buildings and long‑term empty homes should come first. In my town, a disused mill and several empty shops sit idle while new homes creep onto the edge of the Green Belt. If planners could fast‑track conversions and councils were given stronger powers to compulsory purchase and bring these properties back into use, we’d gain affordable homes much quicker and without wrecking landscapes. Brownfield sites should be prioritised over Green Belt release, with strict quality standards so the new homes are pleasant and energy efficient.

On energy, I support higher standards for new builds but the big burden is retrofits. A funded retrofit programme for existing houses and empty properties would reduce bills for tenants and protect landlords from disproportionate costs. In short, better use of existing stock, smart regeneration, and targeted retrofits—not more Green Belt development—would deliver affordable, good quality homes.

From where I live in Wales, the push to mandate higher energy standards for new builds and to fund retrofits may seem wise for bills and climate, but it risks pricing many would-be buyers and renters out of affordable homes. In our area, a modest 3-bedroom scheme I looked at last year faced an extra 15-20k per unit after energy-compliance costs, delaying delivery and nudging rents higher. That simply contradicts the aim of affordability.

I would prefer that supply reforms focus first on regeneration, infill and conversions of vacant buildings and long-term empty homes, before releasing any greenfield land or green belt. We should robustly prioritise reusing existing stock and improving energy efficiency in existing homes to reduce bills, rather than building new at higher cost.

Additionally, we need better local data, stronger developer accountability and dedicated funding for councils to plan, enforce and deliver. In my county, planning delays and a lack of enforcement mean promised affordable units vanish from the delivery timetable. We need binding delivery agreements with penalties, faster consents for brownfield sites, and more support for councils to build capacity. These steps would increase supply without pricing people out.

I support reforms that focus on regenerating towns, filling gaps with infill housing, and converting vacant or long-term empty homes before any greenfield development. Only then should we consider releasing Green Belt land to protect landscapes and character.

I live in England and rent a small flat with friends, so I’m close to the realities of how housing supply and bills affect people in the private rented sector. The proposal to reform and accelerate energy efficiency in homes feels like the right direction to both increase the supply of affordable, good-quality housing and cut bills in the long run. My sense is that the best reforms are those that couple stronger standards for new builds with substantial funding and practical support to upgrade existing homes, especially in the private rented sector where a lot of turnover happens and where tenants often shoulder the burden of high energy costs.

First, mandating higher energy standards for new builds is sensible, provided it is done in a way that does not stall supply. I’d support aiming for net-zero-ready or EPC A-rated homes within the next decade, with a fabric-first approach: heavy insulation, airtight construction, high-performance windows, and ready-to-install heat pumps or other low-carbon heating systems. But to avoid bottlenecks, the policy should include clear transitional timelines, flexible compliance routes for innovative but proven technologies, and strong pre-approved supply chains so builders aren’t waiting months for materials.

Second, funds for retrofits matter enormously for affordability and climate targets. A significant portion of the housing stock in our cities is old and inefficient, and tenants bear the brunt of high bills. A properly designed retrofit program—focused on the private rented sector and social housing—could pay for essential upgrades like cavity and external wall insulation, loft insulation, draught-proofing, double or triple glazing where feasible, solar gains, and efficient low-carbon heating systems such as heat pumps. There should be funding models that protect tenants from rent increases tied to retrofit costs. For example, grants or low-interest loans could be used to upgrade an entire block or street, with the repayment wrapped into long-term energy savings rather than added to rents.

In practice, I’d like to see a simple, city-scale or borough-scale delivery approach: one-stop retrofit services that handle surveys, design, and procurement; bulk procurement to drive down prices; and straightforward planning approvals that recognise the constraints of working in occupied homes. Local authorities could lead by prioritising the worst-performing properties and communities, including those with high energy poverty, and using public land or council energy procurement to accelerate upgrade schemes.

There should also be robust support for landlords, especially small ones, so reforms don’t price them out of the market and reduce supply. Grants or tax relief could be available for a landlord who upgrades multiple units at once, with clear timelines and expectations about quality and safety. A “pay-back” model that shares energy savings with tenants could help keep rents stable while delivering the upgrades. In addition, we need strong enforcement and quality checks to make sure retrofit work isn’t rushed or shoddy—quality training for installers and clear standards will be essential.

From a tenant’s perspective, these reforms must deliver tangible, short-term relief and long-term security. Reduced energy bills should be a real outcome of the upgrades, not an excuse to raise rents elsewhere. I’d support a public dashboard showing progress—how many homes upgraded, what the expected energy savings are, and the average impact on bills—so communities can hold agencies and landlords to account.

A personal example helps illustrate why this matters. In our street, several terraces have old, poorly insulated walls and windows. A landlord who could access retrofit funding would likely upgrade those properties; families in those homes would see lower bills in winter, warmer rooms, and better air quality. That stability makes housing feel more affordable and encourages longer tenancies, which in turn supports a more stable local housing market and better conditions for communities to thrive.

I’m aware of the risks: supply chain constraints, upfront costs, and the possibility that some reforms could push rents up if not carefully designed. So the reforms must be gradual and well targeted. For instance, new-build standards should be phased in, with exemptions where land constraints or costs would unreasonably slow supply, while retrofit funding focuses first on the most inefficient and energy-poor homes. Policies should include protections for tenants during works and ensure that savings are actually passed through to residents, not absorbed by higher rents elsewhere in the building. 

Overall, I believe the reforms you’re proposing—strong energy standards for new builds coupled with well-funded, well-designed retrofit programs—can unlock more affordable, higher-quality housing while also helping the UK meet climate targets. With careful implementation, a supportive funding model for landlords, and transparent accountability, we can reduce energy bills for tenants, lower emissions, and create a housing market that grows in a way that’s fair to renters and beneficial to communities.

Living in England, I’ve learned the debate about affordable, good‑quality homes isn’t just about numbers on a plan. On our street, a derelict plot has sat empty for five years, and every time I walk past I wonder how many more people will need to leave because there isn’t a sustainable mix of housing and services nearby. The reality is that even when new homes appear, families worry about whether schools, GP surgeries, and reliable bus routes will cope with change. I’d welcome reforms that look beyond building more units to the wider ecosystem: better upkeep of existing housing, retrofit schemes to lower energy bills in older homes, and services that actually scale with population shifts. For instance, several nearby terraced houses have damp problems and high energy costs, which makes them unaffordable in practice—even if the market price is lower. If new developments came with robust retrofit plans, improved public transport connections, and protections for parks and green spaces, communities might feel more confident about growth rather than viewing it as a separate policy exercise.

I welcome proposals to reform housing supply and affordability. Living in England as an older person on a modest pension, I see how high private rents can bite and make essential upkeep harder for landlords too. I support considering rent caps or stabilisation as part of a careful package to improve affordability, but only if we guard against harming supply or investment. That’s why pilots are essential. 

Local pilots could cap rent rises for existing tenancies in selected areas, with sensible exemptions for new builds and for landlords upgrading homes to higher energy efficiency and safety standards. They should be independently evaluated and time-limited, with clear criteria and published results. I’d want solid evidence on how caps affect the number of rental homes, maintenance quality, and how many landlords stay in the market vs exit. If a pilot shows rents stabilise without a sizeable drop in supply, we could consider expanding it.

Alongside caps, speeding up planning, using public land for affordable homes, and ensuring a portion of new developments is genuinely affordable would help. Support for private landlords to upgrade properties could maintain quality while rents stay within reach. Overall, a cautious, evidence-led approach with pilots and robust monitoring seems right to me.

As an organisation representing residents and good-quality affordable housing in England, we welcome the government's focus on reforming planning to accelerate delivery. In our experience, the biggest barrier is not lack of land alone but the length and complexity of planning decisions. We have seen viable sites sit idle while multiple authorities chew over the same issues, and small and mid-sized builders walk away rather than escalate disputes. Streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines, while keeping environmental safeguards, would unlock sustainable growth and reduce uncertainty for developers, communities and funders alike.

We propose reforms around the following:

- Fixed timelines with transparent consequences: set statutory timelines for major, minor and change-of-use applications (for example, 16-20 weeks for major schemes, 8-12 weeks for smaller ones), with automatic approval if the authority misses the deadline unless there is a justified reason for delay. This preserves due process but removes open-ended delays that push up costs and rents.

- Proportionate zoning and clear expectations: develop simpler zoning categories at the national or regional level with clear density targets and affordable housing requirements, while preserving meaningful local input and design standards. This would enable faster decision-making on routine schemes that meet agreed criteria, freeing up capacity for more ambitious, high-quality developments.

- Digital, streamlined planning processes: a single digital planning portal with standardised validation, pre-application advice, and real-time case tracking so communities can see progress. This should include a formalised pre-application stage at lower cost to help small builders and community groups understand requirements early.

- Robust but efficient environmental safeguards: retain biodiversity net gain, climate resilience standards and energy efficiency (like on-site renewables and fabric-first approaches), but ensure these checks are integrated into the early feasibility work rather than becoming last-minute delays. We want good-quality homes that perform well, not hurried designs that fail to deliver long-term savings.

- Accelerated local plan development: ensure local plans are produced and reviewed on predictable cycles, with up-front public engagement and clear deliverability tests. When sites meet the plan's criteria, decisions should be quicker; if they don't, there should be a straightforward route to adjust plans without fragmenting the process.

- Infrastructure and developer contributions: align S106 and CIL processes to release land more quickly while guaranteeing that contributions genuinely fund needed infrastructure and affordable homes. We favour reforms that shield small schemes from onerous fees while still ensuring high-quality outcomes.

- Support for smaller builders and community-led schemes: provide fee relief, access to low-cost finance, and targeted planning advice to smaller firms who deliver a disproportionate share of affordable homes. They often face the most friction in current systems.

- Community engagement and transparency: publish clear decision rationales and maintain community dashboards showing progress against milestones. People support faster decisions if they can see that their concerns are addressed and design quality is safeguarded.

In practice, we would be happy to participate in pilot programmes in a couple of districts to test fixed timelines, digital tools and zoning criteria, with independent evaluation. If successful, we would scale quickly while ensuring robust environmental safeguards and local accountability.

In summary, reforming planning and zoning to be faster and more predictable—without watering down environmental protections—has the potential to unlock substantial affordable-housing delivery in our area. It would reduce uncertainty for developers, speed up completion of much-needed homes, and help ensure that the homes built are well-designed, energy-efficient and genuinely affordable for local families.

From our organisation based in England, we think reforms to increase affordable, good-quality homes must be paired with funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing is built. Without timely access to these services, new estates can feel unfinished and place extra pressure on residents, especially older tenants who rely on predictable, affordable infrastructure. We would back policies that require developers to fund and deliver timely transport links, safe cycling and walking routes, primary and secondary schools, GP and community health facilities, and upgraded utilities capacity in step with housing. This approach helps ensure communities are service-ready from day one and reduces reliance on car travel that increases household costs. 

Regarding energy, we support higher energy standards for new builds and targeted retrofit funding for older stock, to cut bills, meet climate targets and prevent disproportionate costs for tenants and landlords. We recognise upfront costs, so funding should be clearly allocated and time-limited, with strong accountability and value for money. In practice, phased infrastructure alongside housing with transparent funding would make genuinely affordable, high-quality homes more achievable.

Absolutely, I support reforms to boost affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Better local data and monitoring would show where promises are kept andd where delivery stalls, making sure developers meet their affordablee housing commitments. Giving councils the planning funds and enforcement capacity they need will speed up delivery without lettingg standards slip. In practice, that means clearer milestones, tougher penalties for missed obligations, and transparent dashboards so residents can see progress. Community land trusts, co‑operatives, self‑build schrmes and modern methods of construction are practical routes to faster supply and higher quality. In my town I’ve seen a local community land trust bring forward affordable homes and keep rents below markett levels, while MMC pilots cut build time and improve finish. Supporting these models alongside conventional homes wouldd diversify supply and reduce wait times for young people like me starting out. Higher energy standards for new builds and funding for retrofits are essential. They will lower bills, cut emissions and avoid shifting costs to tenants and landlords. In short, combine stronger planning delivery with innovative housing models and sustainable standards to deliver more affordable, decent homes near work and transport.

In my area, reforms should safely increase supply by mixing two approaches: create purpose-built Build-to-Rent (BTR) schemes with mixed tenure and robust management, and prioritise regeneration and infill over greenfield or Green Belt release. Key steps: 1) incentives and standards for purpose-built rental with long-term affordability covenants (genuinely affordable rents, 5–20 year affordability targets, and on-site professional management to maintain quality and responsive repairs). This would expand secure, long-term rental options without exhausting owner-occupier stock. 2) a clear preference for regenerating brownfield sites, converting vacant offices or long-empty buildings, and infill development before considering any greenfield or Green Belt release, protecting landscapes and local character. In our town centre we have an underused office block and several long-empty retail units that could yield 60–100 homes with modern insulation and energy efficiency if refurbished and managed properly. 3) streamlined planning with strong design guidance, obligatory affordable-housing contributions within mixed schemes, and long-term maintenance commitments to prevent deterioration. 4) local safeguards: tenant rights, decent living standards, and community facilities integrated with new homes. Taken together, these reforms could raise supply while delivering quality, affordable homes and protecting regional landscapes for the long term.

I welcome proposals to reform how we increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. There simply aren’t enough homes that people on ordinary salaries can afford, and too many new developments end up delivering a lot of market homes with only token affordable housing. The reforms I’d back focus on getting better data, stronger accountability for delivery, more support for small and local builders, and a clear role for community‑led models. When these parts work together, we can build faster while keeping standards high and making sure homes stay affordable for the long term.

- Improve local data, monitoring and developer accountability
  - Create a real‑time housing delivery dashboard at council level that shows permissions granted, starts on site, and actual completions by site, tenure mix and affordable share. This would help residents understand what is really being delivered and where delays are occurring.
  - Require binding delivery timetables for major sites and enforce consequences if milestones aren’t met, including stepped payments linked to milestones and, where necessary, clawback or penalties to fund reallocation to genuinely affordable homes.
  - Fund dedicated enforcement and delivery capacity in planning departments so officers can chase stalled schemes, pursue breaches of planning obligations, and keep procurement and planning on track.
  - Publish independent, quarterly reviews of performance against commitments so communities can hold both councils and developers to account.

- Target finance, procurement access, small‑sites policy and planning support for SME/local builders
  - Expand finance routes that specifically support small and local builders—grants or loan guarantees to bridge viability gaps on sites under 50–100 units, matched with clear, publishable criteria.
  - Create procurement frameworks that reserve a meaningful share of local housing contracts for small and medium‑sized firms, with simplified, proportionate due diligence to reduce cost barriers.
  - Provide planning support for small sites: early feasibility work, design guidance, and a streamlined pre‑application process to help local builders bring plots to market quickly without compromising quality.
  - Deploy a local “one‑stop planning service” that coordinates design, highways, drainage and S106 obligations so small sites aren’t drowned in red tape.

- Support community‑led housing models and modern construction methods to increase speed and long‑term affordability
  - Back community land trusts (CLTs) and housing co‑operatives as a route to secure land and keep homes affordable in perpetuity. This could start with pilot projects on surplus council or council‑acquired land where local residents have a say in design and management.
  - Facilitate self‑build and group self‑build on suitable sites through serviced plots, land swaps where appropriate, and clear, locally tailored guidance, so families and community groups can contribute to housing supply with shared risk.
  - Encourage modern methods of construction (MMC) and off‑site manufacture to raise quality, reduce build times, and improve energy efficiency. This would involve upskilling the local workforce, ensuring quality standards, and integrating MMC with local planning requirements to avoid phantom speedups that compromise design or sustainability.

In practice, I’ve seen how delays on permissions and weak accountability slow delivery and push costs up, which ultimately makes homes unaffordable. By coupling better data with firm delivery oversight and targeted support for SMEs, we unlock sites that would otherwise stall. Community‑led models give local residents a stake, help retain affordability, and often deliver better local place‑making and energy performance. And if we combine all this with modern construction practices, we can build faster without lowering standards or neglecting climate and design quality.

If these reforms are funded properly and accompanied by robust monitoring, they can deliver more affordable, high‑quality homes in a way that fits local needs and protects local character. I’d be glad to see clear milestones, published performance data and opportunities for local residents to participate in oversight. Thank you for considering these practical changes to help my area—indeed, many areas—meet the demand for decent, affordable housing.

Agree. Reforms to raise energy efficiency standards and fund retrofits are essential to meaningfully expand affordable, good-quality housing in England. Mandating higher energy standards for all new builds, with a fabric-first approach (insulation, airtightness, efficient windows) and heat pumps where appropriate, will reduce running costs for tenants and attract investment in high-quality schemes. Equally important is robust funding to retrofit the existing stock. Grants or low-interest loans for solid-wall insulation, loft and cavity insulation, draught-proofing, and mechanical ventilation would cut bills and improve comfort, making affordable homes more attractive to renters and buyers. In my area, many older terraces leak heat and energy costs are a real squeeze in winter; a retrofit programme funded by central and local government would stabilise rents and speed up delivery of new affordable homes. Streamlining planning and procurement to require high energy performance without delaying schemes would help developers bring more units to market sooner. This combination keeps costs down for tenants while delivering more good-quality homes.

To increase affordable homes in our area, I support reforms that streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while preserving environmental safeguards. A nationally consistent planning performance framework with fixed decision windows—ideally 12–18 months from enquiry to decision—would reduce uncertainty and speed delivery, especially on brownfield sites. Digital planning portals, standardised pre-application consultation, and clearer viability criteria would cut duplication. These steps must retain protections for biodiversity, air quality and energy efficiency, including biodiversity net gain and high energy standards.

Second, I back substantial public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable social rented homes. This should be long‑term, well‑governed funding with ring‑fenced capital and revenue support, enabling councils to borrow and partner with housing associations for stable delivery. Homes should meet high energy and accessible design standards, include supported accommodation where needed, and ensure local labour and supply chain benefits.

Third, we need more wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes and specialised stock: a mix of M4(2)/M4(3) dwellings, older‑person and supported housing, plus student key‑worker homes where appropriate, tailored to rural and cultural needs. Sites should be planned with services nearby, and funding for maintenance and adaptations.

In my area, planning delays and under‑funding have kept people in unsuitable homes. A coordinated reform package would help deliver affordable, high‑quality housing more quickly.

Housing affordability and stable rental options are by far the most pressing issue in my city, where students and graduates often face rising rents and short-term lets that make it hard to feel settled after finishing a course or starting a first job. I think reforms that encourage purpose-built Build-to-Rent (BTR) and mixed-tenure schemes could make a real difference, but they have to be designed with strong affordability guarantees and high-quality standards from the outset. I’d also push for planning reforms that speed things up without letting developer profits trump local needs or environmental safeguards.

First, Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure developments with affordability covenants can add much-needed long-term rental supply. When a block is purpose-built as rental housing with a professional management team, you tend to get better repairs, predictable tenancy terms, and clearer expectations about upkeep. In my experience and from stories I’ve heard around other cities, BTR can deliver better-managed blocks than fragmented buy-to-let portfolios, where landlords move out at short notice and maintenance often languishes. The key, however, is to tie rents to a genuine affordability benchmark over the long term and to cap service charges so that near-university or city-centre residents aren’t squeezed by escalating costs. Ideally, a portion of BTR units would be reserved for genuinely affordable rents for the next 30 years, with outcomes reviewed regularly to reflect local incomes and housing need. Professional on-site management should be mandatory, providing timely repairs, resident liaison, and community amenities designed to reduce isolation and support mental wellbeing—things that matter a lot to younger people starting their careers.

Mixed-tenure schemes are also vital. If a development includes social or affordable housing alongside private rental blocks, it prevents the “all market” bubble that pushes people out of the area over time. The covenants should be robust and enforceable, with independent monitoring to prevent gaming. And design matters: accessible homes, good insulation, energy-efficient systems, and layouts that suit modern lives (flexible spaces, bike storage, good digital connectivity). My friends and I want to see livable spaces with real provision for green transport and outdoor spaces, not a sea of tall towers with little community connection.

On planning reform, I’d support streamlining and simplifying processes while keeping environmental safeguards intact. Right now, delays in planning decisions—especially for mid-sized sites—can stall projects that would otherwise bring much-needed homes online quickly. A clear, predictable timetable would help developers and local councils plan better and reduce uncertainty. My suggestion would be to introduce a fast-track track for well-designed affordable or mixed-tenure schemes, with a maximum decision window—for example, 12 weeks for straightforward applications and 20 weeks for more complex ones—paired with mandatory pre-application discussions. A single digital portal could track milestones, enable early community consultation, and insist on cross-department collaboration to avoid last-minute policy changes.

That said, speed cannot come at the expense of environmental and social safeguards. Any reform must retain high standards for energy efficiency, flood-risk management, biodiversity, and green space. Brownfield-first policies should be reinforced, with rigorous requirements for flood mitigation and climate resilience, plus incentives for retrofit where appropriate. I’d also want local communities to have genuine input through design panels or public forums, and for authorities to have the resources to supervise developments and enforce covenants over time.

Incentivising delivery without creating a race to the bottom is crucial. Councils need funding and capacity to plan, assess, and monitor developments, including the long-term performance of BTR schemes. If reforms deliver faster planning decisions, better building standards, and strong affordability commitments, I think they could unlock a steady pipeline of homes that are genuinely affordable for young people starting out—without compromising quality or local character.

In short, I’m cautiously optimistic. yes to purpose-built and mixed-tenure projects with enforceable affordability covenants and professional management; yes to streamlined planning with clear timelines; but no to shortcuts that erode environmental safeguards or community input. If implemented with robust accountability and long-term affordability in mind, these reforms could meaningfully increase the supply of good-quality, affordable homes in my area.

As an organisation operating in England, we welcome reforms to boost affordable, good‑quality homes. First, release surplus public land and capture planning uplift through levies or taxes to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. In practice, releasing council‑owned sites that are underused—such as former depots or schools—could unlock hundreds of affordable homes. A planning uplift levy or equivalent would channel receipts into council‑home building and essential elements like roads, parks, flood defences and utilities, ensuring new sites become lasting neighbourhoods rather than temporary settlements.

Second, encourage purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to increase long‑term rental supply. Where BTR delivers 20–30% affordable homes with clearly managed rents and maintenance standards, it reduces housing waiting lists, improves tenant security and quality of life, and provides stable, well‑managed communities.

Third, require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure service‑ready communities. Planned delivery of a new bus corridor, a primary school and a GP clinic alongside a large development would prevent strain on existing services and support sustainable growth.

Taken together, these reforms would deliver more homes faster, with better quality and resilience, supporting communities across the region.

Thank you for the chance to submit thoughts on how we can genuinely increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. From where we stand, the reforms most likely to deliver real change are not about tinkering with tenancy labels or waving through more planning applications alone. They require tightening accountability, strengthening delivery capability in local authorities, and ensuring long‑term stewardship of homes. Without that, uplift in supply will be short‑lived or poor in quality.

Key reforms we believe are essential:

- Improve local data, monitoring and developer accountability
  - Create a transparent delivery dashboard for every major site that shows planning consent, affordable units promised, units delivered, and actual occupancy. This should be produced quarterly and be publicly accessible.
  - Introduce enforceable milestones with penalties for non‑delivery and clawback mechanisms for subsidies if milestones are missed. If a developer cannot deliver a site on time, homing the funds into a council delivery plan or into viable community housing schemes should be automatic.
  - Require upfront viability tests that are robust and independently checked, so we can distinguish genuine market risk from under‑delivery driven by poor project management or intent to maximise profits.
  - In our area we’ve seen a large site obtain consent years ago and sit largely undeveloped while promises of affordable homes evaporate. A stronger data framework would have flagged delays earlier and prompted corrective action.

- Fund and strengthen council planning and delivery capacity
  - Increase core funding for planning departments and delivery teams so decisions are timely and well coordinated with housing associations and builders who share a long‑term stewardship view.
  - Support option agreements where councils take a more active role in delivery through joint ventures or pass‑through arrangements with trusted housing associations, so delivery risks aren’t all borne by the public purse or by private developers.
  - Establish local pre‑application and validation pathways that speed up quality development while maintaining high design and environmental standards.
  - In practice, capacity gaps at a local level stall projects and push up costs, reducing the effective supply of affordable homes when they’re most needed.

- Strengthen developer accountability and long‑term outcomes
  - Fix the expectation that affordable housing is optional or optional‑once; require clear, enforceable commitments for affordable units on‑site or via fully funded offsite contributions with strict delivery timelines.
  - Build‑to‑Rent (BTR) and mixed‑tenure schemes can help, but only if they come with affordability covenants and professional, responsive management, and if a meaningful share of units remains affordable for the long term.
  - Ensure BTR schemes have transparent service charges and a guaranteed model of property management that protects tenant welfare rather than extracting rents over time.
  - In your area, a number of BTR proposals have promised affordability but failed to secure long‑term covenants or have governance structures that allow rents and conditions to drift away from what was expected. Stronger accountability would prevent this drift.

- Licensing, enforcement, quality standards and longer tenancies balanced with small landlord viability
  - Strengthen selective licensing and mandatory national minimum quality standards for private rentals, with a clear path to enforcement when standards slip.
  - Promote longer tenancies where appropriate, with good tenancy support and clear, fair break clauses, so households can stay in stable homes, while ensuring landlords receive appropriate incentives to maintain properties.
  - Protect small landlords by offering targeted support to upgrade properties (energy efficiency, vital repairs), simplifying regulatory burdens where possible, and ensuring that policy cost increases do not push these operators out of the market, which would shrink supply rather than grow it.
  - Our local experience shows that heavy regulation placed uniformly on all landlords without targeted support can reduce the number of available units, particularly for smaller landlords who are a meaningful chunk of the supply in many neighbourhoods.

- A cohesive, place‑based approach
  - Reforms must be tailored to the local context: job access, transport links, and energy efficiency standards all shape what works where. A one‑size‑fits‑all policy risks distortions that either fail to increase supply or degrade quality.
  - Where possible, couple supply reforms with commitments to energy retrofit and ongoing property maintenance, so new homes don’t become energy‑hungrier as soon as the occupier moves in.

In short, we need a credible, resourced delivery pipeline: better data and accountability, stronger council capacity to plan and deliver, transparent and enforceable commitments from developers, responsible growth of Build‑to‑Rent with genuine affordability covenants, and a fair but robust framework for private rented housing that protects tenants and does not unintentionally squeeze small landlords out of the market. If those elements are in place, the actual number of affordable, good‑quality homes will rise, and they will stay affordable for longer, which is the core aim of this consultation.

I welcome reforms that will increase affordable, good‑quality homes in our area by making sure new housing comes with the services it needs. I would support requiring funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or even before housing is built. In practice this means development plans tied to long‑term infrastructure funding, with each housing tranche delivering its share of roads, GP capacity and schools. In our area a large new estate was approved but the roads were not ready and local clinics were already stretched; that mismatch reduces demand for the homes and harms communities. 

I also back community‑led models—community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction. These approaches can deliver affordable homes quickly and to a high standard. I’ve seen a CLT near us stabilise prices for local families, and modular, timber‑frame builds can cut construction time and waste while meeting high energy standards. 

Release surplus public land and capture planning uplift through levies or taxes to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. If councils identify suitable sites and apply a community‑benefit levy, we can fund schools, transport and green space without pushing rents up further. 

Overall, a coherent mix of infrastructure‑led planning, community‑led delivery and reform of land values is the way forward.

I live in England and I’m 18-24, paying high rents and watching the housing market tighten around me and my friends. I’m not convinced that pouring public money into big council or housing association building programmes will reliably deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes fast enough to make a real difference for low‑income households in our area. The trouble with these large, public‑sector build schemes is they tend to move slowly, get bogged down in procurement and political cycles, and end up costing taxpayers more than intended while the resulting homes don’t always stay affordable for the long term. 

What I’d rather see are reforms that unlock more supply from faster, more flexible routes—without losing sight of genuinely affordable rents and decent quality. In my area, where private rents are high and job security is uneven for young people, we need a steady flow of homes that people can actually afford to live in for the long haul. Here are the reforms I think would work best. 

- Speed up planning and unlock land for housing, especially on brownfield sites near town centres and transport hubs. If developers know there’s a predictable, time‑bound planning process, they’ll bring more sites forward. We should simplify and standardise design controls so every new development is built to high quality standards, but without years of delays waiting for approvals. It’s not about letting anyone build anything anywhere; it’s about creating a fast, fair route to bring forward sites that can deliver affordable homes as part of mixed‑tenure schemes.

- Use private capital with strong safeguards to deliver affordable homes quickly. Public money on its own is slow and expensive; instead, offer targeted incentives, guarantees, and viability supports to private and housing‑association builders to deliver a bigger share of genuinely affordable homes on site, with rents linked to local incomes for the long term. The key is long‑term affordability, not temporary subsidies. Units should be locked in at social rent levels or capped affordable rents for 30–60 years, so today’s subsidy isn’t undone by tomorrow’s market price rise.

- Rebalance the balance between market and affordable. Mandates on affordable housing must be clearer and more enforceable, and the affordable portion should be on‑site where possible, with strict penalties if sites are delayed or changed to higher‑end units. Where on‑site delivery isn’t viable, ensure robust off‑site contributions that genuinely fund new social rented homes elsewhere, not just cash that dries up in administration costs.

- Modern methods of construction and better procurement. Using modular and factory‑built components can slash build times and improve consistency in quality and energy efficiency. A streamlined procurement framework, with a single, capable client body at the local level, would cut the admin drag that often slows schemes to a halt.

- Make use of public land and existing stock, but with tighter oversight. Local authorities hold land that could be released for affordable housing more quickly if there are clear, binding timelines and transparent bids. Also, refurbishing and re‑configuring vacant public buildings or underused spaces can deliver faster, smaller‑scale social renting opportunities while larger schemes are still in the pipeline.

- Ensure quality, inclusivity, and long‑term stewardship. New homes must meet high energy efficiency and accessible design standards, with robust ongoing maintenance and tenancy support. Young residents need homes that aren’t cold, damp, or poorly maintained and that won’t implode financially due to rising costs or poor upkeep. Long‑term tenancy security and pathways to independent living should be built in from the start.

In practice, I’ve seen local schemes stall because of funding rounds, complicated procurement, and uncertain long‑term viability. That’s not a good signal for anyone trying to plan a life here. If reforms prioritise speed, value for money, and long‑term affordability—while keeping quality high—we’ll see more genuinely affordable homes come on line sooner, and they’ll stay affordable for the people who need them most. Public investment can play a role, but it must be part of a broader, more agile package that couples delivery speed with strict affordability controls and high building standards.

Overall, the reforms I’m calling for would, I think, produce more affordable, good‑quality homes faster than a big, public‑sector building programme alone. They would also reduce the risk of long wait times and help younger people like me and my peers find secure housing without being priced out of the area we rely on for work and study.

Living in England, I see the urgent need to boost affordable, good-quality homes in our area. Reforming Section 106, CIL, and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding would be the most effective approach. In my town, a sizeable development promised affordable housing but, under current viability practice, the on-site quota slipped and much of the money for roads and schools went elsewhere. That delays homes and burdens local services.

Reforms should require a clear, binding affordable housing percentage on site, with realistic phasing and robust penalties if delivery slips. Viability assessments must be independent, publicly disclosed, and based on up-to-date finance data. CIL should be predictable and ring-fenced for local infrastructure, including schools, GP surgeries, and sustainable transport, with transparent accounting so residents see the benefits.

I also think there should be a simple, mandatory reporting framework so communities can track progress and hold developers to account. In short, align incentives so developers deliver affordable homes and timely infrastructure, not just planning approvals. This combination would help increase supply without compromising quality, energy standards, or access to services.

Agree. To genuinely boost affordable, good‑quality homes in England, reforms should prioritise purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent (BTR) and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional on‑site management. BTR delivers long‑term rental supply with consistent standards and proactive maintenance, reducing tenant turnover and rogue lets. When developers commit to long leases and high management standards, rents stay more predictable and blocks are well cared for over time. 

All BTR and mixed‑tenure developments should include a share of affordable homes secured by affordability covenants, with rents linked to local incomes so families aren’t priced out as the market shifts. Professional management supports timely repairs, tenancy rights, and community safety, which matters to households like mine who want stable, decent homes in good neighbourhoods. 

I also support pilots of rent caps or stabilisation in areas with acute affordability pressures, provided they’re carefully designed and evaluated. These pilots must be evidence‑led, with clear milestones, sunset clauses, and close monitoring of impact on investment, landlord exit, and new supply. 

Finally, sensible planning reforms and accessible finance for BTR would help deliver more of these homes sooner. In my area I’ve seen well‑run BTR blocks delivering quality homes and stable, professionally managed tenancies, which makes a real difference to daily life.

From my vantage point in a small town in England, I support reforms to boost affordable, good-quality homes. There is real pressure on rents and on local services. Releasing surplus public land is sensible. Our council owns a former hospital site and several unused parcels near the town centre; if uplift from planning is captured via levies or land value capture, those parcels could fund affordable homes and improved infrastructure like GP surgeries and transport links. In practice, we could redevelop such sites with a mix of affordable rent and shared ownership.

I also back purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. That approach can deliver long-term rental stock, good maintenance, and predictable standards, rather than one-off speculative towers. In nearby towns, modest BTR with 20-30% affordable units would help families and older residents.

Finally, we must prioritise wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes and dedicated units for older people, with suitable housing for key workers and students in rural and culturally sensitive ways. Delivering such homes on reformatted sites would meet our demographics and reduce isolation.

absolutely there is no simple fix, but I support reforms that mix community-led models with smarter planning to deliver affordable, good‑quality homes quickly.
