In our area, community land trusts and housing co‑operatives show what long‑term affordability looks like when local people have a say and a stake. Encouraging more self‑build and using modern methods of construction could speed up delivery and lift quality, as long as there are clear standards, robust maintenance arrangements, and proper local oversight. 

On planning rules, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing is essential. We need transparency—publish viability assessments and criteria, with predictable thresholds for affordable homes and infrastructure contributions. Local authorities must be able to secure on‑site affordable homes or enforce credible, well‑funded off‑site packages, and funding must be traceable and timely. Safeguards are needed to protect design quality, green space, and long‑term stewardship, and to prevent small builders from being squeezed out by complex procedures. 

If implemented with strong governance and local accountability, these reforms could unlock faster delivery of affordable homes while ensuring they are well‑built and lasting for communities and older residents who want to stay local!

In my area in England, the squeeze on affordable homes is real for my generation. Long waits for social housing and rising private rents push many people, including graduates and apprentices, to look elsewhere. To fix this, reforms should combine major public investment with practical steps that unlock local builders.

First, a sustained public building programme led by councils and housing associations to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. That kind of pipeline would stabilise rents, reduce homelessness risk, and strengthen communities.

Second, targeted finance, procurement access, and a small-sites policy to help SME and local builders. Let councils bundle small sites, use local firms, and shorten pre‑qualification hurdles so projects start quickly on sites like redundant garages, derelict lots, or underused brownfield parcels near town centres.

Third, streamline planning while preserving safeguards. Create faster timelines for straightforward schemes and provide clear, locally grounded planning guidance, but keep environmental protections and neighbourhood input. Also require high energy efficiency and future‑proofing so homes stay affordable to run.

With these reforms, our area could deliver at least a few dozen new social‑rented homes each year, alongside a mix of market homes that genuinely meet local need and support young people staying close to work and study.

From where I live in England, I don’t think simply speeding up planning or encouraging more private development will reliably deliver affordable, high‑quality homes. Without strong affordability covenants and professional management, Build‑to‑Rent and other private schemes can become expensive and inconsistent in upkeep, harming long‑term community stability. 

I believe reforms should prioritise purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes that include affordability covenants and on‑site or local professional management to secure long‑term quality and price stability. These approaches can boost rental supply if they are paired with robust regulation and ongoing oversight. 

More importantly, new communities must be funded with transport, schools, healthcare and utilities either in place or sequenced early. That means requiring funded, phased provision alongside or before housing, so residents aren’t left with overwhelmed GP services or overcrowded schools. In my experience, a recent development near me promised green space and great access but arrived with limited bus routes and insufficient local services, making it less appealing and more costly for families. 

If these targeted reforms are adopted, we would gain not just more homes, but homes that communities can actually rely on.

I’d back a mix of targeted finance for SME builders, small-sites planning support, and community land trusts or co-ops, plus self-build and modern methods of construction; fund and phase higher energy standards and retrofit programs to avoid cost shocks.

absolutely from where I live in England, rents have crept up faster than wages, making it hard for first-time buyers and renters alike. I think we could increase supply by two linked reforms. First, roll out carefully designed rent stabilisation pilots. Cap annual rent increases for existing affordable units at CPI plus a small margin, with clear exemptions for new builds and social/affordable rent units, and with hard timelines. Require independent evaluation after 2-3 years to measure effects on maintenance, new investment, and landlord exit. If pilots prove rents stabilise without chilling supply, expand gradually; if not, adjust or sunset. Also offer incentives or guarantees to landlords who retain management of affordable units to prevent sudden exits. Second, commit to funded, phased provision of infrastructure alongside housing. New communities should bring transport improvements, GP and school capacity, and utility upgrades in place or under construction before or at the start of occupation. Use upfront infrastructure levies, S106/S106A contributions, and government-backed borrowing to accelerate this. In my area, where infrastructure lags, delivery timescales push up costs and push people to rent unsustainably. With service-ready developments, affordable homes become more desirable and sustainable in the long term!

From my experience living in England, I’m wary that reforms focused mainly on speeding up planning and widening sites will not reliably boost genuinely affordable, good-quality homes. I want reforms that actively encourage purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management, supported by robust planning requirements.

Long-term rental supply is most secure when properties are designed for rent, with decent maintenance and transparent management. In my area, several new flats were marketed as affordable but lacked enforceable price controls or management standards; over time tenants faced rents creeping up and maintenance delays. A policy framework that mandates affordability covenants in BTR developments and requires professional, accountable management would help prevent this.

We should streamline decision timelines but not at the expense of environmental safeguards or local input. Quick approvals without proper design quality or infrastructure planning just shifts the problem. I’d like to see dedicated funding for local authorities to negotiate mixed-tenure schemes, with periodic reviews to ensure rents stay affordable and units remain well-maintained.

In my area of England, the core challenge is really about getting more good‑quality homes that people can actually afford, without strangling the market for builders and landlords who deliver supply. I’m approaching reforms with a cautious, mixed view: I want results, but I also want to avoid unintended consequences that could slow development or push rents up elsewhere. I’d support a package that blends targeted pilots with long‑term funding and careful safeguards.

First, on rent controls or stabilisation: I can see the logic of using temporary, evidence‑driven pilots to stabilise costs for tenants who are being squeezed. A cap or stabilisation scheme could help families in tight spots while we gather robust evidence on what actually works. However, there’s a real risk that overly strict or indefinite caps reduce landlords’ appetite to invest or to stay in the private rental market, particularly in places where supply is already tight. My preference would be to trial limited, time‑bound schemes in a few wards with clear sunset clauses and independent evaluation. If results show that supply or maintenance is being adversely affected, we should wind it down or adjust the design. Any pilot should also include protections for quality and energy standards, and access to a transparent route for tenants to report issues without fear of retaliation.

Second, releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift: this feels like a straightforward lever to reduce land costs and unlock housing. Councils hold a lot of underused sites, from former schools to council housing blocks, and even land owned by NHS trusts in some places. Releasing this land for affordable housing, with planning uplift captured through levies or taxes to fund affordable homes and local infrastructure, could help close the funding gap. The crucial details would be: ensuring land is prioritised for genuinely affordable housing (not just marker for market schemes); applying uplift capture in a predictable way so developers aren’t guessing at value; and using the funds transparently for affordable homes, flood protection, schools, and public transport upgrades that otherwise make sites viable. I’d want to see a strong local oversight body, clear viability tests, and community benefit requirements so local residents don’t feel the gain goes only to developers.

Third, from a more critical perspective, I’d like to see more emphasis on community‑driven and faster delivery models. Community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build, and modern methods of construction can all boost affordability and quality when designed with proper support. CLTs and co‑ops can lock in long‑term affordability and give residents a stake, which helps with upkeep and community cohesion. In practice, this requires early‑stage funding, access to land, and capacity building—plus simple, predictable procurement rules that don’t penalise small builders who want to work with these models. Self‑build and modular/MTC (modern methods of construction) can shorten project timelines and improve energy efficiency. If public bodies partner with reputable manufacturers and provide pre‑approved modular designs, we could accelerate the pipeline of high‑quality homes while meeting modern standards (insulation, air quality, heat loss, retrofit potential).

In terms of implementation, I’d propose: (1) a three‑year, ring‑fenced programme combining a small number of rent stabilisation pilots with independent research comparing tenancy outcomes, maintenance quality, vacancy rates, and overall cost to tenants; (2) a land release plan tied to a clear uplift‑capture framework, with annual public reporting on land sales, how much planning uplift was captured, and how dollars are reinvested; (3) dedicated grant streams or low‑interest loans for community land trusts, co‑ops, and MMC‑driven schemes, plus technical assistance for residents to form and manage these models; (4) local authority fast‑track corridors for consent on proven, quality designs that meet climate and energy targets, but with robust protections for local communities and tenant rights.

On balance, I’d like reforms to be growth‑focused and people‑centred: speed up supply where it’s feasible, while protecting affordability in the longer run. A mixed approach—carefully piloted rent stabilisation, strategic use of public land and uplift revenue, and stronger support for CLTs, co‑ops, self‑build, and MMC—seems the most promising path to deliver more affordable, high‑quality homes in my area. If we get the policy design right, we can attract the investment needed and reduce reliance on expensive subsidies over time, while ensuring residents see visible improvements in local housing supply and living standards.

Living in Scotland, I don’t think reforms focused mainly on planning delays or red tape will deliver affordable, good‑quality homes quickly unless they are paired with targeted changes that empower local builders and communities. We need a package that prioritises SME and local builders, strengthens procurement access, and supports community-led housing models, while still protecting the environment.

Targeted finance and procurement access: unlock finance lines specifically for small and medium builders, with guarantees and simpler equity terms through regional development banks or credit unions. Local firms often face high deposit requirements and opaque bidding processes. A dedicated fund to bridge start‑up costs for small sites would help them take on projects that bigger firms won’t touch. Public procurement should introduce tiered pre‑qualification, longer payment terms, and a local‑benefits criterion so councils can back nearby builders delivering genuinely affordable tenures.

Small sites policy and planning support: councils should be required to identify and release serviced small plots each year and provide a one‑stop planning service for SMEs, with real pre‑app advice and clear timetables. In my area, several small sites have stalled for years due to complex processes; simplifying these while preserving standards would unlock quicker delivery.

Community land trusts, co‑operatives, self‑build and MMC: scale up support for CLTs and housing co‑ops, with land‑transfer permissions and long leases, and make self‑build and modern methods of construction easier to access and finance. Modular homes can raise quality and speed if procurement and planning are aligned.

If reforms stay dominated by scale developers or expansive planning reforms alone, affordable, high‑quality homes will remain out of reach for too many communities.

I support reform of Section 106, CIL and viability with stronger transparency and enforceable on-site affordable homes and infrastructure. Prioritise regeneration and infill over greenfield/Green Belt release, and ensure funded, phased transport, schools and health services alongside housing to avoid service gaps.

Focus finance and procurement support for small and local builders, expand small-site policies; prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant and long-term empty homes before any Green Belt release; streamline planning and decision timelines while retaining environmental safeguards.

I strongly support reforms that would increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area by tying housing delivery to properly funded services and well‑managed rental options. Too often, new homes go up without the infrastructure to support them, leaving residents to cope with crowded transport, delayed GP appointments, and schools full to bursting. This undermines the real affordability of those homes and pushes up living costs for everyone.

Key reforms I’d like to see:
- Funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing. Planning conditions should require infrastructure plans and funding commitments that match housing milestones, with clear delivery timetables and consequences for delays.
- Encourage purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. BTR can provide stable long‑term rental supply, while covenants help keep rents within reach and professional management maintains high standards in blocks and shared spaces.
- Additional measures such as energy‑efficient designs, accessible housing, and nearby community facilities (libraries, day centres) to reduce running costs and support older residents.

As a pensioner who values security and predictable costs, these reforms would help attract families and sustain the communities we’ve spent years building, while ensuring services always catch up with new homes.

From my point of view as someone who has watched local housing supply wobble for years, I strongly disagree with these reforms as a silver bullet for affordable housing. Major public investment in councils and housing associations is the right direction in principle, but without proper capacity, timely procurement, and firm funding guarantees it will stall or overrun, leaving vulnerable households waiting decades. In our borough, several social-rent developments were started only after multiple delays; costs rose, and the promised on-site units shrank after viability reviews.

On reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with more transparency and enforceable obligations: I’m sceptical this will deliver more affordable homes. Too often viability assessments are used to cut back on affordable quotas rather than to improve clarity about finance, and communities rarely see the detailed outcomes. If we cannot ensure enforceable, on-site delivery, the reforms will simply shift risk from developers to taxpayers and tenants.

Prioritising regeneration, infill and converting vacant buildings before releasing greenfield or Green Belt land sounds prudent, but in practice it slows new supply and pushes up land prices elsewhere, delaying real access to affordable homes. We need a clear, accountable pipeline of genuinely affordable homes with predictable funding, not procedural compromises that bake in delays.

I back releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes. Lower land costs will unlock affordable homes and fund needed local infrastructure, helping my area stay affordable for families and pensioners.

absolutely agree. Reforms to raise energy standards for new builds and to fund retrofits are essential in Wales to increase affordable, good-quality homes and to meet climate targets without overburdening tenants or landlords. When new homes are built to higher energy standards, heating costs are lower from day one, which is crucial for pensioners on tight budgets. Retrofitting existing stock—insulation, draught-proofing, efficient boilers or heat pumps—will drastically cut bills and improve comfort, making homes affordable to run long term. 

I support mandating minimum energy performance for all new housing (ideally EPC B or better) and directing funds for deep retrofits in private rented and owner-occupied sectors, prioritising older terraces and rural housing stock common in Wales. Use a mix of grants and low-interest loans funded nationally with matched local schemes, to avoid rent increases and share the costs fairly. In our community, similar retrofitting in social housing has cut bills and kept rents stable. 

Overall, these steps will boost supply by making renovation economically viable, encourage developers to build to higher standards, and protect vulnerable households from escalating energy costs!

I welcome reforms that release surplus public land and capture planning uplift through levies or taxes to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. In my area, there is public land held by councils and public bodies that remains untapped while families struggle to find decent, affordable homes. Releasing that land for genuinely affordable housing, combined with a levy on uplift when land is rezoned, would bring down upfront costs and unlock money for schools, roads and green spaces.

Reform of Section 106, the Community Infrastructure Levy and viability testing is also essential, with greater transparency and enforceable obligations. Too often viability work allows discounts or deferrals of affordable housing. I’d like a clear framework: a defined proportion of homes on site, with robust on-site delivery or timely, ring-fenced contributions, and publicly available viability assessments reviewed by independent consultees. That would help our council plan with confidence and ensure local communities see direct benefits. When land delivers affordable homes alongside infrastructure, it strengthens neighbourhoods and keeps rents realistic for long-term residents.

I understand the drive to unlock land and streamline viability, but these reforms on their own won’t reliably increase affordable housing. Releasing surplus public land is not a panacea; if land is sold to the highest bidder or used for higher‑value schemes, affordability won’t improve for ordinary buyers. It could also erode greenspace and local services in areas where capacity is already tight. Even with planning uplift levies and taxes, the risk is higher land costs elsewhere and developers passing costs to new homes, keeping affordability out of reach for many. 

Similarly, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with more transparency sounds good in theory, but in practice it can delay schemes and push developers to seek loopholes. That can reduce on‑site affordable homes and put infrastructure funding at risk. For small builders, overly complex viability assessments create uncertainty and deter contributions. 

What would help more: targeted use of surplus public land with strict affordability requirements, protected greenspace, and dedicated funding; clearer, independent viability tests; faster approvals for schemes delivering real affordable housing; and shared investments in local infrastructure funded alongside predictable grants.

i strongly believe yes. Require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities with new housing, and back community land trusts, co-ops, self-build and modern methods of construction to boost affordable, high-quality supply quickly!

In our area of England, the need for affordable, good‑quality homes is clear to many of us, especially for families and older residents who face long waiting lists and rising private rents. I support reforms that release surplus public land and capture planning uplift to lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. This could mean councils and public bodies identifying unused sites, reusing them for genuinely affordable homes, and using levies or planning gains to pay for new housing, school places, roads and GP surgeries. It’s important that any uplift is reinvested locally and that there are clear safeguards to prevent land speculation and bidding wars, with transparent rules about how much uplift goes to housing and how much to infrastructure. Quality matters too: homes need good insulation, accessibility, and low running costs, especially for older residents who wish to stay in their communities.

I also see merit in major public investment through council and housing association building programmes to deliver long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. This should come with predictable funding, strong construction standards, and a robust plan for maintenance and management. In my experience, stable, affordable rents and well‑built, age‑friendly homes help communities endure changes in the local economy. The reforms must be coordinated with infrastructure, services, and local planning to deliver a lasting, quality supply that families can actually rely on.

i really think i’m responding as a Welsh resident in the 25–34 age group, and I strongly welcome reforms that would increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes that people can actually live in today and for years to come. In particular, I think we should prioritise three linked strands: wheelchair-accessible and adaptable homes, service-ready new communities, and a planning system that speeds delivery while protecting the environment and local character.

First, homes that work for everyone. We need a steady increase in wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes and a clear plan for older‑persons and supported accommodation, as well as housing suited to students and key workers who keep our towns functioning. In my circle I’ve seen how a lack of accessible design creates extra costs and exclusion for disabled friends and relatives. A practical reform would be to require a minimum proportion of new affordable homes to meet high accessibility standards (M4(2) adaptable and M4(3) wheelchair-accessible) with targets set locally based on need. Importantly, these homes should be designed to be flexible—ground-floor entrances, step-free access, wide doorways, good storage, adaptable bathrooms—so families can stay in the same home as circumstances change. In rural areas, that also means multi-purpose spaces that can act as home offices, study rooms or small clinics when needed, plus culturally sensitive design that supports our Welsh language and community life.

Second, service-ready communities. New housing should be planned with infrastructure in place or funded in parallel, not tacked on later. In practice, that means phased provision of transport links, schools, healthcare facilities and utilities alongside housing—ideally before or in tandem with occupancy. For example, extending a bus route or providing a reliable shuttle service to a new estate, expanding a nearby GP practice or schools, installing high‑speed broadband and upgrading water and waste facilities. I’ve witnessed a proposed development stall because the local transport and health services weren’t secured upfront; families and workers faced uncertain timelines and it made the project financially fragile. If developers are required to fund and deliver these service elements in phases, new communities become sustainable from day one and people can move in with confidence, not after lengthy delays.

Third, a streamlined planning system that keeps safeguards in place. The current process can feel slow and uncertain, which pushes up costs and delays delivery. I’d support a simplified, faster planning pathway for smaller sites, with a clear national framework and robust local input to protect flood risk, biodiversity and local character. Digital planning, pre‑application advisory services, and one‑stop processes would help applicants understand requirements early, reduce back-and-forth, and shorten decision times. But speed should not mean weaker environmental protections. In practice, this could look like standardised digital submissions, a guaranteed decision window (with penalties for avoidable delays), and pre-agreed conditions that can be quickly checked and signed off when infrastructure milestones are met. For rural and culturally unique areas, proposals should include community consultation and consideration of Welsh language needs, with opportunities for community hubs, green spaces and access to local services woven into the design.

Concrete, local examples matter. In my town, a mid-sized affordable scheme stalled for months because the servicing commitments (bus, GP capacity, school places) were not aligned with the timetable for housing delivery. If the reforms I’m proposing had been in place, the site could have moved forward with occupancy earlier, reducing pressure on private rents and supporting local livelihoods. On the ground, that also translates into better outcomes for students who need affordable, accessible housing near university facilities and for key workers who keep hospitals and care homes running.

Overall, these reforms would help deliver a bigger supply of affordable, high‑quality homes that meet diverse needs—accessible and adaptable homes for all ages, service-ready communities in place from the start, and a planning system that moves faster without compromising our environment or values. That means more stable, inclusive towns across Wales where people can live independently, work locally and participate in community life!

I think reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing should be more transparent and enforceable to ensure affordable homes go where they are needed. In our area I’ve seen a large development promise a portion of affordable housing, but the details and delivery timelines are murky, and progress slows. I would support requiring on-site affordable homes wherever viable, with clear thresholds, a defined share of units for social or affordable rent, and robust penalties for late or non-delivery. Viability testing must not be a cover for cutting obligations; there should be independent oversight and annual public reporting detailing what is delivered, what is withheld, and why. 

Major public investment in council and housing association building programmes would make a real difference for low‑income households. Long‑term social rented homes provide stability and security, especially for younger people facing high private rents. In Scotland, rents keep rising while waiting lists grow; new council housing would relief pressure and keep communities together. 

Additionally, improving local data, monitoring and developer accountability is essential. A public dashboard showing current and planned affordable homes, and the infrastructure tied to them, would help residents track commitments. We should fund planning enforcement and capacity in councils and support smaller builders to participate, not crowd them out.

Thank you for the opportunity to feed into this consultation. I live in England and, like many households in my age group, I’ve watched the pressures on affordable housing build up over the last decade. My sense is that we need a practical mix of approaches that can deliver quality homes quickly, while protecting our neighbourhoods and the environment. In this spirit I’d encourage reforms that combine community-led models with smarter planning and targeted testing of rent stabilisation, all underpinned by strong delivery and quality standards.

First, I see real potential in expanding community-led housing models—community land trusts, housing co-operatives, and opportunities for self-build—alongside modern methods of construction (MMC). These approaches offer local control over land and design, which helps safeguard affordability in the long term and encourages high-quality, energy-efficient homes. In my area there are pockets of good practice where residents have come together to secure land, develop carefully designed housing, and manage it through a long-term covenant. If we scale this up with proper funding and planning support, it could mean more genuinely affordable homes that are well suited to local needs, not just market-rate developments that may drift out of reach over time.

Second, planning and decision timelines have to become more predictable without compromising environmental safeguards. We need a planning system that supports delivery but remains rigorous on flood risk, biodiversity, and climate resilience. Practical steps could include binding deadlines for decisions (for example, initial determinations within a set window and mandatory two-stage processes with clear milestones), enhanced pre-application advice, and more robust use of design codes for repeatable, high-quality schemes. Digital submissions should be the default, with clear feedback loops so communities see progress rather than endless delays. Importantly, we should fast-track genuinely community-led and high-quality schemes by offering targeted planning support and, where appropriate, flexible land-use rules that still respect environmental limits.

Third, rent stabilisation or targeted caps could help households at risk of rapid rent increases, but they must be designed with care to avoid unintended consequences for supply. I would favour pilots in high-demand areas that are paired with robust evaluation. Features should include sunset clauses, clear eligibility criteria, and mechanisms to protect landlords who invest in quality maintenance. Any cap should be area-based and time-limited, with periodic reviews and transparent data on effects for vacancy rates, new investment, and the upkeep of existing stock. We must avoid a blanket policy that dissuades private landlords or deters new investment; pilots must be accompanied by evidence on how to preserve incentives for maintenance, improving turnover conditions, and routes for landlords to exit where necessary without destabilising overall supply.

I also think there is a strong case for aligning these reforms with active land release and public land use. Local authorities should be empowered to reuse vacant or underutilised public land for affordable schemes, including CLTs and MMC-assembled homes. I’d like to see accessible finance channels for community ventures—grants, revolving funds, or blended finance—to cover early stage costs like site assembly, planning, and construction punch lists. I’m concerned that the proposed reforms to speed up housing delivery – by streamlining planning, zoning and decision‑making timelines while keeping some environmental safeguards – won’t deliver genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes in practice. In our area, I’ve seen how bureaucratic delay and uncertainty can stretch project timelines for years, but I’m wary of any approach that prizes speed over local scrutiny, design quality and infrastructure capacity.

On planning and decision timelines, the intention to accelerate development sounds sensible in theory. In reality, councils are already stretched thin and capacity is uneven. I’ve watched a number of schemes stall because of a lack of planner resource, conflicting local policies and the need to prove viability with ever‑changing assumptions. If speed is the only measure, we risk cutting corners on drainage, schools, GP capacity and transport links. A rushed decision can also undermine the meaningful involvement of local residents and town‑planning expertise that keeps schemes appropriate for their place. It’s not just about getting houses up; it’s about what those houses sit alongside (schools, infrastructure and green space) and how the development respects the character of the town. Any reform must attach hard, enforceable infrastructure and design‑quality requirements to speed, not just vow to cut the red tape.

That links to the affordability question: faster approvals won’t help if the homes built aren’t affordable or are poorly built. The idea of simplifying planning is attractive, but it shouldn’t be a box‑ticking exercise that allows developers to push through schemes with minimal affordable housing contributions or skim off viability assessments. In several local schemes I’ve seen, viability loopholes mean that the promised affordable homes are later reduced or quietly dropped. I’d want reform to guarantee a binding affordable housing target upfront on sites above a reasonable threshold, with independent reviews of viability and penalties if obligations aren’t met.

Regarding energy standards for new builds, mandating higher standards is desirable in principle for climate targets and bills, but it must be funded and costed properly. If higher fabric standards add thousands of pounds per home and there’s no commensurate support for delivery or for retrofits in existing stock, rents and house prices could rise and overall supply could shrink. The reality in private rented sector properties where energy costs are already a heavy burden means the cost must be shared fairly between developers, landlords and public funding, rather than simply passed on to tenants.

A practical concern in our area is that much of the land with potential for affordable housing sits on brownfield sites with existing infrastructure gaps. Even with faster planning, if schools, health centres, roads and public transport aren’t expanded in parallel, these developments won’t be genuinely sustainable or affordable in daily life. The proposals should be paired with a strong infrastructure plan and a dedicated funding stream for energy retrofit across the existing housing stock, so households can benefit from lower bills without having to wait years for new builds to materialise.

What would work better, in my view, is a package of reforms that combines speed with rigour and equity:
- A guaranteed, enforceable affordable housing quota on all significant sites, with independent oversight and penalties for non‑delivery. Use a mix of on‑site, off‑site and council‑led affordable homes so communities aren’t left with poorer options.
- Ring‑fenced funding for local infrastructure, including schools, GP capacity and public transport, tied directly to the housing supply timeline. No more projects delivered without the necessary amenities to sustain them.
- A clear, time‑limited planning process that prioritises quality design, environmental safeguards and drainage/infrastructure checks, but with extra resources for councils to meet these expectations so delays aren’t simply shifted to developers.
- Higher energy standards conditioned on robust funding: offer grants or low‑interest loans for energy‑efficiency upgrades in both new builds and existing stock, and ensure retrofit funding is long‑term and accessible to tenants and landlords alike.
- A more predictable, transparent viability framework that closes loopholes used to erode affordable housing contributions, with public dashboards showing how much affordable housing has been promised and delivered.

In short, speed is not the sole objective. Any reform must deliver affordable, well‑built homes with the necessary infrastructure and lower energy bills for tenants. Without that balance, we risk more developments that look good on a map but fail our communities once people move in. If reforms are pursued, I’d want tight guardrails, clear delivery targets, and dedicated funding streams that make affordable housing and climate goals genuinely achievable in practice.

From where I’m standing in England, I don’t think releasing surplus public land and using planning uplift through levies or taxes will reliably deliver the affordable, good‑quality homes my area needs. It feels like a quick fix that shifts costs around rather than actually making homes affordable for people like me who are trying to get on the ladder or even rent without spending half our wage on rent.

First, land release alone doesn’t guarantee affordable homes. If the uplift levy is added to the price of the site or passed on through higher rents, you end up squeezing the same market that you’re meant to help. The land might be cheaper to buy, but developers can still price homes at market rates once they’ve paid for the site, planning fees, and the levy. That means the end result isn’t a big step toward affordability; it’s more expensive homes with a few “affordable” units sprinkled in that often aren’t affordable for people on graduate salaries or rents paid with student debt.

Second, the process is slow and unpredictable. Releasing land and calculating uplift requires complex negotiations, planning approvals, and sometimes redesigns to satisfy local concerns. In practice, this can take years. By the time a scheme is finished, the housing market may have shifted, costs have risen again, and the anticipated infrastructure like roads, schools, and cycle routes may still be underfunded. For a young person just starting out, waiting five or six years for a new housing project to materialise isn’t helpful.

Third, there’s a risk that the funds raised by uplift levies aren’t spent where they’re most needed. My local area already struggles with congested roads and underfunded schools, and there’s no guarantee uplift revenue will be prioritised for the exact neighbourhoods that need housing and infrastructure most. Without strict, ring-fenced commitments to delivering genuinely affordable homes and local infrastructure in the places that need it, the money can drift into general budgets or be spent on projects with less direct impact on housing affordability.

Fourth, the approach can fundamentally miss the core problem: real affordability for young people. Wages for many graduates and young workers aren’t keeping pace with house prices and rents. Even when land is cheaper, deposits, mortgage costs, and the prospect of long private rents stay out of reach. We need housing policies that directly address affordability in a way that aligns with people’s incomes today, not schemes that rely on future planning gains.

What would work better, in my view, is a package that prioritises direct investment in affordable housing and reforms that actually lower the cost of living and staying in a home here and now:
- Significantly ramp up public and non‑profit house-building, including social housing and build‑to‑rent with long‑term stewardship and predictable rents. This should be funded through direct borrowing by local authorities and national guarantees, not just planning receipts.
- Strengthen inclusionary zoning with clear, enforceable quotas on all large private schemes (for example, 30–40% affordable on sites of a certain size) and fast-tracked approvals to make sure these homes are delivered quickly.
- Support community-led and community land trust models. Releasing public land should be conditional on long‑term affordability and local control, ideally via long‑term leaseholds to non-profit groups rather than outright sale to developers.
- Reduce construction costs and timeframes through modular/build‑to‑rent approaches, standardised designs, and robust procurement frameworks that keep quality high but prices lower.
- Ensure capital receipts and uplift funds are explicitly ring‑fenced for local affordable housing and infrastructure, with strong local accountability and clearly defined outcomes.
- Improve tenure security and quality: secure, well-maintained homes with energy efficiency standards, and rent controls where appropriate to stop prices from chasing market rents.

In short, I don’t think the proposed reform—releasing land and capturing uplift—will, by itself, unlock the homes we need. A more direct, accountable approach that builds affordable homes, improves planning efficiency, and links new development to tangible local infrastructure in the places people actually live would be a better route for my generation to find decent, affordable homes here and now.

I live in Northern Ireland and see rents rising faster than wages in my area, so I welcome reforms that can boost the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes while protecting tenants. I’d support carefully scoped pilots of rent stabilisation in the private rented sector, but only if they are time‑limited, evidence‑driven and independently evaluated. A cap linked to CPI with reasonable allowances for maintenance or refurbishment, plus a clear sunset clause, could ease year‑on‑year pressure for families on modest incomes without extinguishing landlord investment. The pilots must monitor rent levels, supply response and any landlord exit risk, with protections for vulnerable tenants, fast conflict resolution, and exemptions for essential works so the market isn’t unduly distorted.

Secondly, releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure makes practical sense. In our area there are underused council and NHS sites that could be brought forward for affordable housing if repurposed with planning conditions—ideally 25–40% affordable units on large sites. A local uplift levy or a transparent planning gain mechanism, ring‑fenced for housing, roads and schools, could reduce land costs and accelerate delivery. It must be transparent, with regular reporting on how funds are spent and robust quality standards for energy efficiency and long‑term maintenance. A combined approach—pilot rent controls with principled land release and uplift capture—could start delivering real results without derailing investment.

i really think from where I’m standing in England, the biggest barrier to affordable, good-quality homes isn’t a lack of demand but the way money and permission flow to the biggest players. My view is that targeted finance, more accessible procurement, a smarter small-sites policy, and stronger planning support are the four reforms most likely to deliver diverse, local housing quickly and to a decent standard.

Finance that truly reaches SMEs and local builders
- Create dedicated, locally deployable funds backed by public guarantees to cut risk for banks and building societies when lending to SMEs. - Link public land releases and pre-approved sites to finance gateways that SMEs can access without jumping through endless hoops. In practice, local builders I know have been blocked not by demand but by the difficulty of getting affordable finance for pre-development or early construction costs.

Procurement access that levels the playing field
- Reform procurement to be SME-friendly: two-stage tendering, light-touch prequalification, and longer tender windows so small firms can realistically compete against larger bidders.
- Introduce an explicit pipeline of local authority housing projects where a minimum share is reserved for SMEs and local builders, with simpler payment terms to protect cash flow.
- Create “local supplier” pre-qualification and dynamic registers that are easy to join, regularly updated, and transparent about performance metrics, so SMEs aren’t filtered out before they even bid.
- Encourage modular/offsite construction where SMEs can partner with established manufacturers, enabling fast delivery without sacrificing quality. This would reduce site risk and unlock capacity in areas with skilled but small tradespeople.

Small-sites policy and planning support to accelerate local supply
- Expand the small-sites policy to guarantee a planning pathway for sites of 1–20 homes, with planning permission in principle where appropriate and a fast-track viability assessment that is proportionate and predictable.

Planning support and practical improvements on the ground
- Front-load planning support: pre-application meetings, viability checks, and early discussions about energy standards (passivisation, heat networks, and accessible design) should be standard, not exceptional.
- Digital tools: a simple, transparent planning portal that tracks applications, speeds up information sharing, and flags when a site is ready for decision can dramatically cut delays that hit small builders hardest.
- Clear, timely decisions: set explicit decision windows for small-scale schemes and publish reasons for any delays to reduce uncertainty for local builders.

In my area, I’ve watched a capable local SME struggle to get finance due to risk-averse lenders, while a large developer with deeper pockets moves ahead on comparable sites. The outcomes would be more diverse housing types, closer to town centres, with better design and energy standards, delivered at a pace that matches demand.

Overall, the reforms need to tilt the balance back toward SME and local builders, who are often the real engines of affordable, good-quality housing. Without that shift, the bottlenecks will just move from one part of the system to another, and the homes we need will stay out of reach for too many families!

We welcome reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area and strongly agree with policies that prioritise purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes backed by affordability covenants and professional management. I welcome and strongly support reforms that will genuinely boost the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area. Deliver more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable, older‑persons, supported and student key‑worker homes tailored to demographic, rural and cultural needs. Streamline and simplify planning, zoning and decision timelines while retaining environmental safeguards to accelerate housing delivery and reduce developer uncertainty. A coherent energy standard policy, paired with retrofit funding, would also help new residents feel confident that where they live won’t be a financial burden on top of rent.

Overall, these reforms would deliver not just more homes but better homes: accessible, context‑sensitive designs; quicker, more predictable planning; and energy‑efficient living that reduces bills and climate impact.
