It’s not glamorous, but it feels controllable, affordable, and better suited to what families actually need: predictable rents, decent insulation and energy efficiency, and a stake in the place they live. It won’t move as fast as a big BTR scheme, but the risk of perpetual rent increases and detached management feels lower.

In sum, I think reforms should prioritise land access for community models, financing that supports long‑term affordability, and planning pathways that accelerate delivery without sacrificing quality or local accountability. Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes can play a role, but they should not be the default answer. If policymakers want to genuinely increase affordable, high‑quality housing, they should empower community‑led housing and modern construction methods at scale, with strong protections to keep homes affordable for generations rather than just for the next market cycle.

From where I live in England, reforms to Section 106, the Community Infrastructure Levy, and viability testing should aim to deliver more affordable, good-quality homes without stifling development. I would welcome greater transparency: publish the assumptions and outcomes of viability appraisals, show how much on-site affordable housing is expected, and how funds are allocated for local infrastructure. On-site delivery should be the default, with legally enforceable obligations and independent monitoring; in-lieu payments should be allowed only when truly necessary, and only if funds are ring-fenced for nearby schools, roads and GP access. In my area, a sizeable scheme negotiated 25% on-site affordable housing, but a subsequent viability review reduced that share, leaving fewer homes for local families and relying on later payments. The system must prevent gaming and ensure delivery sits alongside building quality and sustainability. Fast-tracking planning and clearer cost assessments would help, provided they maintain appropriate protections and community input.

As an older resident in England, I strongly support reforms to Section 106, the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and viability testing, with greater transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on‑site affordable homes and infrastructure funding. In our area a large new estate was approved with around 20% affordable homes, yet delivery has lagged and the council has limited oversight. Strengthening the regime so on‑site affordable homes are the default, with clear milestones, robust viability tests, and independent checks, would turn promises into homes. If a site cannot accommodate affordable housing, there should be proportionate, ring‑fenced contributions for local housing and essential infrastructure, funded promptly to relieve pressure on schools, GP surgeries, and roads.

Beyond that, better local data, monitoring and developer accountability are crucial. A public planning dashboard showing land supply, approvals, delivery timelines and affordable completions would help residents understand progress. The council needs more planning‑enforcement capacity and a dedicated team to chase milestones and troubleshoot delays. These reforms would ensure commitments are delivered and that the benefits of new development reach communities sooner, not just on paper.

Stronger energy standards for new builds and funded retrofits are essential to cut bills and carbon, but scale must consider the cost to tenants. Also need more wheelchair-accessible and older-people housing; pilot rent-stabilisation to test effects on supply before wider rollout.

From where I live in England, I see a clear shortage of affordable, good-quality homes. I would welcome a major public investment by councils and housing associations to build genuinely affordable social rented homes for low‑income households. Long‑term funding and strong standards are essential; without them, homes may be affordable at first but deteriorate or not stay affordable. In my area, the council’s latest social housing scheme delivered a slate of 40 units, but the programme stretched over several years and waiting lists remain long. A coordinated pipeline of builds, with sites near town centres, would help.

Rent caps or stabilisation could help families, but I worry about unintended consequences for investment. Pilot schemes should accompany robust monitoring on how they affect new builds, maintenance funding, and landlord viability. If rents are kept artificially low, private lenders may withdraw or costs shift elsewhere.

I also support targeted provision for wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes and stronger supported and older‑person housing, plus some student key‑worker accommodation where appropriate, especially in rural or culturally diverse areas where care staff commute far. Faster planning, modular construction, and clear design standards would help deliver quality homes quickly while keeping costs predictable.

While I understand the aim of making rents more affordable, I’m sceptical that rent caps or stabilisation will, on balance, increase the supply of good-quality homes. Caps tend to reduce the incentive for landlords and investors to commit capital, especially in areas where construction costs are high. In our neighbourhood I’ve seen properties neglected when returns are capped, and some landlords exit the market rather than endure red tape and capped rents. Pilots in other councils have shown short‑term stabilisation of rents but with slower new build rates and, in some cases, poorer upkeep as costs are squeezed. 

What would help more is reform that actually unlocks building: releasing council and NHS land for affordable homes, speeding up planning decisions, and providing targeted support for small builders and community housing groups. Also pair reforms with stronger enforcement to keep existing private stock safe and well maintained. Any use of caps should be temporary, evidence-based pilots with clear exit rules, and should exclude exemptions for genuinely new builds or substantial refurbishments to avoid chilling investment.

I strongly support reforms that tackle the housing shortage by making the most of the homes we alreadyy have, rather than unlocking new greenfield land or releasing Green Belt areas. In Wales, the quickest way to deliver affordable, good‑quality homes for people my age is to prioritise regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant or long‑term empty buildings. This protects our landscaprs while giving towns and cities a nrw lease of life. In my area, there are srveral empty shops and an old factory building that’s been standing unused for years. I’ve seen friends struggle to find somewhere affordable nearby, and it’s frustrating that good spaces sit empty while rents rise. Converting those empty or underused facilities into well-designed, energy‑efficient homes could provide much-needed accommodation quickly and with less harm to our countryside than building on new sites. What reforms would help most: - Make brownfield-first the default planning rule. Local plans should set ambitious targets for conversions and infill every year, with clear milestones for reducing long‑term vacancies. This would make it easier to bring homes back intoo use without touching Green Belt land. - Create strong incentives for conversions and regeneration. Grants or low‑interest loans for building conversions, VAT relief on renvoation work, and more generous support for converting offices, shops andd factories into homes woul unlock projects that developers overlook today. - Empower councils to reclaim long‑term empty properties. Strengthened compulsory purchase order powers, a dedicated fund to bring vacant homes back into use, and streamlined processes would convert dereliction into dwellings and community spaces. - Streamline planning for change of use, while guarding design quality. Fast‑track approvals for well‑designed residential conversions, subject to high standards on energy efficiency, accessibility and local character. That way we protect the lookk and feel of our towns while adding homes. - Ensure homrs are affordable and of good quality. Require high energy efficiency by design (fabric‑first approaches), decent space standards, and protections so rent stays affordable for young people. Tie affordable units to genuine affordability targets, not just numbers on a plan. - Invest in infrastructure to support new homes. Ensure new builds come wit good access to public transport, schools, clinics and jobs so new residents don’t add pressure to already stretched services. - Protect landscapes and avoid Green Belt release until alll options are exhausted. Any release of greenfield or Green Belt land should follow a strict brownfield‑first test and be accompanied by landscape protections and habitat considerations. - Involve communities and young people. Plans should be tested with local residents and tenants, with properr opportunities for input on design, density and parking to avoid alienation and to ensure new homess fit with community needs.. - Use and share good data. A Welsh‑wide picture of empty homes, brownfield stock and regeneration opportunities would help target funds whrre they’re needed most and track progress year by year. By focusing on regenerating and reusing the buildings we already have, we can create affordable, high‑quality homes moree quickly, support local economies, and keep Wales looking the way people love—without sacrificing our landscapes. I’d like to see pilots in a few Welsh towns to prove these reforms work and then roll them out more broadly. Thank you for considering thiss approach.

I support releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift to fund affordable homes and local infrastructure, and streamlining planning with safeguards to speed delivery. Pilot rent caps to improve affordability while testing impacts on supply.

Agree. To increase affordable, good‑quality homes quickly in our area, I support reforms that empower local groups to deliver housing, including community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction. CLTs keep land in community ownership and ring‑fence it for permanent affordability, which helps stabilise prices for first‑time buyers and renters alike. Co‑operatives give residents real influence over design and management, often delivering well‑built homes at below market rents because profits are reinvested locally.

In my neighbourhood, a community group has begun exploring a CLT and a small housing cooperative, and I’ve seen how residents’ involvement can streamline planning discussions and ensure high‑quality design that fits the street. Self‑build and modular approaches could compress build time and reduce costs if supported by clearer procurement routes and access to affordable land, enabling experienced households to spearhead projects without heavy speculative risk. Modern methods also offer higher quality controls and less waste.

I’d like reforms that: (a) provide grant/loan support and clear guidance for CLTs and co‑ops, (b) guarantee land at accessible terms, (c) streamline planning for small, local builds and for modular methods, and (d) set robust quality standards for contractors. This combination would unlock faster, affordable homes that communities can be proud of.

I support reforms that strengthen local data, developer accountability, and delivery capacity, while streamlinin planningg and raising energy standards. In our area, affordable homes stall because milestones slip and information sits in silos. If councils had better local data on housing need, pipeline schemes, and developer performance, they could track commitments, allocate resources where delivery is slow, and publicly report progrrss to residents. A funded planning and enforcement capacity would help ensure developers meet their milestones and that grants or starts aren’ lost to administrative delays. For example, a number of schemes waited months for decisions or for clarifications that should have been straightforward. Streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines—while retaining environmental safeguards—would reduce uncertainty for builders and speed up delivery. A clear, digital planning portal with defined timelines would help households plann and bid for homes. Finally, mandating higher energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits of existing affordable homes would cut tenants’ bills, support local green jobs, and keep development costs in check over the long term. Combined, these reforms could meaningfully increase supply of affordable, good-quality homes.

Thank you for inviting views on how to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in Scotland. I’ve lived in Scotland for many years and, like others in my age group who are renting or looking to settle families here, I’m acutely aware that affordability and decent standards must go hand in hand with real options to build and maintain homes. I broadly support a balanced reform package that can stabilise rents and improve quality without squeezing supply or pushing small landlords out of the market.

First, I think there is a strong case for well‑designed rent stability pilots. A limited, time‑bound rent‑stabilisation approach could help households budget and stay in their homes, particularly for those on modest incomes. The design would matter: cap annual rent increases to a predictable measure such as CPI with a modest top‑up (for example CPI plus 1–2%), with clear exemptions. New-build homes, major renovations, or cases where a landlord is addressing urgent disrepair should be outside the cap, to protect investment and maintenance. Pilots should be run in a handful of diverse council areas and evaluated independently after 2–3 years, looking not only at affordability but also at any effects on investment, new supply, and landlord exit. If the evidence shows negative impacts on supply, the policy can be adjusted or paused; if it brings stability without choking investment, it can be scaled up. In practice, this would offer households a predictable path while ensuring builders and landlords still see a viable return where needed.

Second, strengthening licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards is essential. A robust, transparent licensing framework—with a public register—helps ensure all private landlords meet basic safety and quality requirements. I’d welcome mandatory electrical safety checks, gas safety, working carbon monoxide detectors, and timely response to repairs. A clear standard, aligned with SHQS expectations, would drive improvements in damp, mould, insulation and heating. Enforcement needs to be adequately funded in local authorities so that violations are not merely noted but acted on. Importantly, this should not become an unnecessary burden on legitimate small landlords; instead, the regime should be proportionate, with practical guidance and support for landlords to meet the standards.

Third, promoting longer tenancies can deliver stability for families and older tenants who value certainty. Longer fixed‑term agreements (for example 3 years or more) with clear terms for renewals, and deposits protected through established schemes, would reduce constant moving and related costs. This should be paired with reasonable rent reviews tied to agreed benchmarks to maintain fairness. To make this viable for small landlords, there could be incentives such as tax reliefs or access to grants for energy efficiency upgrades, and a simpler, lower‑cost route for compliance with the licensing and quality standards. The aim is steady tenancies that benefit tenants and give landlords predictable income, while still allowing landlords to exit if they choose, provided there is a process that protects tenants from sudden loss of their home.

Fourth, targeted support to protect small landlords while expanding supply is crucial. A balance must be struck between regulation and viability. It would be sensible to cap the cumulative administrative costs imposed on small portfolios and offer targeted support for energy efficiency improvements, so rented homes become cheaper to run and more attractive to tenants. The Scottish Government could also provide guidance and small grants for essential repairs and upgrades, helping landlords meet higher standards without forcing them out of the market.

Fifth, planning and delivery reforms should unlock more affordable homes. Streamlining planning processes for modest, well‑designed developments and enabling conversions of brownfield and vacant properties into homes can boost supply without expanding pressure on green belts. Encouraging Build‑to‑Rent projects that include affordable components and clearer long‑term obligations on management and maintenance would help steady the market. Local authorities should be supported to bring land to market more quickly and to prioritise energy‑efficient, well‑designed homes that meet needs in both urban and rural parts of Scotland.

Finally, any reform should be accompanied by robust data collection and evaluation. Pilots must be closely monitored with independent evaluation on affordability, supply, tenant outcomes and landlord viability. If a policy proves effective, scale it with the lessons learned; if not, adjust or pause. In short, a cautious, evidence‑led approach that combines affordability tools with strong quality standards and supportive planning could deliver more affordable, good‑quality homes without undermining the market that currently supplies most of Scotland’s private rental stock.

I know a careful, well‑funded package like this can deliver better housing choices for families, older residents, and people on modest incomes right across Scotland. I’d like to see pilots evaluated quickly and transparently so we can learn what works best and build on what protects both tenants and the ability of landlords to maintain and invest in their properties.

In my area in England, the shortage of affordable, good‑quality homes is an everyday reality for many families and older residents like myself. I would welcome reforms that speed up delivery, but only if they preserve environmental safeguards, high building quality and true affordability over the long term. My view is cautiously supportive: streamline planning and decision timelines to reduce delay and uncertainty, while embracing purposeful, well‑designed Build‑to‑Rent (BTR) and mixed‑tenure schemes that include durable affordability covenants and professional management.

On the planning side, the current system often feels glacial, with applications dragging on beyond reasonable expectations. A clear, plan‑led approach is essential. I’d like to see faster determinations for straightforward schemes and a predictable timetable for larger developments, ideally with a target window of a few weeks for pre‑application decisions and a maximum overall processing time that communities can plan around. A single digital, transparent planning portal could shorten back‑and‑forth and reduce the need for repetitive viability negotiations. That said, speed must not erode safeguards: biodiversity net gain, protection of flood risk areas, energy efficiency standards, and quality design should be non‑negotiable, not casualties of rush. Local plans should continue to guide where growth happens, with brownfield sites given priority and infrastructure within reach.

A major concern I’ve observed locally is the repeated renegotiation of affordable housing contributions when viability is marginal or unclear. That creates uncertainty for small builders and blemishes the credibility of the housing supply system. I’d support a more consistent, straightforward viability framework and a cap on late‑stage changes to affordable housing requirements. If reforms make it easier to unlock plots—especially small and medium sites—without eroding local environmental and design standards, we’ll see more delivery and better placement of homes near schools, work and transport links.

Turning to Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure approaches, there is clear potential to stabilise long‑term rental supply and improve living standards. Purpose‑built schemes with professional management can deliver well‑maintained blocks with reliable repairs, on‑site facilities, and predictable rents tied to local norms. To make this work for communities, I’d like to see: (a) a meaningful proportion of BTR or mixed‑tenure units covenanted as affordable over the long term (for example, 15–30% depending on scheme size and local need); (b) long‑term, career‑level property management that actively engages residents and maintains common spaces and services; (c) rents and letting standards aligned with the local housing market and income levels, with clear routes to affordable options; and (d) guarantees that BTR activity does not simply substitute for social or affordable housing elsewhere but complements it, preserving a balanced housing ladder.

In practice, this could mean a BTR site near a transport hub or town centre delivering a mix of one‑ to three‑bed units, a portion covenanted for affordable rent, and a portion retained under professional management with long‑term stewardship. A mixed‑tenure approach on larger developments—combining social/affordable rent, shared ownership, and market homes—would help create sustainable communities rather than exclusive clusters. It’s important that such schemes include accessible design, energy‑efficient build quality, and ongoing retrofit plans so older residents can remain comfortable in a changing climate.

From a personal perspective, as someone in the 55–64 age group, I value homes that are adaptable, affordable to heat, and well maintained over time. I’d like to see infrastructure improvements (schools, GP services, transport) coordinated with delivery so new homes are genuinely fit for purpose, not just a number on a tally. Retrofitting emphasis should accompany new build; fabric‑first energy efficiency and low‑carbon design should be standard rather than optional add‑ons.

In short, I support reforms that speed up housing delivery without weakening protections or quality. Streamlined planning and decision timelines, if applied consistently and transparently, can unlock land and reduce uncertainty. Pair that with robust, well‑regulated BTR and mixed‑tenure schemes that include long‑term affordability covenants and professional management, and you can increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes while sustaining vibrant, mixed communities. Crucially, any reform must be accompanied by infrastructure funding and honest, community‑level engagement to ensure growth benefits current residents and future generations alike.

Agree: releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure; prioritising regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant/empty homes; and simplifying planning timelines while safeguarding the environment would boost supply and keep landscapes protected.

While I understand the aim to increase affordable homes, reforms that simply prioritise boosting supply through faster approvals or looser zoning risk repeating past mistakes. In our area, land price remains the single biggest barrier. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes would help bring land costs down and raise funds for affordable housing and for local infrastructure like roads, schools and GP capacity. I’ve watched a council-owned site on the edge of town sit empty for years because viability hinged on land costs; a proper uplift capture mechanism could convert idle land into homes and funded services.

But reforms must not rush housing without readiness. I would insist on funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing to ensure new communities are sustainable. Without that, new homes become commuter dormitories with congested services and poor outcomes for residents. Any levy should be transparent and ring-fenced for local benefits, not diverted to general budgets.

In short: unlock public land, capture land value to fund affordable homes and infrastructure, and require service-ready delivery in step with housing rather than simply accelerating approvals.

In Scotland, housing should be paired with funded, phased transport, schools, healthcare and utilities to create service-ready communities, while expanding finance access and small-sites planning support for SME builders; consider rent stabilisation pilots with careful monitoring.

i strongly believe i understand the climate aim, but mandating higher energy standards for all new builds and funding retrofit schemes, as proposed to increase supply of affordable homes, risks having the opposite effect. Higher build costs push up sale and rent prices, making genuinely affordable homes scarcer, particularly in Scotland where pressure on supply is acute. In my experience as a landlord in Scotland, developers have faced lengthy planning approvals and hefty compliance costs to meet new energy standards. Even with retrofit subsidies, the burden ends up with tenants via higher rents or with councils if schemes are delayed or scaled back. A better approach would be to streamline planning and approvals to accelerate affordable-housing construction, and to strengthen targeted support for the worst-performing homes rather than blanket standards. Use public funds for energy-efficient improvements in existing social housing and in private rentals only where costs are recouped through grants, not rent increases. Expand grant schemes for low-income tenants and require developers to deliver a higher proportion of genuinely affordable units through negotiated planning obligations, with robust delivery timelines and price caps to prevent cost leakage. Local authorities should be empowered to buy land and deliver council housing quickly, with energy standards that are ambitious but proportionate. This balanced package would increase supply without pricing people out!

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I support reforms that require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing, so the new communities are service-ready from day one. Over the years I’ve watched new housing rise, but the essential services lag behind, leaving families and especially older residents to cope with overcrowded clinics, longer journeys to schools, and patchy transport. This makes affordable homes harder to use and often deters people from moving into those areas.

In our town, a plan for a 300-home estate on the edge was approved some years ago. The promised primary school and expanded GP facility were not funded upfront, and now the new families are trying to access services that are already stretched. The result is longer journeys for school runs, more crowded buses, and increased pressure on the hospital. For people like me, reliable local transport and a safe, easy route to the clinic are vital; when these aren’t in place, even affordable housing becomes less attractive and harder to sustain in the long term.

To make reforms work, I would like to see several practical steps:

- Infrastructure-led masterplans with binding delivery triggers: Planning should not be granted unless councils and developers can show a funded schedule for roads, bus routes, schools, GP slots and utilities that aligns with housing phases. If milestones aren’t met, permissions should be revisited rather than left to drift.
- Front-loaded funding for essential services: Create a mechanism to secure upfront commitments for the first 5–10 years of a new development. This could be through an enhanced Community Infrastructure Levy or a dedicated pooled fund, so that a new estate isn’t bought at the expense of existing residents waiting for a doctor appointment or a reliable bus timetable.
- Transport and connectivity as a core project: Guarantee a funded bus service, safe walking and cycling routes, and, where feasible, rail connections. Services should be scheduled to match school hours and clinic needs, so older residents and families can plan with confidence.
- Utilities and digital connectivity: Ensure water, sewerage, electricity and robust broadband capacity from the outset. A new estate without reliable connectivity risks isolating residents from telehealth, work, and social networks.
- Quality standards and accessible design: Build affordable homes to high energy efficiency standards and with adaptable design (level access, wider doorways, accessible kitchens and bathrooms). This helps older residents stay in their homes longer and promotes mixed, inclusive communities.
- Local involvement and oversight: Create a citizen-delivery board with representatives from local residents, tenants and volunteers to monitor progress and publish clear updates every six months. People want to see promises becoming real actions.
- Longevity of place: Plan for ongoing maintenance of roads, lighting and green spaces, with a sustainable budget for upkeep. Without this, new estates quickly feel neglected and less safe.

If these reforms are embedded in policy and law, developers, builders and councils will have a clear roadmap for delivering homes that are genuinely affordable because the surrounding services are ready. My experience shows that housing alone cannot solve affordability if schools are full, GP appointments are hard to come by, or transport is unreliable. A truly affordable home is one that comes with a functioning, well-funded support system—delivered in a coordinated, phased way that keeps communities sustainable for the long term.

In Scotland's rural and ageing communities, we need more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older people, student key workers, and other essential workers, plus targeted finance and small-sites planning to help local SME builders; meanwhile, promote purpose-built Build-to-Rent with affordability covenants and professional management.

Yes, I support reforms that focus on improving local data, stronger monitoring, clearer developer accountability, and giving councils the capacity to plan, enforce and deliver. In practice this would mean a live, publicly accessible housing delivery dashboard showing planned, started and completed affordable homes by site, tenure and funding source, updated quarterly. Local authorities often lack up-to-date information and that delays decision-making; better data would help households plan and help funders see progress. We need independent quarterly audits of major sites and publish milestones and penalties for delays to keep schemes on track. Developers should be required to publish build-out timetables and face penalties if milestones slip, with funds clawed back to reinvest in new affordable homes. Councils must have ring-fenced funds to recruit and retain planning, enforcement and delivery staff, plus streamlined processes to avoid needless hold-ups. In our area, a site with dozens of affordable units has lingered for years due to slow monitoring; improved capacity would have prevented that. This would help families and older residents who need secure, good-quality homes close to services.

I live in England and I’m responding as an individual. I strongly support reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. The core of my view is that better local data, closer monitoring and stronger accountability for developers are essential. Councils need accurate housing and infrastructure data, delivery milestones and clear consequences if commitments are not met. In practice, that would mean more staff for planning delivery, sharper enforcement and transparent reporting so residents can see when a site’s affordable homes actually appear.

I also back targeted finance, easier procurement access and a robust small-sites policy to help SME and local builders contribute more diverse, local housing. Small builders often lack finance or the simplified procurement routes they need; giving them priority access to finance and a local, streamlined planning path would unlock more homes across well‑tried brownfield sites.

Finally, new communities must be service‑ready. I welcome a funded, phased provision of transport, schools, GP surgeries and utilities alongside or before housing as part of a credible delivery plan. That keeps families moving in and ensures the homes aren’t left with inadequate infrastructure.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I live in Scotland and, like many in my community, I want affordable, good-quality homes, but I’m wary that these reforms to speed up housing delivery could come at the expense of local protections, service capacity, and environmental safeguards. Delivering more homes must go hand in hand with healthy communities, not at the cost of greenspace, schools, GP surgeries, or our climate commitments.

On planning and decision timelines: there is a real danger that streamlining planning rules and speeding up decisions could erode essential public scrutiny. Local people deserve to see high-quality design, appropriate density, and proper consideration of flood risk, biodiversity, and carbon emissions. In my area, a proposed development was fast-tracked and approved with only a cursory look at ecological safeguards; the promised tree-planting and habitat restoration were vague, and the project now faces long-term maintenance questions. If speed becomes the priority, it’s those checks that get squeezed—and the long-term costs fall on communities and public services.

Infrastructure sequencing and service readiness: I agree there must be reliable connectivity between housing and services, but mandating funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing sounds sensible only if there is credible, funded delivery. In practice, the public purse is finite and councils already struggle to plan and fund essential infrastructure. My experience in a border town is that a 60–70 home scheme was consented quickly, yet the new primary school, bus services, and water upgrades were never delivered on time. Families faced longer commutes, crowded clinics, and higher traffic congestion while developers argued the market would fund the gaps later. That is not sustainable growth; it merely shifts the burden onto residents and public services.

Reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing: there is widespread concern that viability assessments are used to reduce affordable housing and local infrastructure contributions. In Scotland, too many projects have cited viability problems to dodge on-site affordable housing or to delay necessary amenities. If these reforms are to work, there must be transparency and enforceable obligations that ensure on-site affordable homes and critical infrastructure are delivered promptly. I would insist on independent, publicly accessible viability appraisals, with a clear, mandatory threshold for affordable housing on-site and robust penalties if obligations are not met. Off-site contributions should only be permissible where there is a concrete, delivered plan for affordable housing and infrastructure, not simply “cash in lieu” that never materialises.

Specific concerns and practical illustrations:
- A large brownfield site near my town was given outline consent quickly, but the agreed affordable housing was proposed as off-site units many miles away, with no concrete timetable. That undermined community cohesion and left the local school and GP unable to plan for demand.
- In another case, a new housing project promised infrastructure upgrades in a separate funding package, yet the local authority had no assurance of delivery timelines, so residents faced years of traffic issues and extended hospital and school delays.
- Even where contributions are paid, I’ve seen little evidence of regulated monitoring or public reporting on how those funds are spent and what outcomes they deliver for the community. Transparent, auditable reporting is essential.

What I’d like to see instead, to genuinely increase supply while protecting communities:
- Strengthened, well-resourced local planning with statutory deadlines and consequences for excessive delays, paired with clear design quality standards and environmental safeguards.
- An infrastructure-led approach that ties housing to a credible delivery plan for transport, health, education, and utilities, with a public capital commitment and a shared risk model so delays don’t fall on residents while developers wait for profitability.
- Reform of Section 106/CIL that is transparent, publicly auditable, and enforceable, with a default preference for on-site affordable housing where feasible and clearly defined timelines for delivery. Off-site contributions should be used only where there is verifiable, deliverable need and a strict timetable.
- A focus on brownfield-first development, with high-quality design, energy efficiency, and access to public transport and digital connectivity. That means giving communities real say in place-making decisions and ensuring climate resilience and biodiversity protections are built into every plan.
- A public-interest assessment as part of viability discussions to guard against under-provision of social infrastructure and to keep land values from extracting affordability from future residents.

In short, I want reforms that accelerate delivery without sacrificing environmental protections, place-making, and social infrastructure. Without robust safeguards and transparent accountability, faster approvals will simply erode the quality of homes and the resilience of new communities.

Thank you for considering these points. I want Scotland to build more homes, but to do so in a way that strengthens, rather than weakens, our public services and our environment.

Prioritise regenerating brownfield sites, conversions, and long-term empty homes over Green Belt release; back major public investment in social housing; use surplus public land and planning uplift to fund affordable homes and local infrastructure, but ensure landscape protection and delivery efficiency.

Rents in Northern Ireland have soared and long-term security is lacking. I disagree with reforms that rely mainly on more owner-occupied housing or piecemeal private renting. Instead, the reforms I think would most effectively increase supply are to actively promote purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management. Planning should set aside land near towns for BTR and mixed tenure projects, with affordability covenants locked for 20-25 years and rents tied to local income levels. Developers should provide on-site management, responsive maintenance, and high energy efficiency standards. This approach delivers scale, quality, and predictable costs, helping people like me avoid endless private-rental stress. In my circle, friends have faced sudden rent increases and short tenancies; BTR offers long-term leases and greater stability. Also prioritise brownfield sites close to transport links and jobs, with clear local allocation to those in need. A credible pipeline of such developments would boost supply without compromising quality or affordability.

I strongly support reforms that would raise the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area. Key is better local data and stronger council capacity to plan, monitor, and enforce delivery; that means a public, up-to-date pipeline showing which sites have permission, what affordable-share is planned, and when homes are due to be built. In our town, several sites with outline consent have stalled for years; improving developer accountability and providing ring-fenced funding for planning and enforcement would help ensure commitments are kept or reallocated. Robust monitoring would help us spot shortfalls early and adjust viability tests to protect affordable housing. I also back mandating higher energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits for the existing stock. This would cut bills for residents and tenants, meet climate targets, and avoid shifting costs onto renters or small landlords. Finally, releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift via levies or taxes on developers would lower land costs and generate funds for affordable housing and essential local infrastructure. If used transparently, it could unlock more genuinely affordable homes without inflating rents.

Thank you for the opportunity to share my views. I live in Scotland and I want to see more affordable, good‑quality homes available locally, built by capable local and SME builders, with strong community and public backing. As someone in my late twenties who hopes to stay in a place with good jobs, schools and green spaces, I believe reform packages that unlock finance, streamline procurement for small builders, empower community-led housing, and back long‑term social housing programmes will deliver the most meaningful increase in supply. In my area I’ve seen small projects struggle because the financial and planning steps are costly and slow. A realistic, well funded package that cuts red tape while protecting quality would bring many more homes on site much sooner.

To be concrete, here are reforms I think would work best, with reasons and a bit of local context:

- Targeted finance and easier procurement access for SME/local builders
  - Create dedicated development finance lines and blended funding that are accessible to small and medium‑sized builders, with simpler eligibility, quicker decisions and longer repayment terms. In our community, a small housing cooperative struggled to secure affordable finance for a 6‑home scheme; the terms from private lenders were steep and the process lengthy. If there were a government‑backed, SME‑friendly finance option and a procurement framework that explicitly prioritised local firms, we’d see more local builders competing for and delivering sites.
  - Strengthen procurement pathways that reserve a meaningful share of council and housing association contracts for local SMEs, with streamlined pre‑qualification and clear, predictable timelines. This would help diversify the supply chain, create local jobs and keep construction costs closer to home.

- Small‑sites policy and planning support to help SME/local builders
  - Accelerate the release of small sites (under, say, 5–15 homes) by providing pre‑approved design packs, adaptable standard house types, and shorter pre‑application processes. A planning performance agreement with fixed timelines would give developers confidence and help projects stay on track.
  - Increase planning support for community‑led and SME schemes, including dedicated case officers, early pre‑app advice, and clearer routes for local designs that meet energy efficiency and tenure targets. In practice, this means fewer delays and less wasted time on paperwork, especially for sites that local builders know well.

- Support for community land trusts, co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction (MMC)
  - Release land for community-led housing where appropriate and provide land and finance packages specifically designed for CLTs and housing co‑ops, so land price isn’t a barrier to affordable homes. These models help keep homes affordable long‑term and build community resilience.
  - Back self‑build and community‑led sites with access to low‑cost finance, technical advisory support, and up‑skilling of local trades. Combining self‑build with modern methods of construction (MMC), such as modular or off‑site timber framing, can accelerate delivery and improve quality and energy performance. I’ve seen MMC work well on other projects in Scotland and the north of England, delivering well‑built, greener homes in a fraction of the time.
  - Promote land trusts and co‑ops as a credible route to rapid, affordable housing supply on brownfield and smaller sites, keeping land in community stewardship and rents affordable in the long term.

- Major public investment in council and housing association building programmes
  - Provide a sustained, multi‑decade pipeline of investment to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. A predictable funding envelope would allow housing associations and councils to plan, recruit and train local workers, and to spread costs and risks across projects.
  - Tie investment to strong energy efficiency and climate targets, using modern construction standards and retrofit where appropriate. This not only lowers running costs for tenants but also aligns with Scotland’s climate commitments and energy‑safety standards.
  - Support a blended approach where social rent homes are complemented by affordable private rental and low‑cost ownership options, all delivered with robust tenancy protections and good-quality standards.

In practice, a coherent policy package would look like a combined framework: finance and procurement support for SMEs, a proactive small‑sites planning regime, a strong emphasis on community‑led delivery and MMC, and a long‑term public investment programme focused on genuinely affordable social housing. The key is coordination across national and local governments, councils, housing associations, and the building sector, plus clear metrics and a transparent delivery timetable.

If implemented, these reforms would not only increase the number of affordable homes more quickly but would also improve the quality and energy efficiency of those homes, support local jobs and skills growth, and help communities stay vibrant and affordable for years to come.

I’d be happy to discuss these ideas further and participate in any pilot work or consultation to help shape practical, on‑the‑ground reforms.

I support reforms that prioritise regenerating town centres, converting empty homes and infill before any Green Belt release; back SME builders with finance and planning support; and expand Build-to-Rent with affordability covenants and professional management for stability.

Living in England and observing housing costs in my area, I believe the most effective reforms to boost the supply of affordable, good-quality homes rest on two linked pillars. First, a substantial public investment programme through councils and housing associations to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low‑income households. Second, a streamlined planning system that speeds up delivery without compromising environmental safeguards. Both are needed if we’re serious about reducing the pressure on local housing waiting lists and ensuring stable, decent homes for families who would otherwise be priced out of the market.

On the public investment side, I’ve seen how our local council could unlock real progress if it had a clear, multi-year pipeline of projects backed by appropriate funding. There are several brownfield sites and surplus public land that sit unused for years, where we could build social rent homes quickly if there were stable financing and certainty about planning approvals. A 10-year or longer, ringfenced programme with capital grants and affordable borrowing powers would let councils and housing associations plan, partner with builders, and deliver scale. In practice, this could mean, for our area, several thousand additional social rented homes over the next decade—homes that are genuinely affordable, designed for families, with good energy standards and accessible layouts. The plan should require that a substantial proportion of new builds are social rent, with rents pegged at a level that protects households on the lowest incomes and helps sustain the overall viability of communities.

Public investment must be paired with a strong focus on quality and longevity. It’s not enough to create more units; they must be well-built, energy efficient and designed to last. That means higher standards for insulation, air tightness and low running costs; adaptable layouts for changing family needs; and accessible design for older or disabled residents. It also means using energy-efficient construction and, where possible, on-site renewable energy, so that homes remain affordable over the long term. In our town, a recently completed housing association scheme delivered well-built flats but the long waiting lists elsewhere show the shortage remains acute. A sustained pipeline would change that, allowing households to move out of overcrowded or temporary accommodation into secure homes and giving communities long-term stability.

Turning to planning reform, I support streamlining and simplifying planning, zoning and decision timelines while retaining environmental safeguards. The obstacle isn’t the need to protect the environment—it’s the delays and complexity that deter councils and developers from moving swiftly. A clearer, faster pathway would reduce uncertainty for builders and help housing associations accelerate delivery. Practical steps could include a nationally set timetable for decisions, with automatic extensions only granted for genuine site-specific issues, and a simplified viability process that reduces protracted negotiations over Section 106 contributions. In our area, major sites stall for years while detailed discussions on affordable housing percentages and infrastructure contributions drag on. A streamlined framework with predefined, transparent thresholds would deliver quicker approvals for sites that clearly meet affordable housing criteria, subject to robust biodiversity, flood risk and energy standards.

Environment safeguards must not be watered down. We should retain biodiversity net gain, flood risk assessments, and clear energy performance requirements, but reduce duplicative consultations and off-ramps that stall projects. A “brownfield-first” approach, with a prioritised register of public land and underutilised sites, would accelerate delivery without compromising climate goals. A one-stop digital planning portal, standardised design codes, and pre-application planning support would help developers and housing associations align their proposals with local needs from the outset.

Implementation should be accompanied by accountability and clear outcomes. Authorities should publish annual delivery plans, with milestones for the number of social rented homes completed, and independent monitoring to ensure that gains materialise. A portion of the gains from planning reforms—the uplift in land value and development fees—should be reinvested directly into affordable housing. This could help sustain a steady stream of socially rented units and keep rents affordable for low‑income families.

In short, the most credible route to more affordable, good‑quality homes in my area is a long-term, publicly funded building programme led by councils and housing associations, combined with a faster, clearer planning process that still protects the environment. When these two elements work together, we can replace waiting lists with real choices for families and communities, and deliver homes that are affordable to live in today and sustainable for decades to come.

I’m writing as someone living in England, in the 55-64 age band, and I’m not convinced the reforms as described will reliably increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in my area without creating new problems for services and local democracy. In practice, housing delivery seems to stall when infrastructure and services aren’t funded in parallel with building, and I’ve seen this locally more than once. A few concrete points from my experience and observations below.

- Service-readiness must come first. It’s not enough to promise more homes if there isn’t capacity for transport, schools, GP capacity, utilities and broadband to keep up. In our town area, a plan for several thousand homes sits in the planning queue, but the new primary school is not funded to meet demand and the local health centre already has lengthy waits. If homes are completed and people move in without appropriate services, you create bottlenecks that push rents up, reduce quality of life, and undermine the purpose of affordability. Any reform should require a funded, phased provision of critical infrastructure and services alongside or even before occupancy, with independent milestones and regular audits to prove readiness before residents move in.

- Public investment in genuinely affordable social housing is essential, but not a silver bullet. The idea of “major public investment” into council and housing association building programmes is welcome in principle, but it must be long‑term, well-governed and cost-controlled. I’ve witnessed past schemes run over budget and time, producing units that are affordable on paper but costly to maintain or poorly designed for energy efficiency. We should widen the toolkit to include public land reuse, community‑led housing models, and robust long‑term stewardship with clear commitments on rent levels and repairs. Without an explicit guarantee that new homes stay affordable for the long term and that maintenance won’t erode that affordability, the social value gets diluted.

- Planning reform must preserve quality and community voice. Streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines is attractive in principle, but I’d be wary of moving too fast at the expense of design quality, environmental safeguards and local accountability. In my experience, haste can produce cookie-cutter developments with insufficient parking, insufficient space for cycle routes, and poor energy standards that cost residents more in the long run. It’s vital that any speedier process retains robust environmental protections and a real opportunity for local communities to shape schemes through meaningful consultation and effective local appeals processes. Dumbing down planning checks to chase speed risks the very thing we want to avoid: poor-quality housing that becomes a burden rather than a home.

- A practical reform package would mix and match ideas with guardrails. If we are to accelerate delivery, I’d support reforms that tie faster planning to clear, enforceable standards: mandatory, shovel-ready infrastructure packages; a dedicated, long‑term fund for affordable housing that covers both construction and ongoing repairs; performance targets for energy efficiency and low maintenance costs; and a default expectation that a portion of every new development is genuinely affordable rental or sale units, with rents and prices indexed to local income levels and not speculative market levels. More explicitly, I’d want to see public land brought into play, with long-term leases to housing associations or community land trusts to ensure long-term affordability and stewardship.

- Local impacts matter. In my area, new housing without commensurate services has tangible downsides: overstretched schools, crowded buses, longer journeys to doctor appointments, and more traffic. Any reform should require a credible plan for transport and health services to scale in step with housing, ideally funded by a combination of government grants, developer contributions, and efficiency in public procurement that reduces unit costs without compromising quality.

In short, I’m not against increasing affordable homes, but I am wary of reforms that prioritise speed over service readiness, or that rely on public investment without robust safeguards for affordability, maintenance and community input. The reforms I’d back would insist on infrastructure-first milestones, long‑term social housing funding with strong governance, and planning rules that secure high-quality design and local democracy while still removing unnecessary delays that stall good projects. Only then can we deliver genuinely affordable, well‑located housing that sustains communities rather than just adds numbers to a housing column.

I strongly support reforms that increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in Wales. Strengthening licensing, enforcement and minimum standards, alongside longer tenancies, would raise safety and energy efficiency in the private rented sector. In my street I’ve seen tenants living in damp, poorly heated homes because upgrades are too costly for small landlords; clearer standards and targeted support would encourage compliant landlords to invest, while still protecting tenants. A stable tenancy of three to five years would give families real security and help communities.

On planning, streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines, with retained environmental safeguards, would cut unnecessary delays and reduce developer uncertainty. In practice, local schemes stall because of slow processes and conflicting signals. Digital submissions, standardised application forms and earlier pre‑application engagement would speed delivery of affordable homes while protecting green spaces and flood risk.

Consider rent stabilization pilots to improve affordability while evaluating risks to supply. I’d back targeted caps in high‑pressure areas, combined with monitoring, exemptions for new builds and support for landlords to modernise properties, funded by evidence collected through pilots.

From my home in Scotland, aged 65+, I’ve watched neighbours and families struggle to find affordable, good‑quality homes close to the services we rely on. I support reforms that empower SME and local builders to increase local supply. Targeted finance and easier procurement for small firms would help—simpler access to public funding, and procurement frameworks that recognise smaller bidders, not just large developers. A clear small‑sites policy would make councils identify and release compact brownfield parcels in towns and villages, with robust pre‑application planning support to shorten timescales and improve site viability.

Planning reforms should prioritise local design quality and energy efficiency, while ensuring new homes are adaptable for an ageing population Obviously.... However, I’m wary of schemes that push housing in isolation; we must require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure sustainable, service‑ready communities. In our area, transport upgrades and GP capacity often lag housing delivery, which undermines the very benefit of new homes.

Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes could lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. There is unused council land near the town centre that could deliver 80–120 affordable homes if land costs were reduced and uplift revenue ring-fenced for community facilities.

Reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with more transparency sounds appealing, but in practice it risks choking off new housing. Even with better transparency, the system will still add negotiation overhead, create more delays, and raise costs that get passed on to buyers and renters. In my town, a 180-home scheme aimed to deliver 40% affordable on-site. The viability assessment kept being re-run, and the council's decision pushed back by months; by the time it finally started, the affordable homes were pushed to a scattered off-site contribution or delayed indefinitely. The infrastructure funding relies on developers' margins; when margins shrink, infrastructure and social housing commitments are the first casualty. I value openness, but not if it means fewer homes get built. We need to fix the bottlenecks that slow up planning and land release: unlock brownfield land, standardise viability criteria, expedite decisions, and ensure upfront, enforceable obligations are embedded in the planning conditions without crippling delivery times. In short, better processes must lead to more, not less, affordable homes on-site.

i strongly believe from my vantage in a small town in England, the reforms that would most help increase affordable, good-quality homes are threefold. First, prioritise regeneration, infill, and conversion of vacant buildings and long-term empty homes over any release of Green Belt or greenfield land. Our town has a derelict factory near the river and several empty shops above the High Street; converting these into well-designed flats would add stock quickly without harming landscapes. Simplify planning rules for conversions and ensure high design standards so the new homes sit well in their surroundings, with regard to parking, accessibility, and public spaces.

Second, I’m cautiously in favour of major public investment in council and housing association building programmes, provided there are tight cost controls, local jobs, and long-term upkeep guarantees. The need for genuinely affordable social rented homes for low-income households is clear, but delivery must be efficient and with transparent oversight.

Third, mandate higher energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits to reduce bills and meet climate targets. Our older homes are energy hogs; retrofits and better insulation pay back over time, but costs must be shared fairly between tenants and landlords, with accessible grants!

Release surplus public land but fund the uplift via levies to lower land costs and pay for affordable housing and infrastructure; streamline planning timelines while preserving environmental safeguards; target finance and procurement support for SME and local builders through small-sites policy.

I believe the reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in our area are twofold: raise energy standards for new builds and invest in retrofits, and prioritise regeneration and the conversion of vacant or long-term empty buildings before releasing Green Belt land. Mandating higher energy efficiency for all new homes, with funding to upgrade existing stock, would cut bills for residents and reduce energy demand, helping both tenants and landlords manage costs without sacrificing comfort. In our town, many older homes could be heat upgraded and insulated, and a rolling retrofit fund could enable households to access heat pumps during the colder months. 

Second, prioritising regeneration and infill would bring homes on brownfield sites or within town centres first. We have disused mills and empty shops that could be converted into affordable flats, supporting local services and avoiding countryside loss. Efficient planning processes and small grants for these projects would speed delivery. Only after these avenues are fully exploited should we consider Green Belt releases, to protect landscapes and the character of our area.

Reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area should focus on energy efficiency and the long-term affordability of ownership and rents, while enabling builders to bring more units to market. First, mandate higher energy standards for new builds. A fabric‑first approach—tight insulation, high‑performing windows, airtight construction, and ready infrastructure for heat pumps—should be the baseline. Aiming for EPC B (or better) by 2030 would cut running costs for future tenants, help meet climate targets, and reduce energy poverty, while still being attractive to developers who can use off‑site manufacture and modular techniques to keep prices down. Second, fund retrofits of existing homes, especially social and affordable stock. Long‑term, low‑interest loans and grants for landlords and leaseholders to upgrade insulation, heating systems and draught‑proofing would dramatically reduce bills and help keep rents affordable. In my street, older terraces suffer from drafts and under‑performing boilers; retrofits would unlock more livable homes without pushing rents up. Third, align planning and funding with supply by streamlining approvals for energy‑efficient schemes and offering predictable subsidies tied to performance. If upfront costs rise, ensure grants or tax relief cover the extra, with safeguards to prevent rent spikes. Overall, these reforms would boost supply by making homes cheaper to operate and more appealing to developers, while protecting tenants.

I live in England and respond as an individual. I welcome the aim of increasing affordable, good‑quality homes, but I’m not convinced by reform packages that lean heavily on market‑led Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants. In practice, these can lock in private ownership structures and management that prioritise returns over long‑term affordability and social cohesion, with rents that drift beyond local wages. In our area, several BTR blocks have gone up quickly, yet long‑term affordability and upkeep have sometimes lagged when management fees rise or repairs are slow. 

I see more robust potential in community‑led approaches: community land trusts and housing co‑operatives keep the price of homes tethered to local incomes and give residents real influence over design and upkeep. Self‑build groups and modern methods of construction can accelerate supply if supported by streamlined planning and access to skilled labour. The small‑sites policy, targeted finance, and easier procurement for SME builders are essential; they enable local firms to deliver a diverse mix of homes without being squeezed by national developers.

Any reform should pair rental provision with accountable, resident‑led governance and ensure affordability remains genuinely affordable for local people, not just for the next decade.

I support reforms, but only if local data and monitoring are robust and developers are held accountable; councils must have funding to plan, enforce, and deliver commitments to affordable, quality homes.

From our organisation in Wales, tackling housing affordability in our communities, we see a two‑pronged approach as most promising, provided it is tightly monitored and funded.

First, better local data and stronger accountability: a public dashboard tracking land supply, planning permissions, and delivery against affordable-housing commitments. We’ve seen sites with permission for 60 affordable units stall for years while the rest of the scheme progresses; councils are strained, and monitoring is inconsistent. A statutory role for enforcement and dedicated delivery capacity within planning departments would help ensure obligations are met, with clear milestones and clawback if delivery slips.

Second, release of surplus public land and land value capture: freeing council and Welsh Government assets would lower land costs; applying uplifts via levies or targeted taxes (like CIL or planning gain) could fund affordable homes and local infrastructure. In our experience, where land costs are high, affordable homes struggle to compete with market sale prices; earmarking uplift receipts for genuinely affordable housing and roads, schools, and GP capacity would help.

We urge pilots in willing authorities to test dashboards and levy schemes and publish results publicly.

From where I’m standing in England, with family members who rely on mobility aids and a local university campus just up the road, I don’t think simply piling more generic homes on the market will fix the shortages or deliver the right kind of housing for most people. The reforms that will actually increase affordable, good-quality homes are those that prioritise wheelchair‑accessible, adaptable homes, plus dedicated older‑person and supported housing, and student key‑worker accommodation, all tailored to rural realities and cultural needs.

Two big reasons frame my view. First, a lot of the stock being built now is inaccessible or only modestly adaptable. My mum’s bungalow wasn’t designed for a wheelchair, and the cost of retrofitting is high, time‑consuming and sometimes not feasible in older stock. In rural areas like ours, where wheelchairs and carers must contend with uneven pavements, long driveways, and limited local services, a family can burn through money trying to make a home usable. If we had housing designed from the start to be accessible and adaptable, households would spend less on later alterations and could stay in their communities longer.

Second, the people who need affordable homes aren’t just first‑time buyers. We also need supply that supports older residents who want to downsize into more appropriate accommodation, and student and key‑worker housing that keeps essential services close to where they work and study. In our town, nurses, healthcare assistants, and teachers commute long distances because there isn’t affordable, nearby housing with the right design for their shift patterns. Delivering dedicated funded schemes for student‑key workers near campuses and clinics would help recruitment and retention and reduce strain on household budgets.

Proposed reforms I’d like to see implemented include:

- Make accessible design standard in new affordable housing. Require a meaningful proportion of new affordable homes to meet M4(2) accessible and adaptable standards, with a subset that is M4(3) wheelchair‑user capable. This isn’t cosmetic; it means wider doorways, step‑free access, ground‑level living space, and bathroom layouts that work for wheelchairs from day one. In practice, that reduces the need for disruptive renovations later and helps people stay independent longer.

- Fund retrofit and expansion of specialist housing in rural areas. Create a dedicated Accessible Housing Retrofit Fund for existing stock and for expansions of supported housing, where care and social support services are built in. This would be aimed at older people and those with disabilities, so they can move into appropriate homes without needing to relocate far away from families or services.

- Expand supported housing for older people and for people with disabilities. Develop more “extra‑care” or supported living schemes within existing communities, with on‑site or nearby care provisions. In my experience, the ability to receive support in a familiar local area vastly improves quality of life and can cut hospital discharge times and social care costs.

- Create targeted student‑key‑worker housing near universities and health campuses. Ring‑fenced funding, simpler viability assessments for these schemes, and shared equity or rental models that prioritise affordability for staff and students would help keep essential workers close to the services they support. It’s not just about students; it’s about keeping a pipeline of nurses, teachers, and carers who can live near where they work and study.

- Tailor developments to rural and cultural needs. Allow for flexible layouts that suit multi‑generational living or cultural norms around family space while still meeting accessibility requirements. Plan for transport‑constrained areas by locating housing near bus routes and essential services, and use community land trusts or cooperative models to preserve affordability and local control in rural settings.

- Simplify planning and funding procedures for these schemes. Remove unnecessary hurdles for specialist housing and ensure viability assessments recognise the higher upfront costs of accessibility and support services. Clear funding streams for both new build and retrofit will unlock development quickly rather than stalling projects that meet real needs.

- Measure and report outcomes. Tie reforms to concrete targets, such as numbers of accessible homes delivered, occupancy by older people, take‑up by key workers, and resident satisfaction in rural areas. Transparent data will reveal what works and where to improve.

If these reforms are pursued, I believe we would see a real step change in the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes that fit people’s abilities and daily lives. Buildings that are accessible by design, supported housing that keeps families together in their communities, and student‑key worker homes that reduce travel and recruitment hurdles—these are the kinds of fixes that reflect how people actually live and move in England today.

To increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area, the reforms that would work best are releasing surplus public land and capturing the uplift from planning decisions through levies or taxes. Local authorities hold sites that could deliver affordable homes with good design if land costs are lowered and the uplift receipts ring‑fenced for housing and infrastructure. A value‑capture approach—whether a planning uplift levy, tweaks to the Community Infrastructure Levy, or a targeted land value tax—can reduce development costs and fund roads, flood defences, schools and health capacity alongside the homes themselves. In our district we’ve discussed former council depots and NHS land that could be transformed into genuinely affordable housing with energy‑efficient standards and durable maintenance commitments. The aim should be a mix of affordable tenures and high quality design, with receipts recycling back into local communities.

I’d also consider rent stabilisation pilots as a supplementary tool, but only with robust safeguards: time‑limited trials, clear success metrics, exemptions for new builds or major refurbishments, and support to landlords for maintenance and exits. The risk is that poorly designed caps dampen investment or reduce supply. Overall, land release and uplift capture should take priority, with measured pilots to test affordability without chilling development.

From where I live in England, I’m sceptical that simply pouring public money into council and housing association building programmes will reliably deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes fast enough to meet need. In practice, the scale of funding needed, the time it takes to navigate planning and procurement, and the ongoing costs of maintenance mean outcomes can lag far behind demand. And when schemes do materialise, I worry some simply swap public subsidies for more debt or grant dependence without addressing the underlying supply constraints we all see in our day-to-day lives.

If the aim is to actually increase affordable housing quickly and sustainably, reforms should go beyond hammering more money into state-built stocks. Here are practical levers that could move the needle without relying solely on large public building programmes:

- Planning and land release reform: accelerate planning permissions for brownfield and town-centre sites, and prioritise up-zoning near employment hubs to unlock land for affordable homes. Create clear, time-bound delivery milestones tied to affordable housing outputs, so schemes aren’t left languishing for years in bureaucratic queues. Make it easier for councils to acquire and assemble land when viability is still sound, rather than letting parcels sit empty.

- Control costs and improve certainty: impose standardised, cost-conscious designs for social housing where appropriate, with common components and modular construction where quality can be guaranteed. Streamline procurement and permit faster, high-quality MMC (modern methods of construction) to reduce build times and variance in costs. This would help stretch every pound further; currently, price volatility and delays inflate budgets and delay homes for households in need.

- Mixed-tenure and community-led delivery: encourage a broader mix of delivery channels, including private sector partnerships with social obligations, longer-term build-to-rent with affordable elements, and community-led models such as community land trusts. These can deliver more units faster, diversify communities, and reduce reliance on public capital alone. In many places, community groups understand local needs better and can maintain affordability over the long term if backed by stable grant or loan funding.

- Use and refurbish existing stock first: accelerate the refit and conversion of empty homes and substandard existing stock, with strong retrofit programmes to improve energy efficiency. This not only raises quality quickly but can also reduce ongoing costs for tenants and councils, making affordability more sustainable while new-build may be delayed.

- Targeted, time-limited public support with guardrails: provide subsidies or guarantees that are explicitly linked to short and medium-term outputs, with strict performance reporting and protections against cost overruns. Tie affordability to actual long-term rent levels and occupancy obligations to avoid stock drifting into higher rents or sales in the future.

- Protect tenants and quality: ensure any new social housing stock comes with robust tenancy rights, energy efficiency targets, and high maintenance standards; avoid creating properties that look affordable on paper but deteriorate quickly due to poor upkeep.

I’ve seen cases locally where families wait years on council lists (and often end up in expensive private rentals with rising rents and poor conditions) while shiny new schemes take ages to materialise, or the units fail to get retained as truly affordable housing. There’s a real danger that large-scale public investment ends up as a slow, costly route that doesn’t actually expand the affordable stock in a meaningful, timely way.

In short, the reforms that will most effectively increase supply are the ones that remove bottlenecks in delivery, diversify the routes to affordable housing, and ensure cost control and long-term affordability. Public investment can play a role, but it must be part of a broader, reform-led strategy that speeds up delivery, uses land wisely, and leverages the strengths of private and community-led delivery to get homes built and kept affordable for those who need them most.

I don't think releasing surplus public land and using levies to capture planning uplift will meaningfully increase affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Land values are the real driver, and uplift charges can simply raise prices for all new homes instead of creating genuinely affordable options for ordinary households. Instead, reforms should prioritise community control and proven construction methods. For example, community land trusts and housing co‑operatives can hold land in trust and preserve affordability in perpetuity, while locally run development on underused sites can keep profits in the community. In places with CLTs, affordable rents have stayed stable longer than in conventional market schemes, which suggests a better long‑term outcome. We should also back self‑build and modern methods of construction to speed up delivery and improve quality - what a surprise. Allow small builders and community groups access to publicly owned sites with long leases, simplify planning for modular or timber‑frame homes, and ensure robust quality standards. Funding should come from targeted local sources (grants, local borrowing, dedicated funds) rather than broad uplift levies that raise costs for everyone. These approaches would deliver affordable, high‑quality homes quicker and with lasting community benefit.

I believe the reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area are rooted in sustained, public investment in council and housing association building programmes. This isn’t a quick fix; it’s about delivering genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households that are secure, energy efficient and well‑designed for the communities they serve. My own experience in our town shows why this approach is so necessary, and why it should be backed with robust funding and practical reforms rather than simply slogans.
