If public funding is used, it should come with strong cost controls, transparent governance, and a ring-fenced maintenance fund to prevent the stock from deteriorating after handover. Consider long-term leasing/management arrangements with private sector partners only where there are strict limits on rent escalations and clear social value commitments.
- Strong emphasis on energy efficiency and accessibility. Any new homes should be built to keep running costs low for decades, be adaptable for changing needs with universal design principles, and comply with high fire-safety and safety standards from day one.
- Improve the private rented sector alongside council housing. Better regulation of private rents and stronger incentives for landlords to maintain decent energy efficiency can reduce pressure on social housing demand. A healthier overall market will free up stock for those who truly need social rents.

In short, more homes are necessary, but the biggest gains would come from improving what already exists, not just pouring public money into large new builds that can take years to materialise and may not remain affordable in the long term. I’d like to see reforms that empower local communities, accelerate practical improvements, and ensure every new or refurbished home really remains affordable, well maintained, and accessible for the people who need it most.

i really think disagree that broad top‑down reforms alone will swiftly deliver affordable, high‑quality homes. Real progress comes from empowering communities—invest in community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build, and modern methods of construction to lock in long‑term affordability and speed up delivery!

While I share the aim of more affordable, good‑quality homes, I cannot support the reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing as currently drafted. They risk weakening delivery and pushing more payments into in‑lieu funds rather than on‑site homes, which would put extra pressure on local services and infrastructure. In our area a large estate recently approved promised half the homes as affordable under S106; in practice only a minority were built on site and the rest was paid as a cash contribution. Consequently, there is no lasting affordable supply in the community, and roads and GP capacity already struggle.

Reforms must be differently framed: require on‑site affordable housing as the default for most sites, with binding obligations; ensure viability assessments are transparent—publish costs, assumptions, and the independent checks; cap the ability to reduce obligations through optimistic margins; ensure receipts from CIL and S106 are ring‑fenced for local infrastructure and housing in the same area, with regular monitoring and penalties for late delivery.

In short, better transparency and enforceable obligations are welcome, but only if they guarantee real on‑site affordable homes and timely infrastructure funding, not vague promises or cash payments that delay development.

Yes, I support reforms that unlock major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low-income households. In my area, the social-rent waiting list is long and few new homes are built to replace those lost to demolition or right-to-buy, leaving pressure on families in insecure private tenancies. A multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlement for councils and housing associations is essential, with councils empowered to borrow against the Housing Revenue Account to finance new sites. Planning reform should prioritise social housing on brownfield land and streamline approvals for modest developments, with a clear cap on fees and delays. Use public land and right-to-buy receipts to back new social rented homes, not just market housing. Encourage modern methods of construction to bring costs down and speed up delivery, while maintaining high standards of energy efficiency and quality. Long-term affordability must be protected by rents tied to local income levels and secure allocation policies, with tenants involved in design and stewardship. If these steps are accompanied by strong local oversight, we can genuinely increase supply and relieve hardship without compromising standards.

i really think i support reforms that require all new homes to be wheelchair-accessible and adaptable, with more older-persons, supported and student key-worker housing targeted to rural and cultural needs. However, ensure stable funding, clear delivery plans, and long-term maintenance to keep them affordable!

While the aim of increasing affordable, good‑quality homes is welcome, I oppose the reforms as drafted. Relying mainly on purpose‑built Build‑to‑Rent and large mixed‑tenure schemes risks pushing rents up and handing control to private developers, without a guaranteed long‑term supply of genuinely affordable homes or real community fit. In my area, new BTR blocks went up quickly but very few units were truly affordable, and the management and service charges can undermine stability for older residents and families alike.

I believe reforms should prioritise community‑led and cooperative models: community land trusts, housing co‑ops, self‑build, and modern methods of construction, which can deliver good homes faster with local accountability and lower long‑term costs. Any energy standards must be higher for new builds and, crucially, funded for retrofits so bills stay affordable and responsibilities don’t shift onto tenants or landlords.

Practically, that means enabling local groups with land, unlocking finance for affordable units, cutting unnecessary planning delays, and enforcing robust affordability covenants within developments. Only by combining strong local control, professional management, and substantial retrofit funding will supply be genuinely affordable and sustainably high‑quality for people like me in later life.

THANK YOU FOR THE OPPORTUNITY TO RESPOND. IN OUR AREA THE PRIVATE RENTED SECTOR PLAYS A BIG PART IN HOUSING THE LOCAL WORKFORCE AND FAMILIES, BUT THE QUALITY OF SOME HOMES REMAINS VARIABLE. I’VE LIVED IN RENTED ACCOMMODATION FOR OVER A DECADE AND ALSO OWN TWO SMALL RENTAL PROPERTIES. I’VE SEEN DAMP AND POORLY INSULATED HOMES, AND THE STRESS ON TENANTS WHEN MAINTENANCE ISN’T PROMPT. I BELIEVE REFORMS CAN RAISE STANDARDS AND AFFORDABILITY WHILE KEEPING THE SECTOR VIABLE FOR SMALL LANDLORDS LIKE ME AND OTHERS WHO RELY ON A MODEST PORTFOLIO TO FUND OUR MORTGAGES AND RETIREMENT. THE KEY IS BALANCE: TOUGHER STANDARDS AND ENFORCEMENT, BUT WITH SENSIBLE PROTECTIONS FOR SMALL LANDLORDS AND TARGETED SUPPORT WHERE IT’S MOST NEEDED. BASED ON MY EXPERIENCE, THE REFORMS THAT WOULD MOST EFFECTIVELY INCREASE SUPPLY OF AFFORDABLE, GOOD-QUALITY HOMES ARE AS FOLLOWS:

- CREATE A CLEAR, CONSISTENT BASELINE FOR LICENSING AND MINIMUM STANDARDS
  - ESTABLISH A NATIONAL FLOOR FOR LICENSING THAT COVERS ENGLAND BUT ALLOWS LOCAL AUTHORITIES TO RAISE THE BAR WHERE NECESSARY. THIS SHOULD BE UNDERPINNED BY A SIMPLE, PUBLIC ONLINE SYSTEM SO LANDLORDS CAN APPLY ONCE AND UPDATE AS NEEDED.
  - FUND ENFORCEMENT PROPERLY SO INSPECTORS AREN’T ENDLESSLY BACKLOGED. QUICK, PREDICTABLE COMPLIANCE TIMELINES HELP LANDLORDS PLAN AND TENANTS KNOW WHAT TO EXPECT.
  - ALIGN LICENSING WITH A UNIVERSAL SET OF PROPERTY STANDARDS (DECENT HOMES, SAFE GAS AND ELECTRICAL WORK, WORKING HEATING AND HOT WATER, NO DAMP OR MOULD): IF A PROPERTY MEETS THE STANDARD AT RENEWAL, THAT SHOULD BE RECOGNISED TO AVOID REPETITIVE INSPECTIONS.

- INTRODUCE PROPORTIONATE, TARGETED MEASURES TO PROTECT SMALL LANDLORDS
  - USE A TIERED APPROACH SO LANDLORDS WITH ONLY ONE TO THREE PROPERTIES FACE A LIGHTER, STREAMLINED REGIME AND FEES, WITH CLEAR EXEMPTIONS FOR GENUINE MICRO-LANDLORDS WHO MANAGE A SINGLE HOME.
  - CAP OR CAP-RELATIVE LICENSING FEES AND ENSURE COSTS ARE TRANSPARENTLY SPENT ON ENFORCEMENT AND PROPERTY IMPROVEMENT SCHEMES IN THE AREAS THEY COVER.
  - ENCOURAGE ACCREDITATION SCHEMES THAT OFFER BENEFITS (E.G., REDUCED INSPECTIONS, ACCESS TO LANDLORD SUPPORT SERVICES) FOR THOSE WHO MEET HIGHER STANDARDS AND MAINTAIN GOOD COMPLIANCE HISTORY.

- STRENGTHEN ENFORCEMENT AGAINST ROGUE LANDLORDS WHILE SUPPORTING LEGITIMATE ONES
  - INCREASE PENALTIES FOR THE WORST OFFENDERS BUT PROVIDE A CLEAR, TWO-STAGE REMEDY PROCESS FOR IMPROVING NON-COMPLIANT PROPERTIES, WITH TARGETED HELP FOR LANDLORDS TO MEET ESSENTIAL STANDARDS.
  - CREATE A JOINT LOCAL-GOVERNMENT/LANDLORD PARTNERSHIP THAT SHARES DATA TO AVOID DUPLICATIVE INSPECTIONS AND TO FOCUS RESOURCES ON PROPERTIES MOST AT RISK OF POOR CONDITIONS.

- PROMOTE LONGER TENANCIES WITH SENSIBLE PROTECTIONS
  - DEFAULT TO LONGER TENANCIES (FOR EXAMPLE THREE-YEAR TERMS) WITH AUTOMATIC RENEWAL UNLESS THERE ARE CLEAR, SUBSTANTIATED GROUNDS TO END THE TENANCY. THIS GIVES FAMILIES AND WORKERS STABILITY AND PREDICTABLE HOUSING COSTS.
  - PROVIDE A FRAMEWORK FOR FAIR AND TRANSPARENT RENT REVIEWS, AND ENSURE THERE IS A CLEAR, EFFICIENT PROCESS FOR END-OF-TENANCY NOTICES WHEN JUSTIFIED, SO NEITHER TENANTS NOR LANDLORDS FACE PERPETUAL UNCERTAINTY.
  - TIE LONGER TENANCIES TO PRACTICAL INCENTIVES FOR LANDLORDS: ACCESS TO ENERGY-EFFICIENCY GRANTS, LOW-INTEREST LOANS FOR ESSENTIAL REPAIRS, AND SIMPLIFIED TAX OR REGULATORY RELIEF FOR PROPERTIES MEETING HIGHER STANDARDS.

- INVEST IN IMPROVING QUALITY AND ENERGY EFFICIENCY, ANCHORED BY TENANT AFFORDABILITY
  - USE GOVERNMENT-BACKED SCHEMES TO FUND INSULATION UPGRADES, MODERN HEATING SYSTEMS, AND VENTILATION IMPROVEMENTS, PRIORITISED FOR HOMES WITH DOCUMENTED DAMP OR HIGH ENERGY COSTS. IN MY EXPERIENCE, EVEN MODEST IMPROVEMENTS CAN MAKE A HOME SIGNIFICANTLY HEALTHIER AND CHEAPER TO HEAT.
  - ENSURE ANY MEASURES ADDRESS BOTH SAFETY AND COMFORT: UP-TO-DATE ELECTRICAL SAFETY, GAS SAFETY, SMOKE/CO ALARMS, AND VENTILATION TO PREVENT MOULD—BECAUSE LONG-TERM HEALTH AND ENERGY COSTS MATTER TO TENANTS AND LANDLORDS ALIKE.
  - SUPPORT TENANTS WITH CLEAR INFORMATION ABOUT RIGHTS, RESPONSIBILITIES, AND THE OPTIONS FOR LONGER TENANCIES, INCLUDING ACCESS TO INDEPENDENT ADVICE IF DISPUTES ARISE.

- PROVIDE A PHASED ROLLOUT WITH LOCAL LEARNING
  - START WITH PILOTS IN WILLING COUNCILS TO TEST LICENSING EFFECTIVENESS, ENFORCEMENT CAPACITY, AND LANDLORD SUPPORT MECHANISMS. USE THE RESULTS TO REFINE NATIONAL STANDARDS AND TO SHARE BEST PRACTICES ACROSS REGIONS.
  - MANDATE ROBUST DATA COLLECTION ON PROPERTY CONDITION, TENANCY DURATION, RENT LEVELS, AND EVICTION OUTCOMES SO WE CAN MEASURE WHETHER THESE REFORMS DELIVER MORE AFFORDABLE, HIGHER-QUALITY HOMES AND STABLE TENANCIES WITHOUT SHRINKING SUPPLY.

IN SHORT, I SUPPORT RAISING THE BAR FOR QUALITY AND SAFETY IN RENTED HOMES AND ENCOURAGING LONGER TENANCIES, BUT I WANT TO SEE THESE REFORMS IMPLEMENTED WITH FAIRNESS FOR SMALL LANDLORDS AND TARGETED INVESTMENT TO IMPROVE ENERGY EFFICIENCY. IF DONE THOUGHTFULLY, THESE MEASURES CAN MAKE THE PRIVATE RENTED SECTOR MORE TRUSTWORTHY AND STABLE, WHICH SHOULD LEAD TO MORE HOUSEHOLDS BEING ABLE TO CHOOSE GOOD-QUALITY, AFFORDABLE HOMES WITHOUT DETERRING RESPONSIBLE LANDLORDS FROM OFFERING THEM. I’M HOPEFUL FOR A PRACTICAL, PARTNERSHIP-BASED APPROACH BETWEEN GOVERNMENT, COUNCILS, TENANTS, AND LANDLORDS THAT DELIVERS REAL IMPROVEMENTS ON THE GROUND.

Thank you for the opportunity to share my views. Living in England and watching local housing costs creep up over the years, I’ve come to believe that real change will come from two clear reforms: making better use of public land and ensuring new homes are genuinely affordable to run, not just to buy. As a pensioner, I’ve seen how energy bills bite and how difficult it can be for ordinary families and older residents to stay in the communities they’ve helped build.

First, releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes offers a practical route to lower land costs and fund essential services. There are plenty of sites owned by councils, NHS trusts, and other public bodies that sit idle or are used inefficiently. A sensible policy would require local authorities to publish a clear register of surplus land with timelines for disposal, and for developers to contribute to affordable housing and local infrastructure via a transparent uplift mechanism. This could fund new council houses, shared ownership properties, and genuinely affordable rented homes, as well as improvements to schools, GP surgeries, and roads. In our area, for example, a former hospital site and a couple of empty council plots near town centres could accommodate small blocks of one- and two-bedroom flats designed for older people and younger key workers. If the land is released at sensible values and uplift is reinvested in the community, it would reduce the cost of new homes and help communities grow sustainably rather than chasing ever higher land prices.

Second, raising energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits is not a luxury but a necessity. Stricter energy efficiency standards—aligned with current climate targets—will reduce bills for households and lessen the burden on the national grid. For new builds, mandating better insulation, efficient heating systems, and heat pump readiness will pay dividends over the life of the home. For existing housing stock, an active retrofit programme is vital. My concern as a pensioner is that poor energy efficiency translates into unmanageable bills and cold, damp homes. It’s essential that the upfront costs of improvements are supported by public grants, low-interest loans, or subsidies, so tenants and landlords alike are not penalised by higher rents to cover expensive upgrades. A coordinated retrofit fund could prioritise blocks of flats and council housing, but also extend to private rentals where the energy performance is poor.

To make this effective, I’d like to see clear safeguards. Uplift revenues should be ringfenced for affordable housing and local infrastructure and should not simply subsidise higher-end development. The planning process should be streamlined enough to avoid delays, but robust enough to insist on quality design, accessibility, and long-term maintenance plans. We must also ensure that new homes incorporate accessibility features—level access, wider doorways, and adaptable bathrooms—so older residents can stay in their communities as their needs change.

Putting these reforms together would not only increase the number of affordable, good-quality homes but also create communities that are less energy intensive and more resilient to energy price swings. Releasing public land offers a tangible opportunity to bring down land costs and fund local services, while higher energy standards and retrofit funding protect households from spiralling bills and help meet climate targets. In my experience, such coordinated reforms deliver lasting benefits for current and future residents alike, securing better homes and stronger local facilities for our towns and villages.

From my experience in England, the most effective reforms would unlock finance and land for small and local builders, and improve planning support so they can deliver more diverse, affordable homes quickly. Key measures:
- Targeted finance: create a dedicated, patient fund for SME/local builders with longer tenors, lower rates and simpler drawdowns; provide guarantees or equity support to de-risk small-site schemes; ensure preference for mixed-tenure, affordable homes. On a recent local site, a promising bid stalled when a major lender pulled back; with accessible funds it would not have fallen over.
- Procurement access: widen eligibility in public and social housing contracts; set aside quotas for SMEs; cap minimum lot sizes to allow 4-15 unit schemes; streamline pre-qualification and allow shorter tender windows so small firms can compete.
- Small-sites policy and land supply: systematically release council and surplus church/education land for small-scale builders; create a 'small-sites first' stream within planning to prioritise infill and brownfield plots under 1 acre.
- Planning support: offer early viability advice, standardised pre-apps, and time-limited decisions; give local authorities a clear lead-in with a planning performance agreement.
This needs to be paired with robust quality controls to ensure long-term affordability and design standards.

I strongly support reforms that put major public investment into council housing and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. In our area in Wales, the lack of secure, affordable homes pushes families into costly private rented accommodation or into homelessness support services. A bold, well-funded programme would not only give people a stable base to live and work from but would also stabilise neighbourhoods and reduce pressures on emergency and health services that arise when people are crammed into unsuitable housing.

Key reforms I think would work best are:

- Scale up public investment specifically for social and affordable housing: provide ring‑fenced, long‑term capital grants to councils and housing associations to build and modernise homes that are genuinely affordable for low‑income households. Use a mix of direct public builds and partnerships with housing associations to ensure speed and quality.

- Leverage finance without compromising affordability: enable affordable borrowing backed by government guarantees where appropriate, so projects can be delivered faster while rents stay within what families can reasonably afford. Long‑term affordability should be built into the model, with rents linked to local income levels rather than market rates after a short subsidy period.

- Make land available and reduce delays in planning: release publicly owned land (including surplus local authority and Welsh Government assets) for social housing with streamlined planning processes. Sit alongside clearer local design standards that prioritise quality, energy efficiency and durability rather than short‑term cost saving.

- Prioritise energy efficiency and quality in build standards: every new social home should meet high energy‑efficiency standards, with modern, durable construction that reduces fuel bills and upkeep costs for tenants. This makes genuinely affordable homes affordable in the long term and supports climate goals.

- Use modern construction methods to speed up delivery and lower costs: wherever appropriate, use modern methods of construction (modular, off‑site build, etc.) to shorten build times while maintaining quality and safety. This helps deliver more homes faster and can bring costs down without compromising tenants’ experience.

- Focus on long‑term stewardship and tenant involvement: ensure councils and housing associations retain ownership and responsibility for maintenance and tenancy management. Involve residents in design choices and ongoing governance to build trust and ensure homes meet real needs.

- Targeted approaches for areas with acute need: data‑driven planning to identify hotspots where pressure on housing is highest, with flexible funding to respond to local circumstances—rural, coastal, and urban communities all have specific challenges that public investment can address.

- Build a pipeline with skilled local jobs and apprenticeships: create procurement rules that prioritise local jobs, training, and fair work. A social housing programme can be a driver for local economies, keeping investment within communities and boosting lifelong skills.

In my experience, when a council or housing association is clear about a long‑term plan to build affordable homes, it changes expectations and reduces the churn in households that are repeatedly moved around by insecure private rents. A few years ago, a relative faced a lengthy wait for a private‑rented property that was both expensive and unstable; a robust social‑housing programme would have provided a real alternative and saved distress for the family while also freeing up private sector stock for people who truly need it.

Ultimately, reforms must be coherent: decent, affordable homes funded publicly, built to high standards, and managed for the long term by trusted public or quasi‑public bodies. If we can deliver that, we’ll see not just more roofs over heads, but healthier, more stable communities across Wales.

I’m replying on behalf of our organisation because we’re concerned that the reforms being proposed around Section 106, CIL and viability testing, along with the push for tougher energy standards and more SME-focused planning support, could actually reduce the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes rather than increase it. We don’t dispute the aim of delivering affordable housing or cutting bills. But in practice, the way these reforms are framed risks higher costs, slower delivery and weaker local control over what gets built where, which is not what’s needed in our area.

Section 106, CIL and viability testing
- Transparency is welcome, but the key question is enforceability and real delivery. In many schemes we’ve seen viability testing used to justify lower affordable housing contributions, or to blur what is actually being provided on site. If the reforms simply add more reporting layers without requiring binding, on‑site obligations, councils and communities may still see too little affordable housing delivered, while developers pass costs onto tenants in the form of higher rents or service charges.
- On-site affordable housing can be a benefit when done well, but it must be genuinely on site, well managed, and fit for the local area. We’ve seen cases where “in‑lieu” contributions or affordable homes located far from the new development undermine long‑term sustainability, local connections, and the ability of residents to access jobs and schools. If the reforms move away from clear, enforceable on‑site delivery, we fear affordability and community integration will suffer.
- Viability testing needs independent oversight and robust, locally grounded data. Relying on developers’ own figures often means more optimistic projections than the local market can sustain. We’d advocate for explicit, statutory thresholds, independent independent checks, and a rule that if a site can’t deliver a reasonable affordable contribution without compromising safety or quality, the plan should not be approved. Speed and simplicity matter too; protracted negotiations drain scarce council resources and delay housing delivery.
- Our experience in local schemes suggests that when viability and contributions are predictable and linked to deliverable outcomes (for example, clear timelines for construction of affordable homes and explicit performance standards for on‑site management), delivery improves. The reform package must translate into rock‑solid commitments, not just higher paperwork and delayed onset of homes.

Higher energy standards and retrofit funding
- Mandating higher energy standards for new builds is sensible in principle, but in practice it raises the upfront cost of homes. For first‑time buyers and private renters, those costs often get baked into rents or mortgage prices. Without adequate grant support, loan products, and a clear plan for phased implementation, the result could be fewer new homes, or more expensive homes, at a time when affordability is already stretched.
- The retrofit push is equally important for long‑term affordability and climate targets, but funding must be predictable and sufficient. We’ve heard from tenants and local builders that retrofit schemes stall when funding cycles are uncertain or too short to be competitive. A credible retrofit fund should be long‑term, with clear eligibility criteria and a pipeline of work that aligns with local housing stock, energy performance gaps, and local authority needs.
- A practical approach would be to combine a staged, cost‑effective standard for new homes with a comprehensive retrofit fund that prioritises existing social housing and privately rented homes that are most energy‑inefficient. This would curb bills without pricing new homes out of reach or stalling construction. It’s crucial not to pass disproportionate costs to tenants or to small landlords who may already be stretched.

Finance, procurement access, and small‑sites policy
- SMEs and local builders are essential to a diverse, locally grown housing supply. But access to finance, complex procurement rules and planning bottlenecks can disproportionately disadvantage smaller players. If the policy shifts too much risk onto those builders, we’ll see fewer bids, longer project times, and higher prices per unit.
- Procurement processes can be over‑engineered and risk‑averse, favouring larger firms with established procurement teams. This reduces competition, stifles innovation, and can undermine quality if the commissions go to the lowest bidder rather than the best‑quality, value‑for‑money provider. A more equitable pathway would be to offer light‑touch, clearly defined pre‑qualification and a streamlined bidding process for SMEs, with a robust quality and aftercare standard.
- A targeted small‑sites policy could help, but it must come with dedicated planning support, faster decisions, and easier access to land. Local authorities need practical tools: land assembly support, pre‑application advice, and a predictable timetable that lets small builders plan ahead. Critical too is a planning framework that prioritises high‑quality design and appropriate densities, not just speed of approvals.

What we’d like to see instead
- A package that binds affordable housing delivery to specific, enforceable commitments on site, with transparent, independent oversight of viability assessments and a clear timetable for delivery. If a site cannot deliver the agreed on‑site affordable homes, there should be an enforceable back‑stop that ensures early replacement schemes or in‑lieu contributions meet locality needs.
- A credible funding bridge for energy standards and retrofits, with long‑term commitments and simple access for small landlords and developers. This should include grants, low‑interest loans and guarantees that don’t fall apart mid‑ programme and that actually reduce bills for tenants.
- Real support for SMEs: streamlined procurement, relaxed pre‑qualification for small bids, and dedicated planning support to get small sites through quickly while maintaining quality. Invest in local builder capacity, equipment sharing, and supply chain finance so that smaller firms can compete without taking on unsustainable risk.

In short, reforms must be deliverable, locally accountable and cost‑controlled. The aim should be more affordable homes that are genuinely affordable, built quickly, and of high quality, with energy efficiency baked in from day one but not at the expense of supply. If the reforms can deliver on those conditions, they’re worth pursuing; if not, they risk leaving more people stuck in unaffordable private rents with fewer homes being built in the places we need them most.

Rising rents and slow housing development in our town, England, mean we need a mix of approaches to boost affordable, good‑quality homes. Community land trusts can hold land in trust and lock affordability into the long term. Self‑build and modern methods of construction can speed up delivery and improve energy efficiency, provided plots are genuinely affordable and there’s clear planning and skilled fabrication capacity. Policy reforms should include dedicated funding for CLTs and co‑ops, streamlined routes for small, serviced plots and incentives for MMC that guarantee long‑term affordability and quality.

In my area, the most effective reforms would start with regenerating our existing stock rather than opening up greenfield land or releasing Green Belt. There are numerous vacant offices and old industrial sites that could be converted into genuinely affordable, good‑quality homes with much less environmental and community disruption than new builds on greenfield sites. I’ve seen derelict mills and empty shopfronts sit unused for years while demand outstrips supply; converting these spaces into flats or small-family homes would also revitalise town centres and improve energy efficiency through retrofits. We should prioritise infill, refurbishment and conversions before any release of protected landscapes. 

On the supply side, reforms should include faster, simpler planning procedures for brownfield redevelopments, clearer change‑of‑use rules, and stronger incentives to bring long‑term empty homes back into use (with penalties for prolonged vacancy). Local planning must require a meaningful proportion of affordable homes in brownfield schemes and support community-led schemes, not just top‑down delivery. 

Regarding public investment in council and housing association building programmes, I’m concerned they won’t move quickly enough or adapt to local needs. Public schemes should be tightly time‑bound, well costed, and paired with robust maintenance funds. If such investment is pursued, it must be complemented by reform that accelerates modular, energy‑retrofit focused builds and enables local partnerships (e.g., with community land trusts) to deliver stable, long‑term social rent housing that genuinely serves low‑income households.

From where I live in England, the big barrier to affordable, good-quality homes is not just price but the fragility of delivery: land, planning, and funding move at different speeds. Reforms that genuinely shift supply fast are those that empower community-led solutions: community land trusts (CLTs), housing co-operatives, self-build, and modern methods of construction (MMC).

A CLT model keeps land in community ownership and guarantees lasting affordability. In our area, a small CLT has started on a derelict site but progress is hampered by complex funding routes and slow land release. Simplifying land transactions, creating a clear pathway to grant or revolving funds, and giving councils dedicated land for CLTs would unlock many more sites without sacrificing value for money.

Co-operatives work well where residents want a say over design and management; they can offer stable rents and high quality outcomes if supported with professional governance and access to affordable debt.

Self-build and custom-build should be normalised, with serviced plots and one-stop planning that reduces risk and time. MMC — factory-built, well-insulated homes — can cut construction time and improve warmth, if backed by robust quality standards, warranties, and local job opportunities.

Overall, a package of land supply, planning reform, targeted finance, and standards is needed to make these routes work at scale.

What would work better, in my view, is a balanced package of reform: - Targeted planning reforms that speed up routine, low-risk decisions while preserving mandatory environmental assessments and local input. - A mandatory, transparent delivery tracker that publicly shows land supply,, decision datrs, and the status of affordable housing and infrastructure contributions. - Stronger local data capabilities, with real-time dashboards and independent auditing to verify that promised homes are built and tenures are achieved. - Increased council capacity and predictable funding to planning and enforcement, plus a clear framework for penalties or renegotiation if commitments aren’t delivered. - Brownfield first, density in townn centres with good access to public transport, and explicit rrquirements to protect existing green spaces and flood mitigation measures. - Clear,, upfront infrastructure funding guarantees tied to planning permissions so schools, health services and roads can keep pace with new homes. - Community involvement baked into the process, with transparent timrlines and meaningful opportunities for residents to influence designs without derailing delivery. i really think thank you for the opportunity to give my view. In our area there is a real demand for genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes, especially for older people on modest incomes who want to stay local and independent. The last thing we need is more promises that don’t materialise, or schemes that end up delivering a handful of units after years of delay while the housing lists grow longer. On the idea of major public investment in council and housing association building programmes, I am skeptical unless there are tight, transparent delivery controls. Large schemes risk being slowed by planning, procurement and political changes, and they can pile up debt that ultimately falls on the public purse. In practice, I’ve seen sites announced with great fanfare but with years passing before any homes are finished, while waiting lists for social rent remain stubbornly long. When resources are concentrated in a few big projects, there is also a danger of not matching local need: family-sized homes in areas where there are many single occupants, or accessible ground‑floor flats where demand is strongest. A click‑through of the local outcomes often shows cost escalations, design changes and, at times, compromises on quality that later stretch maintenance budgets.

That said, I recognise a role for public involvement, but it must be tightly governed by robust data and accountability. A more cautious, data‑driven approach could unlock better outcomes without the faults I’ve described. I think the foundation for any reform should be improved local data, monitoring and accountability to ensure commitments are delivered and that schemes meet real local needs. In my experience, residents and council officers alike benefit from clear, public dashboards showing:
- current and forecast affordable-housing delivery by development, tenure and size; 
- the proportion of units secured for social rent versus other affordable routes; 
- when delivery milestones are missed and what penalties or remedial steps follow; 
- progress on energy efficiency, accessibility and long-term dwelling quality.

Beyond data, stronger accountability for developers is essential. Section 106 agreements and other planning obligations should be used with greater bite, including published delivery trajectories, explicit nomination rights for councils or housing associations, and enforceable penalties for delays or underperformance. Local authorities should be able to require public interest disclosures from partners if schemes stagnate, and there must be a transparent mechanism to claw back contributions where delivery falters. In some areas, the absence of timely information means money sits unused or projects stall, leaving communities without the homes they were promised.

I also think public investment should be paired with capacity-building at the local level. Funded capacity for planning, enforcement and delivery teams in councils is crucial. If planning departments are overstretched, even good schemes fail to materialise. I’d support a ring-fenced, long‑term fund to recruit and retain skilled planning officers, housing delivery managers and building compliance staff, along with independent project monitoring to prevent conflicts of interest and to keep schemes on track. A more capable delivery ecosystem would help ensure commitments are delivered in the lives of local people who need them most rather than in the political cycle.

In terms of how to deliver more affordable homes effectively, I would favour a mixed approach: increase the use of council or arm’s‑length housing delivery bodies to work with registered providers, but with very clear accountability and performance standards; make better use of public land and underutilised assets for social rented housing, with fast‑track planning for suitable schemes; and explore value‑capture mechanisms where appropriate to reinvest in further affordable housing. I would also want to see a stronger emphasis on quality and resilience: homes must be safe, energy‑efficient, accessible and designed for the long term, not just cost‑effective to build. For the older residents among us, the availability of a reliable mix of one‑ and two‑bedroom homes with good access to care and community support is crucial.

Finally, community involvement should be embedded from the outset. Local residents know what works in their streets—car parking, access to services, and incremental changes to the neighbourhood matter as much as unit counts. Transparent consultation and ongoing feedback loops will help ensure that any reform truly reflects local needs and yields homes that people can and will use for decades.

If policymakers pursue a strategy that combines better data and accountability with targeted capacity funding and streamlined, quality-focused delivery, there is real potential to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. It will require humility to challenge flawed processes, and a stubborn focus on delivering what is promised to those who need it most.

I’m writing as a pensioner living in England and I want more affordable, good‑quality homes near where I’ve lived all my life. I do care about climate targets and lower energy bills, but I believe the reforms suggested would not reliably increase the number of homes available at rents people can actually afford. In fact, I’m concerned they could slow development, push costs down the line onto tenants, or simply deter builders from taking on new schemes. The goal should be more homes built quickly, well‑designed, and affordable from day one, not a package that risks shrinking supply while chasing green labels.

First, mandating higher energy standards for all new builds and funding retrofits sounds sensible in theory, but it creates real practical barriers. Building costs are already high. If every new home has to meet tougher standards, developers face bigger financing gaps and longer permission times. The result can be higher sale prices or rents, and fewer homes built in our towns and villages. I’ve seen a small, much‑needed affordable development stall for months because the cost estimates rose once green standards were added. Retrofitting existing stock, while admirable, is not a universal remedy. Councils often struggle to access funds quickly enough, and landlords of privately rented properties simply don’t have the margin to undertake expensive improvements without higher rents or longer void periods. Instead of a blanket mandate, I’d support targeted, time‑bound requirements where the hardest‑to‑heat homes (and social housing) receive funding first, with predictable, simple access to grants and clear timelines. And any retrofit funding should come with protections to ensure tenants don’t pay higher bills through higher rents, at least until a measured share of the savings is passed on.

Second, the idea of rent caps or stabilization to improve affordability requires far more careful design. Yes, fixing rents in the private sector for existing tenancies in hard‑pressed areas could help households, but blanket caps threaten the very thing we need most: a steady flow of new homes. If returns to builders and investors are squeezed too tightly, development slows, current landlords exit the market, and landlords may convert properties to other uses or let maintenance slide to cut costs. In my view, any rent‑control policy should be trialled with robust evaluation, targeted to specific renter groups, time‑limited, and always linked to a credible plan to increase new supply. Pilots should come with clear exit strategies and independent monitoring to ensure they don’t backfire and reduce the overall number of affordable homes available in the long term.

Third, the proposal to bolster data, monitoring and developer accountability is sensible. Where I live, funding is announced but delivery often stalls because councils lack planning and enforcement capacity, or because there isn’t a reliable pipeline showing which sites will come forward and when. A crucial reform would be to empower local authorities with adequate planning staff, faster decision‑making, and enforceable delivery milestones for developers. A transparent, public dashboard showing planning approvals, construction starts, and affordable units delivered would help residents hold partners to account. In one local scheme, a council enjoyed a warm announcement but several commitments slipped because there was no real mechanism to enforce milestones or punish delay. A ring‑fenced fund to support planning capacity, with penalties for missed delivery targets, would be a genuine improvement.

To my mind, reforms should prioritise removing the bottlenecks in planning and land release, encouraging smaller builders and modular construction, and ensuring energy efficiency is funded in a way that benefits tenants rather than simply increasing rents. We should look to fast‑track permissions for well‑designed schemes on publicly owned land and require longer‑term affordability where public money is used. The money saved on faster decisions and stable planning processes could be redirected into high‑quality, well‑insulated homes that stay affordable for households like mine—not into higher rents that price people out of the area.

In short, I want to see more homes built, faster, at rents people can afford, with real protections that prevent costs from being shifted onto tenants. That means targeted energy efficiency funding, carefully designed and time‑limited controls on rents, and stronger planning capacity plus tough, transparent accountability for delivery. If reforms can deliver that balance, I’d welcome them. But as they stand, I fear the current package risks reducing, not increasing, the supply of affordable homes.

Supporting plots for self‑build on suitable brownfield or municipal land, with streamlined planning checks and access to affordable finance, would empower residents who want to contribute to their housing. I’ve seen how modular and timber‑frame construction can shorten build times and improve energy efficiency, which reduces running costs for residents and helps councils meet climate targets. A practical step would be to create a publicly supported channel for small‑scale builders to access land, finance and a dependable supply chain for MMC components, and to permit quicker planning decisions for self‑build and MMC projects on suitable sites.

Targeted finance, access to procurement, and a dedicated small‑sites policy are essential to widen SME participation. Local builders often struggle to compete with larger firms on public housing or regeneration contracts, even when they have local knowledge and a strong track record. I’d support reserving a portion of public housing work for SMEs, with a simple, transparent bidding process and pre‑tender advisory support to navigate procurement rules. A practical policy would be to reserve a share of pipeline contracts for local small builders and require public bodies to publish a clear, long‑term site pipeline (including brownfield and surplus public land) with expected timelines. In parallel, provide viability support and reduced upfront barriers for small sites—sites under 0.5–1 hectare—so they are not left undeveloped while bigger sites are pursued.

Major public investment in council and housing association building programmes is crucial to delivering genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes. Capital funding must be expanded and sustained, with rents targeted at genuinely affordable levels and long‑term stewardship guaranteed. This is not just about numbers; it is about quality—homes that are energy efficient, accessible and resilient to climate change, built to a high standard with robust maintenance provisions. In many towns, waiting lists for social housing are long, and private supply has failed to meet need. A strong, predictable funding stream for councils and housing associations would unlock a steady pipeline of social renting homes, anchored in local demand and designed to the needs of families and older residents alike. It would also stimulate local jobs and supply chains, benefitting the local economy beyond the flats themselves.

Taken together, these reforms would create a well‑balanced, locally rooted housing system: community‑led models that keep homes affordable in perpetuity; faster, higher‑quality homes built with modern methods; more opportunities for small local builders to participate; and ambitious public investment that guarantees genuinely affordable social housing for those most in need. If policymakers implement these reform strands in a coordinated way—with clear timelines, robust governance, and strong local engagement—I believe we can significantly increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in my area and across England, while delivering broader social and economic benefits.

From my experience renting in England, reforms need to balance speed of delivery with cost and quality. I support raising energy efficiency standards for new builds and funding retrofits to cut bills and hit climate targets, but the funding must be stable and accessible to smaller builders and housing associations, not just large developers. A phased, predictable approach with low-interest finance and clear milestones would reduce the risk of shifting costs onto tenants. 

On planning, I’d combine streamlining with strong safeguards. Local authorities often stall projects through multiple consultations and lengthy decision timelines, which pushes up costs and makes schemes unviable. A one-stop digital planning process, simplified zoning, and prioritised decisions for well-supported schemes would speed delivery, provided flood risk, biodiversity, and community engagement are not downgraded. Infrastructure and public service capacity should be considered at the outset to avoid deals that fail later.

Regarding affordability, pilots of rent stabilization could help in high-demand areas but must be time-limited and evidence-based, with protections for genuine tenants and clear exit routes for investors if harms to supply appear. Targeted housing vouchers or moving-cost support could reduce displacement while reforms are piloted and evaluated.

Overall, I’d welcome reforms that accelerate delivery without baking in higher bills for tenants or eroding developer confidence.

From where I live in England, the urgent task is increasing affordable, good‑quality homes quickly without sacrificing community control or long‑term value. I support reforms that empower community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build, and modern methods of construction, provided they are properly funded and well regulated.

Key levers would be: 1) make land affordable for CLTs and co‑operatives—public or surplus land released on long leases with clear affordability guarantees; 2) simplify planning for community‑led schemes and offer fast‑track consent for small to medium sites, with predictable timetables; 3) fund the setup costs of CLTs and co‑ops (business planning, legal, pre‑development work) and provide accessible loans to help households become members or founders; 4) support self‑build plots and custom‑build mechanisms so local residents can contribute directly to their homes, with ready infrastructure and design templates; 5) invest in modern methods of construction and local offsite supply chains (timber framing, modular units) with skills training and robust quality standards to speed delivery and improve sustainability.

In my area we have idle brownfield land near transport links that could host community schemes if land terms and timelines were clear. The Bristol Community Land Trust shows how long‑term affordability and local stewardship can work, while self‑build and MMC can shorten build times and raise quality. With coordinated funding and streamlined processes, these routes could significantly widen access to good homes while strengthening communities.
